body_text:
Donna Mills tells Fox News Digital what changed her mind about joining the platform — and why she says there's no pressure to bare it all.

"Knots Landing" star Donna Mills is revealing the one unexpected request she refuses to fulfill for her OnlyFans subscribers.

During a Friday appearance on ABC's "Nightline," the 85-year-old actress told correspondent Kayna Whitworth that her content largely consists of glimpses into her daily life but asserted that there is one routine she won’t perform for the camera.

"I do the Peloton," Mills said. "Just, you know, they’re the things of everyday life: having a cup of coffee, you know. They say they like it when you brush your teeth…I’m not going to brush my teeth."

Donna Mills revealed the one OnlyFans request that she won't fulfill. (Disney via Getty Images)

DONNA MILLS DOES 100 SIT-UPS A DAY, PLAYS TENNIS FIVE TIMES A WEEK AT 85 BUT WON'T QUIT DORITOS

When asked if she believes that most of the OnlyFans users who are engaging with her are men, Mills said, "I think so. Yeah. Sometimes you don’t know."

While Mills drew the line at brushing her teeth on camera, she appeared more open to sharing racier content with her subscribers. However, she explained that she does not believe full nudity is necessary to be sexy, pointing to one of her past Playboy shoots as an example.

PLAYBOY'S CELEBRITY-DRIVEN RELAUNCH FACES CREDIBILITY TEST IN ONLYFANS ERA, EXPERT SAYS

The "Knots Landing" star said she plans to sell never-before-seen "Playboy" photos. (2005 CBS WORLDWIDE INC.)

"I think it’s sexier to be not just totally naked, you know," she said. "And have a little imagination about it."

"One of the pictures in ‘Playboy,’ which I think is one of the sexiest things, is me in the shower, in a dress," Mills added.

CRYSTAL HEFNER FELT 'ABSOLUTELY BRAINWASHED' DURING HUGH HEFNER MARRIAGE, REVEALS STRICT PLAYBOY MANSION RULES

The "Play Misty for Me" star said she believed that the never-before-seen "Playboy" outtakes could be particularly enticing for her OnlyFans subscribers.

"I think the probably the most appealing would be the ones that weren't in the magazine, right?" she said. "Because they're from the shoot, the same shoot, but they weren't in the magazine."

'HARRY POTTER' ACTOR SAYS ONLYFANS VIDEOS EARNED HER MORE THAN HER ENTIRE ACTING CAREER

After Whitworth asked how much she might charge subscribers for one of the previously unseen photos, Mills floated a potential price.

Mills launched her OnlyFans page in July. (2024 Getty Images)

"Boy, I'm not sure," she said. "Maybe I'm not sure — $100."

DREA DE MATTEO SAYS ONLYFANS BECAME ‘POLITICAL STATEMENT’ AFTER FINANCIAL STRUGGLES THREATENED HER HOME

"We're thinking you could go up a little higher," Whiteworth told her.

Mills surprised her fans when she announced that she had launched an OnlyFans account in July.

WHY WWE LEGEND DAWN MARIE IS HEADING TO ONLYFANS AT 55

The actress, who became a television sensation playing the glamorous and ruthless Abby Cunningham on "Knots Landing" from 1980 to 1989, said the platform would give her a chance to connect with fans in a more personal way.

Mills said fans were hungry for a behind-the-scenes look at her life, which she noted wasn't possible during her TV heyday.

Mills said she shared a glimpse at her daily life with her subscribers.  (Photo by Michael Tullberg/Getty Images)

'KNOTS LANDING' STAR DONNA MILLS ISSUES URGENT WARNING ABOUT AGING

"They want to know me," she told Variety at the time. "They want to know what I do during the day when I’m home. They want to see my home. They want to know much more about my personal life than we ever experienced back in the ’80s and the ’90s that, you know, the fans were cut off from."

"I've always appreciated the incredible support and encouragement I've received from my fans over the years," Mills said. "Social media has been a wonderful way to stay connected, but I'm excited to join OnlyFans because it offers the opportunity for a more personal and direct connection,"

However, Mills emphasized that she planned to approach OnlyFans on her own terms.

"It’s simply another platform to spend quality time with the people who’ve supported me throughout my career while staying true to who I am," she said.

Andy Bachman, CEO of Creators, Inc., the talent agency that manages Mills' OnlyFans account, noted that the Hollywood veteran isn't switching up her image.

"This is not about changing who she is. It is about giving her longtime fans more access to the personality, style and behind-the-scenes moments they already love," Andy Bachman, CEO of the talent agency Creators Inc., said.

The actress is reportedly making "many six figures." (© 2025 Disney. All rights reserved.)

"Donna has always been fearless and ahead of her time," Bachman added. "She told me, 'YOLO — let's do it,' and that perfectly captures her attitude. She is approaching OnlyFans on her own terms and creating a space that feels authentic, personal and completely true to her."

During an appearance on "TMZ Live" shortly after launching her account, Mills said that she wasn't planning to pose nude but didn't entirely rule out the possibility.

"Who knows? My first answer would be, oh, no, I won’t do that," she said. "But then my second answer is, I don’t know."

"I don’t want to do anything that’s salacious, you know what I mean?" Mills added. "That isn’t my personality. That isn’t what I feel good doing. But if it’s cute and sexy … we’ll see."

In August, Mills appeared on "Creators Inc. Podcast," less than a month after launching her account. At the time, Bachman, who hosts the podcast, shared an update on her page's performance.

"I can say that you are doing incredibly well," he said. "Many six figures, and it’s been early."

Bachman noted that Mills had already received some unusual requests, including "foot kink people" who asked to see the actress "stomping on grapes" with her bare feet in her vineyard.

"I’m gonna do it," Mills said. "I tried to shoot it myself. But you can’t shoot something while you’re stomping, it just doesn’t work."

"I'm going to uh… I'm going to do that very soon… and do it right so that you know people can… really enjoy it," she continued. "I think it's really funny and fun and uh it's the kind of thing that I want to be able to share with the fans."

In an interview with Fox News Digital last month, Mills teased what fans can expect from her future content.

GET ENTERTAINMENT SCOOP DELIVERED RIGHT TO YOUR EMAIL BY CLICKING HERE

"I think what the page will be, will be spicy. That’s kind of always been my thing, to be a little spicy," Mills said. "I think they’ll react to that, they’ll like that, and also it’s my chance to communicate with them through the videos and things like that and talk to them."

Mills teased that her page will be "spicy." (GC Images)

Mills also explained that part of her motivation for launching her OnlyFans was to prove that getting older doesn't mean life gets smaller.

"When I kind of looked at it a few years ago and said, 'What do I want to do with this portion of my life, this chapter in my life?' I said, 'I’d like to be an inspiration,'" she emphasized.

LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

"I’d like to show people, and particularly women, that it doesn’t have to be over. It’s just a new chapter. It’s not the end... It’s just something you can enjoy. You should enjoy. It’s part of your life."

PUT YOUR ENTERTAINMENT KNOWLEDGE TO THE TEST AND SEE HOW YOU SCORE

After playing one of television's most famously ambitious villains, Mills already knows exactly how Abby Cunningham would react to her latest move.

"She would say, ‘Go, girl!’ Without a doubt," Mills said. "Are you kidding? Abby would be all for it. She was for anything that was going to move her forward, that was going to be to her advantage. So, she would be dead on for this. She would love this."

title: Ballon d’Or 2026: Can Barcelona phenom Lamine Yamal become youngest winner?
excerpt:

Those are just a few words that best encapsulate Lamine Yamal’s appeal.

Since making his first-team deb...
body_text:
A once-in-a-generation talent. A superstar in the making. Equal parts audacious and ambitious.

Those are just a few words that best encapsulate Lamine Yamal’s appeal.

Since making his first-team debut three years ago, Yamal has taken world football by storm, compelling fans and players alike to take note of his talent.

His flair on the football field and flamboyant personality off it have made Yamal one of the sport’s best showmen in recent years.

Now, the 19-year-old has set his sights on another big prize to add to his glittering cabinet – the Ballon d’Or, football’s most prestigious individual honour.

No teenager has won the Ballon d’Or in the award’s 70-year history – Yamal is campaigning to become the youngest winner.

So, how does his bid compare with the other leading contenders? Al Jazeera breaks it down:

Very few players can boast such an impressive season as Yamal’s.

In 2025-26, the winger won the FIFA 2026 World Cup with Spain, only days after his 19th birthday. His success in North America came on the back of his La Liga title triumph with Barcelona.

While an injury-marred campaign meant Yamal did not dazzle viewers on his World Cup debut, grabbing just one goal and an assist, the youngster enjoyed far more success on club duty.

Yamal racked up 22 goals and 15 assists in 38 league appearances, playing a major role in Barcelona’s successful title defence. He was also part of the Catalan club’s Spanish Super Cup-winning squad.

The major double of a world title and a domestic title has strengthened Yamal’s claim for the Ballon d’Or.

According to bookmakers, he is among the top three contenders, alongside Bayern Munich’s Harry Kane and Real Madrid’s Kylian Mbappe.

The 2026 Ballon d’Or race is the closest in decades. But Yamal is quite confident of winning the award, singling out Mbappe as his only threat.

“For me, Mbappe and me, we’re the two best players in the world,” the winger said in an interview on Movistar Plus.

“I honestly think that, as the best in the world, maybe there are two of us, and this year I would deserve it because of what I’ve won,” he added.

This self-promotion by footballers is a relatively recent development in a team sport where, until a few years ago, the top individual prize went largely unnoticed until it was time to present it.

But now, the Ballon d’Or dominates football conversations during the following season, and the award, despite carrying no cash prize, brings greater status and worth.

Barca manager Hansi Flick said although he would have preferred Yamal not to have spoken about it, he accepts it as part of the winger’s self-belief.

“He’s exceptional, and it’s a part of this … I would not prefer this, but he’s doing this. He has self-confidence; he wants to win the Ballon d’Or.”

Nominated for the third time, Yamal finished runner-up to Ousmane Dembele of PSG in the 2025 Ballon d’Or race.

Monday’s ceremony in London is likely to revolve around a three-way battle between Yamal, Mbappe and Kane. It is an interesting contest between three players in three different stages of their careers: one in his teens, one in his 20s and one in his 30s.

While Yamal has publicly pitted himself against Mbappe in the battle, he is confident that the trophies in his portfolio will help him beat the Frenchman, who has had no luck with silverware.

However, purely on an individual basis, Mbappe’s statistics are far better than Yamal’s.

Yamal had 25 goals and 20 assists for club and country. Mbappe, on the other hand, had a staggering 58 goals and 13 assists. The 27-year-old also finished the season as La Liga and Champions League top scorer, lifted the World Cup’s Golden Boot and broke the all-time goals record with 22.

Then there is the unstoppable force of Kane, who was in a league of his own. His 73 goals last season were the best haul by a footballer since Lionel Messi’s 82 in 2011-12.

So while Yamal has the shiny trophies to vouch for his Ballon d’Or bid, his solo displays pale in comparison with his seniors, Mbappe and Kane.

Kane’s incredible goal-scoring prowess – even at the age of 33 – is hard to ignore, but Yamal believes simply registering the maximum goals cannot be the criterion for the prize.

“The Ballon d’Or should go to the best player in the world, full stop,” he said. “Not to a player who has scored 80 goals, because if you score 80 goals, you get the top scorer award for that,” Yamal added, seemingly taking a dig at Kane.

“Those are two completely different things that people do not understand.”

Yamal’s fate now lies in the hands of a jury of journalists from 100 countries whose votes will decide whether he can become the youngest Ballon d’Or winner, surpassing Brazilian legend Ronaldo Nazario, who was 21 at the time of his triumph in 1997.

After lifting the Kopa Trophy for the best Young Talent of the year twice, Yamal will hope the third time is the charm, this time stepping up to the biggest stage to bring home the ultimate individual trophy.

title: NFL's French national anthem performer Nina Tonji alters words to La Marseillaise, sparking outrage in France
excerpt:
Greg Gutfeld and the 'Gutfeld!' panel react to Motown legend Martha Reeves singing a heavily criticized rendition of the national anthem at a recent Women’s Pro Baseball League game.

Words often matt...
body_text:
Greg Gutfeld and the 'Gutfeld!' panel react to Motown legend Martha Reeves singing a heavily criticized rendition of the national anthem at a recent Women’s Pro Baseball League game.

Words often matter as much as actions and amid the civil unrest that France has felt in recent days, some French people are apparently angry and offended over the altering of their national anthem before the NFL game between the Pittsburgh Steelers and New Orleans Saints.

And, yes, this has to do with immigrants in France.

Before the game, singer Nina Tonji performed La Marseillaise at the Stade de France. Although she received a warm round of applause afterward, there has been significant online backlash because she modified the lyrics of the song.

NFL OVERCOMES CIVIL UNREST, TRUMP CONCERNS AND CALLS TO POSTPONE AS STEELERS AND SAINTS KICK OFF IN PARIS

Tonji changed "Qu'un sang impur abreuve nos sillons!" to "Qu'un sang uni abreuve nos sillons!," and that was clearly done on purpose because it has political and societal ramifications.

"Qu’un sang impur abreuve nos sillons" means "May impure blood water our furrows/fields." In the revolutionary context of La Marseillaise, "impure blood" referred to enemies and traitors – particularly French immigrants fighting alongside foreign armies.

Replacing impur ("impure") with uni ("united") changes the meaning of the passage from from a call for enemy blood to nourish France’s soil into an appeal for national unity and solidarity that includes immigrants to nourish France's soil.

Pittsburgh Steelers players run onto the field before an NFL game against the New Orleans Saints in Saint-Denis, outside Paris, on Sunday, Oct. 25, 2026. (AP Photo/Aurelien Morissard)

Tonji thus changed the song's tone from violent exclusion of a foreign enemy to a message of unity with foreigners.

She gave immigrants cover that La Marseillaise did not in 1792 when it was written during the French Revolution.

And, yes, this rendition represented a lyrical alteration by the Tonji that departed from the traditional wording of the French national anthem. But it comes at a time when people in France are on edge about immigration and foreigners.

The Soul Rebels perform the US national anthem before an NFL football game between Pittsburgh Steelers and New Orleans Saints in Saint-Denis, outside Paris, Sunday, Oct. 25, 2026. (AP Photo/Steve Luciano)

That’s because at least some of the protesters who took to the streets during the past two weeks of civil unrest were immigrants. Some rallied for anti-Israel causes, while others called for the overthrow of the current political system.

So, predictably, there has been an online backlash.

This is where we also inform you that Tonji was born in Montreal, Canada.

Much of the attention she is now getting has come from media accounts with massive followings.

Cerfia posted the song to its 1.3 million followers and highlighted the changes made.

RMC Sport posted it to its 2.7 million followers, saying the change caused "confusion."

Francetvsport also posted the song to its 297,500 followers.

Saints players warn-up before an NFL football game between Pittsburgh Steelers and New Orleans Saints in Saint-Denis, outside Paris, Sunday, Oct. 25, 2026. (AP Photo/Steve Luciano)

The replies to the viral posts did include some people willing to overlook the change. But a vast majority insulted everything from Tonji's voice, to looks, to the action itself, calling it a "scandal," and "disrespectful" and a "controversy."

Seems some French people have pride in their national anthem.

So here is a common sense approach the NFL should adapt to avoid these public relations black eyes – because the league gets a lot of coverage over national anthem performances that go awry.

ZERO BS. JUST DAKICH. TAKE THE DON'T @ ME PODCAST ON THE ROAD. DOWNLOAD NOW!

The league, which supposedly has a right of refusal over these pregame and even halftime acts, can easily force the artists to sign binding contracts that demand they perform the songs as written.

Sure, interpret all you want, the league can tell the artists. That's what makes you an artist.

But don't alter lyrics to suit a personal agenda or feeling. Because that makes you an activist.

FOLLOW ARMANDO SALGUERO ON X: @ARMANDOSALGUERO

Armando Salguero is OutKick's Senior NFL Writer.

title: Thousands protest in Prague against public media funding reforms
excerpt: Several thousand people have taken to the streets in Prague to protest against plans to change the funding system for the Czech Republic’s public media, accusing the government of stifling press freed...
body_text:
Several thousand people have taken to the streets in Prague to protest against plans to change the funding system for the Czech Republic’s public media, accusing the government of stifling press freedom.

On Sunday, protesters demanded the withdrawal of legislation seeking to abolish household licence fees and replace them with state budget allocations for public radio and television.

The Czech lower house of parliament approved fast-tracking the bill in a rare overnight vote on Saturday after governing coalition lawmakers rushed to open the issue, limiting the opposition’s ability to engage in debate before the vote was held.

The bill, proposed by the governing coalition led by billionaire Prime Minister Andrej Babis, which includes two far-right parties, must still be passed by the upper house before becoming law.

The opposition has pledged to challenge the legislation in the constitutional court. The plan would cut funding for public media by about 15 percent, possibly as early as next year.

At the protest in Prague’s Old Town Square, demonstrators chanted, “We’ve had enough”, “This must not be allowed to pass”, and “4:36”, referencing the early morning hour when the draft was approved by parliament.

Babis has said the plan is not an attack on media independence but a matter of funding transparency.

Critics warn the proposed change would allow the governing coalition to take control of the media. They compare it with the actions of populist governments, such as Hungarian Prime Minister Viktor Orban and Slovakia’s Prime Minister Robert Fico.

Babis and his coalition, whose agenda includes reducing support for Ukraine as it fights off a Russian invasion, have a record of attacks against the media.

Public media staffers announced they would go on strike on November 3. They are backed by labour unions, university rectors, churches, international media organisations and many others.

A rally is also planned at Prague’s Letna park on November 15, two days before the anniversary of the 1989 anti-communist Velvet Revolution that ended more than 40 years of totalitarian government.

title: DAVID MARCUS: The future of the GOP in New England rides on Maine’s Senate vote
excerpt:
Sen. Susan Collins faces a challenge from Democrat Troy Jackson in Maine as Republicans debate the future of centrism and the GOP's place in New England.

The New England region of the United States c...
body_text:
Sen. Susan Collins faces a challenge from Democrat Troy Jackson in Maine as Republicans debate the future of centrism and the GOP's place in New England.

The New England region of the United States comprises six states, more than 15 million people, 21 seats in the House of Representatives, and 12 senators. Yet, of this congressional delegation, only one is a Republican — Sen. Susan Collins of Maine — at least for now.

In the Pine Tree State, Democrat Troy Jackson has a slight lead in the polls. Over her 30 years in the Senate, Collins has pulled a lot of electoral footballs from Democrat Charlie Browns, who thought victory and a Senate seat were a chip shot away.

In Maine, I chatted with Republican State House Representative Laurel Libby — a rising star in the local GOP and possible heir to the kind of centrist Republicanism that Collins has managed to cling to in this mostly blue region.

Libby told Fox News Digital that "[Collins] is great on constituent services and goes out of her way to be in the community," adding, "it's kind of hysterical for Troy Jackson to say she doesn’t hold town halls. Susan Collins is out in the community constantly."

DAVID MARCUS: IN BLUE MAINE, NOBODY BELIEVES SUSAN COLLINS WILL LOSE UNTIL THEY SEE IT

Maine voters share their views on Sen. Susan Collins and the upcoming midterm election. (Fox News Digital)

I pressed Libby a bit on what role, especially if Collins holds on to win, the Maine and broader New England Republican Party can play in the post Trump era — which lies just over two years over the horizon. She replied, "I think we need to be providing the long-term solutions for Maine.

"We’ve seen what a Democrat trifecta [in state government] has done for Maine. During Jackson’s time in the Senate, he is responsible for our electricity costs going up 70%," she said. "He supported a budget that went up 50%."

VOTERS PREPARE TO WEIGH-IN ON TRUMP'S ECONOMY AS COSTS CONTINUE TO SURGE

These were concerns that I also heard from Don, a Vietnam veteran in his late 70s who recently moved into Bangor from a nearby farm after his wife passed away.

"All those Democrats south of [the state capital] Augusta, they just think everyone is made of money, and it's really hurting normal folks," Don said.

Among Republican voters in Bangor, and even some Independents, the word "Augusta," is generally uttered with approximately the level of disdain Jerry Seinfeld had when saying "Newman!"

Dan and Tess, a couple in their 30s, were in town from Massachusetts, of which Maine was once a part. They both see Collins as a strong centrist voice for the region.

"It's a problem when every politician in New England is a Democrat," Dan said. "Especially when the Democrats are out of power."

Maine voters share their views on Sen. Susan Collins and the upcoming midterm election. (Fox News Digital)

Chris, also from Massachusetts, was in Maine upgrading carrier lines. When asked what Republicans could do to get a foothold in the region, he said, "I don't really know, when the state's been Democratic [for so long]. ... Coming together to the people with things that don't pull sides apart, because they have two sides, but they're supposed to meet in the middle."

This is a point that Libby refined in our conversation when asked about the fact that Collins was campaigning this week with former moderate Democratic Senator Joe Manchin of West Virginia, while Jackson barnstormed with far-left New York Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez.

KYRSTEN SINEMA QUESTIONS WHETHER MODERATES STILL HAVE A PLACE IN THE DEMOCRATIC PARTY

"It’s absolutely representative of what they both [would] bring to the Senate," Libby told Fox News Digital. "Susan Collins has proven that she is willing and able to work in a bipartisan manner, to get things done, and during his time in the [state] Senate, did the opposite," including Libby claims a few end runs around the Maine Constitution.

Maine voters share their views on Sen. Susan Collins and the upcoming midterm election. (Fox News Digital)

Manchin is now out of power, mostly owing to his refusal to bow to the far left zeitgeist of the current Democratic Party. This is thus far a fate Susan Collins has avoided over the past decade when she distances herself from Trump and MAGA populism.

If Troy Jackson does manage to topple Collins, the message to Republicans in Maine and New England will be that centrism doesn’t work, that they need bare knuckle brawlers more like Rep. Brandon Gill of Texas, than bipartisan peacemakers like Collins.

Nationally, there are some hardcore Republicans who would welcome a Collins loss in this respect. They see moderate Republicans as more of an obstacle than an asset. But most in the GOP concede that holding the Senate for Trump’s final two years in office outweighs the broader ideological intraparty fights.

Win, lose, or draw for Collins, in the future it will be younger Republican politicians like Libby, who will have to define what a Republican is in Maine, New England, and to some degree in America as a whole.

Democrats exiled Joe Manchin for his lack of political purity; they are on the way to doing the same to Sen. John Fetterman, D-Pa., even though, somewhat hilariously, he really could wind up as the 51st vote in a one-seat Democratic majority next year.

If Maine Republicans can save Susan Collins once again, it will show that the GOP really can, at least in part, and unlike Democrats, embrace moderate and centrist positions — a point that could play heavily in their favor as both parties try to define themselves for the post-Trump age.

David Marcus is a columnist living in West Virginia and the author of "Charade: The COVID Lies That Crushed A Nation."

body_text:

Southwest Airlines will add 11 new nonstop international routes to its schedule beginning in November, giving travelers more options for their next tropical escape.

On Nov. 1, the carrier will start offering nonstop service from Harry Reid International Airport (LAS) in Las Vegas to Puerto Vallarta (PVR), the New York Post reported.

Southwest Airlines already has command of more than 40% of all flight operations at LAS.

SOUTHWEST CAPTAIN ADMITS HIS 'LIP WAS QUIVERING' DURING CO-PILOT DAUGHTER'S SURPRISE SPEECH ON FINAL FLIGHT

In February 2027, the airline will begin offering nonstop flights from Nashville International Airport (BNA) to Liberia, and to Aruba (AUA) in March.

Nonstop service to Nassau, Bahamas via Southwest Airlines will soon be available to passengers. (DANIEL SLIM/AFP via Getty Images)

Demand for travel to Liberia has surged by 11.8% in recent months, according to the New York Post, although there is currently a Level 2 travel advisory in effect.

Additionally, all Americans wishing to go to Liberia must procure a visa before they visit, no matter the length of their trip, according to the U.S. Department of State.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER

In June, BNA will also begin nonstop service to Nassau (NAS) and Providenciales (PLS).

Southwest Airlines will be the only carrier with direct flights for all four of the Nashville routes.

Southwest Airlines is adding eleven new international destinations to its flight schedule beginning in November. (iStock)

Southwest will add four new international routes from Austin-Bergstrom International Airport (AUS) in June, as well.

Flights will go to San José, Costa Rica, beginning in March, and there will be service to Liberia, Punta Cana and Nassau starting in June.

Two more direct flights from Columbus (CMH) and Pittsburgh (PIT) to Punta Cana (PUJ) will be available in March and June, respectively.

Southwest Airlines will soon offer nonstop flights from multiple airports to Punta Cana, Dominican Republic. (iStock)

Southwest Airlines first began service on June 18, 1971, going from Love Field in Dallas to San Antonio and Houston, according to their website.

title: Australia politics live: MPs to pay tribute to Helen Haines as parliament resumes; Hanson says One Nation cartoons ‘not going anywhere’
excerpt:
Get our daily political email, free app or daily news podcast

Crossbench MPs will honour Helen Haines today by placing an orange cockatoo sign on her seat in parliament as lower house members, includ...
body_text:
Get our daily political email, free app or daily news podcast

Crossbench MPs will honour Helen Haines today by placing an orange cockatoo sign on her seat in parliament as lower house members, including the prime minister, Anthony Albanese, will pay tribute and send well wishes to her this morning.

The orange cockatoo is synonymous with Haines. She explained in 2024 that it came about after volunteers for her predecessor, Cathy McGowan, “were like a flock of cockatoos” with their orange shirts on.

double quotation markThe association and symbolism has grown from there, representing a community flocking together to build a vibrant democracy. Volunteers have crafted cockies out of old yard signs and injected much fun, intrigue and conversation into the independent campaigns of Indi.

Haines remains in a serious but stable condition in a Melbourne hospital after she lost both legs following an alleged attack near her electorate office in north-east Victoria a week ago.

The MP’s husband, Phil Haines, provided an update at the Alfred hospital on Wednesday, saying “both her heart and her mind are in good shape”. It’s understood Phil will attend parliament today.

Haines was the first federal politician to sign a civility pledge as part of the Compassion in Politics movement to make politics more respectful. Crossbench MPs will sign the simple pledge and encourage others to do so today.

Independent MP Zali Steggall has called for more respect in times of disagreement, telling ABC that leadership and words matter.

double quotation markWe absolutely need to make sure there is more civility and respect.

Steggall says this issue can be seen on social media.

double quotation markSocial media is a platform where they can send abuse and threats through direct messages, call my electorate office, or send pretty revolting stuff

It’s just quite shocking how disconnected from manners and reality sometimes people get when they launch into their diatribes and make threats.

Steggall says there was an incident that was reported to the AFP and resulted in someone outside her electorate being charged.

Politicians may feel less safe in home electorates than parliament, Tehan says

Following the alleged attack on Helen Haines, security measures have reportedly increased around Parliament House.

But Liberal MP Dan Tehan says the security in parliament is “pretty good”.

double quotation markThere’s been a lot of money and a lot of effort and a lot of thought going into security here at Parliament House.

I think the vulnerability is actually when we’re out doing our job in the community, and that’s probably where we need to put the focus.

Anonymous online voices allow people to ‘do and say anything’, Tehan says

Liberal MP Dan Tehan has raised concerns about the impact of anonymous online accounts on inflammatory political discourse.

double quotation markThe problem we’ve got at the moment is the anonymous voices online.

I’m a big believer in freedom of speech and always have been, but I’ve always strongly believed that you have to put your name to your words. That’s the key.

In the community, those who disagree tend to do so respectfully, he said.

double quotation markWhat you tend to see online is the people who are there, anonymously, will just do and say anything.

Now, whether that then heightens it, I don’t know, but … it’s always the question of balance.

Auditor-general examining if detention in Victorian police cells breaches human rights

The Victorian auditor general is investigating the detention of people in police cells, after Guardian Australia revealed the practice routinely led to the force breaching its own guidelines.

The Victorian auditor general’s office (Vago) confirmed it was set to examine whether Victoria police and the department of justice “manage prison and police cell capacity to support human rights and the efficient functioning of the justice system”.

Guardian Australia reported in November last year that the process of “decanting” was resulting in people being moved hundreds of kilometres across Victoria as the government grappled with tougher bail laws and a shortage of prison beds and corrections workers.

This was also leading to people spending more than the 14-day target in police cells, and in some cases meant they were serving their entire sentences there.

In announcing the audit earlier this month, Vago said:

double quotation markPolice cells are designed to hold people for short periods, such as after arrest and for bail hearings. However, in 2025 there were media reports of police holding prisoners in police cells beyond the recommended 14-day limit.

When cells at one station are full, police may transport individuals to other stations. In some reported cases, police have transported individuals hundreds of kilometres away.

This can mean that prisoners miss their court appearances and do not have easy access to their lawyers and health services. This undermines both prisoners’ human rights and the proper functioning of the justice system.

Vago noted that Victoria’s recent bail reforms were also likely to increase pressure on prison beds and staff capacity.

It said in a statement to Guardian Australia that the audit was under way and was expected to be tabled early next year.

Safety concerns and threats have changed ‘dramatically’ for politicians: Butler

Cabinet minister Mark Butler has said this sitting week offers an opportunity to discuss ways to keep MPs, their families and staffers safe.

Asked by ABC Radio National if much had changed during his time in parliament, Butler said:

double quotation markIt’s changed dramatically in my time.

I’ve been here for almost 20 years and security has changed, and the federal police, in my experience, have been very, very responsive to our requests when there are threats or the possibility of me going to an event.

But just the number and the nature of threats of violence and death, not just to MPs, but to their children and to their partners and to their staff, is like nothing we saw 20 years ago.

Politicians to sign ‘civility pledge’ following alleged attack on Haines

The speaker of the house, Milton Dick, will call for civility in parliament today, and some politicians are expected to sign a “civility pledge”.

Independent MP Helen Haines was the first to sign this pledge before she was allegedly attacked last week.

Fellow independent Kate Chaney, on Monday told ABC radio she would be adding her name:

double quotation markI think there’s something really symbolic about the fact that Helen was [the first] federal MP to have signed this. It is a very simple thing.

It just says ‘in my political life I pledge to act with honesty, respect, and compassion’.

That feels to me like a simple and poignant way to honour the contribution Helen’s made to the parliament and continue to try to embody those values that she personifies in the way that I do my work in parliament.

All Australian women will soon be able to attend a pharmacy for UTI treatment or re-supply of hormonal contraception, as the federal government expands a trial program to lower healthcare costs.

This program was previously restricted to concession card holders, but the health minister, Mark Butler, and minister for women, Katy Gallagher, announced on Monday that it would be expanded to benefit an estimated 900,000 women.

The 12-month trial, to begin from early 2027, will allow Australian women to access pharmacy treatment for uncomplicated urinary tract infections (UTIs) and initiation or re-supply of hormonal contraception.

The federal government will cover pharmacist consultation costs, of up to $38 per visit.

double quotation markFor too long, women’s experiences of the health system haven’t received the attention they deserve. We’re determined to change that. We’re making practical changes that give women more choice, make health care more accessible and help save women thousands of dollars over their lifetimes.

double quotation markWe want to make it easier for women to get care that fits into their lives.

Parliament will mark a solemn start to the sitting week as politicians pay tribute to independent MP Helen Haines, who was rammed by a vehicle outside her electoral office.

The popular crossbencher was allegedly targeted in a deliberate attack when she was struck by a four-wheel drive on the main street of the Victorian town of Wangaratta on 19 October.

She has had both legs amputated and remains in hospital a week after the incident.

The prime minister, Anthony Albanese, will deliver a speech to parliament on Monday, reflecting on the alleged assault and its impact, and invite colleagues to do the same.

Fellow independent MP Monique Ryan described Dr Haines as the parliament’s “most gentle, principled and kind” member ahead of her planned remarks in the lower house.

“People who love her will try to do justice to Helen’s integrity and leadership,” she said.

“I hope that all members will rise to the occasion as Helen would do were she with us.

A fundraiser for charity Save the Children, set up on Wednesday by Haines’ family in lieu of flowers, had surpassed $1.2m in donations by Sunday afternoon.

Pauline Hanson says One Nation’s controversial cartoon series “will not be going anywhere”, after growing outrage over its offensive portrayal of federal politicians including previous depictions of some being run over by motor vehicles.

Hanson said her party’s Please Explain animation series had “nothing to do with the tragic attack on Helen Haines”, and claimed major party politicians wanted the series “censored”.
 
 
 The series has garnered further criticism after videos from 2023 and 2024 were re-circulated online and discussed on Sunday morning political talk shows on the ABC and News24.

In one 2023 video, titled Under the Bus, Hanson appears to drive a bus over independent senator Lidia Thorpe, who had been depicted as lying under the vehicle’s tyres. In another from 2024, titled The State of Melbourne, former Victorian premier Daniel Andrews is shown being run down by a car driven by cartoon character Bluey, with the video ending with suggestions Anthony Albanese was also about to be hit.

Those cartoons, published years before the attack on Haines, have been criticised for portraying violence against politicians. Shadow minister Ted O’Brien said on News24 the cartoons were “not timely”, and while admitting he hadn’t seen them, questioned whether they were “appropriate in the current climate”.

The scrutiny comes after criticism of the cartoon series labelling Liberal MP Andrew Hastie a “traitor” and mocking Jacqui Lambie’s health condition. Hanson previously stood by those cartoons, but later apologised to Lambie and claimed she hadn’t seen that clip.

But Hanson, posting on social media on Sunday afternoon, rejected criticism of the other clips. She claimed “the Labor and Liberal Dirt Units are already back at work, attempting to use this tragedy to silence their critics and deflect from their own failings. Too many media organisations are happy to help them fling the dirt.”

double quotation markThe Please Explain cartoons have nothing to do with the tragic attack on Helen Haines. They will not be going anywhere. Liberal and Labor politicians want our cartoons censored because they don’t like the scrutiny.

Those seeking to exploit this tragedy to silence their critics should be ashamed of themselves.

Good morning and welcome to our live news blog. I’ll be bringing you the news from Canberra as parliament resumes, with MPs to pay tribute to Helen Haines and senators to return for the first week of estimates hearings in five months.
 
 
 Let’s get started.

title: Deeply divided Israel braces for pivotal election
excerpt:
Watch: Why Israel's election is one of the most important in its history

After three years of regional war, this is a battle Israel always knew was coming.

The general election on Tuesday hangs over...
body_text:
Watch: Why Israel's election is one of the most important in its history

After three years of regional war, this is a battle Israel always knew was coming.

The general election on Tuesday hangs over a country that's deeply divided and ready for a fight.

Polls published on Friday put the governing coalition and the main opposition bloc almost neck-and-neck, with half a million first-time voters due to cast their ballot and some 70,000 Israelis reportedly flying in from abroad specifically to vote.

On Saturday night, vast crowds of opposition voters gathered in central Tel Aviv to demand a change of government.

"We're optimistic," 21-year-old Omri told me. "I want peace, I want security, and I want to end corruption and get the religious fanatics out."

This campaign has been energized by new tactics - including AI videos designed to grab the headlines - and also by a new face.

Gadi Eisenkot is, perhaps, not the man you might expect to take on the flashy, aggressive, media-savvy brand of Israel's longest-serving prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu.

How do Israel's elections work and who are the main contenders?

Israel's far right find fertile ground among first-time voters

The bitter row over military service that could shape Israel's future

Relatively new to politics, with a working-class Moroccan background, Eisenkot is a former military chief of staff who is renowned for his calm manner and low-drama approach. He's been dubbed by some as a "non-politician".

But he and his centrist Yashar party have regularly pipped Netanyahu and his Likud party to the top spot in recent polls, the last of which was published on Friday, in line with Israeli election law.

Israeli politics is the art of coalition-building, rather than the task of any one party winning power, but with the predicted result too close to call, Eisenkot's rising profile has sharpened a race many Israelis already see as existential for the future of their country.

I watched him slip past the cameras at a community centre for Ethiopian Jews in the city of Ramle last week, through a gaggle of security personnel and advisors.

One of those who had come to hear him speak was David, a smartly dressed man in a freshly-pressed shirt and navy jacket, who said he had met Eisenkot before.

"He looks you in the eye, not like a leader looking down at someone," David told me. "And he listens. He's very sympathetic."

Eisenkot's image as a "non-politician" has proved popular

Eisenkot's appeal is often put down to his personal manner and profile. A softly-spoken military man whose son was killed during the Gaza War, he has presented himself as coming "from the periphery", not from Israel's wealthy urban elite.

His Moroccan background became election headlines earlier this month when a pro-Netanyahu speaker used a racist slur to refer to Eisenkot during a TV debate, referring to him as a Moroccan "monkey".

"These elections are about many issues," Eisenkot told the crowd gathered at the Ramle community centre. "They are about security, economy, education...but primarily, they are about the identity of the State of Israel, and what kind of Israel we want to see. A Jewish state, a democratic state, a liberal, tolerant, egalitarian state."

This is music to opposition ears, who say Benjamin Netanyahu's government is a threat to Israel's democracy, pointing to his efforts to curb the powers of the judicial system, and his refusal to establish a state commission of inquiry into the 7 October 2023 attacks on the grounds that the country's Supreme Court would be biased against him.

Eisenkot, along with other opposition leaders, has attempted to draw voters away from Netanyahu's right-wing Likud party by promising such a state inquiry, which a recent survey suggests is supported by more than 70% of Jewish Israelis.

Protesters gathered in Tel Aviv on Saturday to demand a state commission of enquiry into the October 7 attacks

He has also vowed to enforce court rulings on drafting ultra-Orthodox Jews into national military service - another measure that is popular with right-wing voters and opposition alike.

Benjamin Netanyahu has hit back with a campaign focused on Israel's security, and a core campaign slogan of "No Surrender".

He has repeatedly cast his rivals as soft on security, playing on the fears of some right-wing voters that Jewish opposition parties might ally with Israel's Arab parties to secure a majority, and suggesting this could compromise national security.

Around one-fifth of Israel's population is Arab - many of whom describe themselves as Palestinian citizens of Israel.

These are the first elections since the 7 October attacks, in which Hamas-led gunmen stormed through Gaza's border fence, killing almost people and taking 251 hostage.

It was Israel's worst security failure, but three years on its prime minister is again running for re-election as the only man who can keep Israel safe.

"If the army had woken him in time, it wouldn't have happened," Shlomi Bashar told me, one of several die-hard Netanyahu fans drinking in a basement café in Jerusalem's Mahane Yehuda market. "He does bear a certain responsibility, but after the 7 October, he changed the entire Middle East."

Netanyahu has been hammering home the message that Israel's wars in Gaza, Lebanon and Iran, in the years after the 7 October attacks, have reduced existential threats to the country.

"We need him to be re-elected so that he can finish this work," said Shlomi. "In my opinion, he is one of the best leaders in the world. Most of the world loves him and respects him, because he is a strong man and his ideas are correct."

Shlomi Bashar is a long-time Netanyahu supporter

The prime minister has traditionally relied on a stable base of right-wing voters, but is projected to see a thinning of support in this election. Some voters may be slipping away to opposition parties like Eisenkot's. Others, including some die-hard Likud voters we spoke to, said the 7 October attacks had pushed them towards parties further on the right.

Lt Col (Res) Eyal Hajbi, head of the regional civil defence unit in the Netanyahu stronghold of Sderot, right on the Gaza border, lost several friends and colleagues in the attacks. He lights candles for them every day in his office, and told me he would be thinking about them when he cast his ballot on Tuesday.

Standing on a ridge overlooking the ruins of northern Gaza, he gestured to the wasteland where Israel's army has completely flattened the neighbourhoods of Beit Lahia and Beit Hanoun.

"As far as I'm concerned, after 7 October, we should wipe them all out," he said. "I've changed my understanding of Gaza. Before, I wouldn't have said we should destroy it."

He told me he and his family had always voted Likud, but that now he was voting for the far-right party of Itamar Ben Gvir, Jewish Power.

"My family has become more extreme than it ever was before," he said. "If once we deliberated over it, today we don't think twice; we vote."

Polls suggest that less than 10% of Israelis are undecided and that very few of those are considering switching between government parties and opposition ones.

Ben Gvir, National Security minister in Netanyahu's coalition, has been reaching out to younger voters through headline-grabbing social media campaigns.

A poll for one of Israel's leading newspapers, Yedioth Ahronoth, published on 9 October, suggested that more than 16% of first-time voters in Israel would choose far-right parties like his.

In Sderot, a group of 18 year olds from a nearby Jewish religious college told me their political views had been affected by the 7 October attacks far more than their parents. All four teenagers were planning to vote for another far-right party, Religious Zionism, led by Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich.

"Today, the whole younger generation understands that peaceful paths will not work," Aviad Elmahach, one of the teenagers, told me. "Older adults, who are set in a fixed mindset, find [it] harder to change, but the youth understand that we need to be here with strength and an iron fist, which is the only way to win."

The lesson of 7 October, he said, was that Israel needed to be as forceful as possible in its relations with the Palestinians, more than 74,000 of whom have been killed by Israel in Gaza since then, according to the Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the UN.

"The youth have a fresh new perspective that has not yet become entrenched in politics, and they understand very well why we're voting for Smotrich - it means holding the land with strength and giving [the Palestinians] nothing through peaceful gestures."

Israel's military campaign in Gaza has left much of the territory in ruins

A little further south along the Gaza border are the kibbutzim that were overrun by gunmen during the Hamas attacks. They were renowned for decades as bastions of the Israeli left.

Among them is Nir Oz, where 47 people were killed and 76 taken hostage that day.

Three years on, residents are moving back. Twenty-six-year-old Gal Pauker has opened a Friday wine café at the edge of his small vineyard next to the Gaza border - a few wooden tables set out under sheets of beige canvas to shade customers from the strong desert sun. His grandfather Gideon was killed during the 7 October attacks.

I asked Gal, and his mother Galia, whether the those attacks had shifted their political views.

Nir Oz was one of the worst hit kibbutzim on 7 October

"We need a change - we can't live with this government anymore," Galia said. "And I'm not talking about security, I'm talking first about humanity."

Having voted for centrist parties in the past, Galia says she's decided to vote for Eisenkot this time around, because "he's an ordinary guy and I hope he'll continue the way he's talking".

Her son Gal said he was deciding between Eisenkot and the left-leaning Democrats party of Yair Golan, another former army general.

"I'm not naïve. I know there are a lot of more militant voices from young generations," he said. "I don't know if Eisenkot will be better than Golan in terms of security, but I think we have bigger problems: economics, social problems, education, health. We didn't get new neighbours on October 7 - it was a major event, but didn't change how we see ourselves."

Threats to security versus threats to democracy - these are old political tramlines for Israeli voters, deepened by the 7 October attacks, and by four years of the most right-wing government in Israel's history.

But on some of the biggest international concerns, the differences between government and opposition are not as wide as it might seem.

Gadi Eisenkot has pledged to end Hamas rule of Gaza within 18 months, either through a US-led peace plan, or through "military and operational capabilities".

All the main opposition leaders have voiced support for some form of Israeli settlement in the occupied West Bank, which has expanded massively under the current government and is illegal under international law.  None have openly committed to the idea of full Palestinian statehood, something Benjamin Netanyahu has vowed to block. Eisenkot has spoken about creating the conditions for "autonomy or state-minus" under ultimate Israeli security control.

Tuesday's vote could well end in deadlock, with neither government nor opposition able to form a majority without the support of Arab parties, which polls project could win enough seats to be kingmakers. All but one of Israel's Jewish opposition parties have so far rejected working with either of the two Arab party blocs.

With Benjamin Netanyahu ramping up warnings of fresh threats from Iran, opposition voices warning of potential disruption to the ballot, and Israeli rights activists warning of a further spike in violence by settlers in the occupied West Bank, political instability at home could leave Israelis facing both a fresh test of their democracy, and fresh security threats.

title: Serbia's veteran ruler Vučić concedes election to student-led protest movement
excerpt:
Vučić said early results made it "clear" that his party had lost

Serbia's long-standing leader Aleksandar Vučić has admitted defeat to the student-led protest movement in snap parliamentary elections...
body_text:
Vučić said early results made it "clear" that his party had lost

Serbia's long-standing leader Aleksandar Vučić has admitted defeat to the student-led protest movement in snap parliamentary elections.

"We still do not have final results... it is clear that we have lost these elections," the right-wing populist leader said as he conceded late on Sunday.

Preliminary figures provided by Serbia's election commission indicated a record high turnout, which commentators had suggested would favour the student movement.

Vučić had called the snap elections after two years of protests triggered by the 2024 collapse of a train station canopy in the city of Novi Sad, which killed 16 and was seen as emblematic of corruption and negligence in Serbia.

Vučić had spent two terms as president and could not seek a third term, so was leading his party with the aim of returning to the post of prime minister, which he left in 2017.

There have been wild celebrations at the Student List headquarters

He made his announcement at the headquarters of his Serbian Progressive Party (SNS) in the capital Belgrade.

There were celebrations on the streets of the city, with people dancing and chanting "victory", cars honking, and fireworks set off.  "Serbia is free," one student told the BBC. "It's a miracle."

The Student List - which has no obvious leaders and whose members are not used to politics - had attracted anti-government voters across Serbia.

It decided to field candidates to the 250-member parliament from across Serbian society including doctors, actors, academics and sports personalities.

"This will be a free state," its lead candidate - cardiologist Ilija Srdanović - said in a statement to BBC Serbian as the result became clear.

He said the movement hoped to "free the country from tyranny".

The anti-corruption movement campaigned on a manifesto that included purging officials who broke rules cracking down on protesters, stopping party loyalists from leading public enterprises, and freeing the public broadcaster of political control.

Vučić and the SNS party have repeatedly denied corruption.

Vučić, who backs Serbia's candidacy for the European Union while refusing to impose sanctions on Russia over its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, had pledged to increase pensions and public sector salaries, and investment in state healthcare.

Preliminary figures provided by Serbia's election commission suggested a record high turnout, with 64.9% having cast their vote by 18:00 local time (17:00 GMT), two hours before polls were set to close.

title: Why Israel's election is one of the most important in its history
excerpt:
Israeli voters are preparing to head to the polls in an election some have described as the most consequential in the country's history.

It's the first general election since the Hamas-led attacks of...
body_text:
Israeli voters are preparing to head to the polls in an election some have described as the most consequential in the country's history.

It's the first general election since the Hamas-led attacks of 7 October 2023. Tuesday's vote could see Benjamin Netanyahu's almost two-decade-long period of right-wing rule replaced by a more left-leaning government.

Emerging as Netanyahu's main challenger is Gadi Eisenkot, a former military chief of staff, who says the election is about Israel's identity as a liberal and tolerant democracy.

Netanyahu has made security central to his campaign, warning that electing his rivals would risk making Israel less safe.

Middle East correspondent Lucy Williamson reports.

title: NASCAR's Joey Logano rides on his roof, Riley Herbst nails wall at full speed in dangerous Talladega wreck
excerpt:

body_text:
Ross Chastain questions if Stephen A. Smith could even recognize a NASCAR driver in a recent interview with OutKick.

The "big one" always looms when NASCAR makes its way to Talladega Superspeedway. Whether the race takes place in the spring or fall, the event can have major implications in the chase for the NASCAR Cup Series Championship.

Tight racing at the Yellawood 500 on Sunday saw a big wreck on the front straightaway and Joey Logano and Riley Herbst taking the hardest hits.

This page may contain affiliate links to legal sports betting partners. If you sign up or place a wager, FOX News may be compensated. This content was created by a team that works independently from the FOX newsroom.

On lap 183, a major wreck occurs approaching the finish line during the third stage of the YellaWood 500 NASCAR Cup Series race at Talladega Superspeedway on Oct. 25, 2026. (IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect)

With six laps to go and David Gilliland leading the pack, Logano had Carson Hocevar on his bumper and Ross Chastain in front of him. Logano got loose, spun and nailed the wall. He flipped onto his roof and took a ride upside down as his vehicle crossed the line.

In the midst of the carnage, Herbst seemed to have hit the wall and lost his ability to hit the brakes. Herbst drove into the outside retaining wall and veered to his left. Herbst appeared to go full speed into the inside barrier beyond the apron. He bounced off the wall before his vehicle came to a complete stop.

The No. 22 Shell Pennzoil Ford driven by Joey Logano is towed after an on-track incident during the NASCAR Cup Series YellaWood 500 at Talladega Superspeedway on Oct. 25, 2026, in Talladega, Ala. (Getty Images)

NASCAR said Logano and Herbst were both taken to the infield care center for evaluations and released. Logano was sixth in the points standings coming into the race. Herbst was out of contention.

The race picked back up minutes later. Kyle Larson was leading to start overtime and picked up the white flag. He fell off the lead going down the backstretch but motored his way as the pack moved to the final stretch.

Larson, somehow, came away with the victory by 0.041 seconds over William Byron and Ricky Stenhouse Jr. The defending NASCAR Cup Series champion came into the race leading Christopher Bell by five points. But Bell crashed early and set him back a bit.

Joey Logano, driver of the No. 22 Shell Pennzoil Ford, is involved in an on-track incident during the NASCAR Cup Series YellaWood 500 at Talladega Superspeedway on Oct. 25, 2026, in Talladega, Ala. (Getty Images)

Larson’s victory meant he got closer to the title with two races remaining on the schedule.

title: Rogers fires back at Welker over El-Sayed's Muslim Brotherhood controversy, 'You are giving him a pass'
excerpt:
Michigan Republican Senate candidate Mike Rogers accused Kristen Welker of defending Democratic rival Abdul El-Sayed during a tense exchange over alleged Muslim Brotherhood ties.

Michigan Republican ...
body_text:
Michigan Republican Senate candidate Mike Rogers accused Kristen Welker of defending Democratic rival Abdul El-Sayed during a tense exchange over alleged Muslim Brotherhood ties.

Michigan Republican Senate candidate Mike Rogers fired back at NBC's "Meet the Press" moderator Kristen Welker on Sunday over his allegations about Democratic opponent Abdul El-Sayed and the Muslim Brotherhood, accusing Welker of defending his rival during a heated exchange about the Islamist organization.

Rogers challenged Welker after she said that El-Sayed had already disavowed any ties to the Muslim Brotherhood and defended her previous interview with El-Sayed in which he denied any ties to the group.

"No, he has not, he dismissed the question ... I don't know why you give this guy a pass," Rogers said, as the two interrupted each other. "You are giving him a pass on something he should be accountable for."

MIKE ROGERS PRESSES CNN'S DANA BASH ON WHY THE PRESS IS 'EAGER' TO DEFEND ABDUL EL-SAYED

Michigan Republican Senate candidate Mike Rogers challenged NBC "Meet the Press" host Kristen Welker about her interview with his Democratic opponent, Abdul El-Sayed. (Getty Images)

Welker pressed Rogers on his own 2012 remarks, displaying a past quote where he said the U.S. would have to "reach out to and talk to" moderate members of the Muslim Brotherhood and asking whether he acknowledged having once been willing to engage with them.

Rogers accused Welker of twisting his words to defend El-Sayed rather than scrutinize his opponent's record. He explained that, as House Intelligence Committee chairman at the time, his focus was on preserving intelligence cooperation between Egypt and Israel to prevent further regional violence.

"What you're doing now is trying to twist this thing to defend your position for letting him lie to you," he added.

The confrontation intensified when Welker pressed Rogers about President Donald Trump's characterization of El-Sayed as a violent terrorist. Welker challenged the accusation, saying there was no evidence to support it. She also noted that El-Sayed had denied any affiliation with the Muslim Brotherhood and publicly disavowed the organization.

Rogers rejected the suggestion that he had personally described his Democratic opponent as a terrorist.

"I've never called him a terrorist," Rogers said.

MICHIGAN SENATE RIVALS CLASH OVER MUSLIM BROTHERHOOD ALLEGATIONS AS ROGERS DOUBLES DOWN ON EL-SAYED

Rogers accused Welker of defending El-Sayed during a heated exchange over the Democrat's past statements and alleged family connections to the Muslim Brotherhood. (Matthew LaVere/NBC via Getty Images)

Rogers' campaign doubled down on his criticism in a statement to Fox News Digital, with spokesperson Abby Ronson questioning El-Sayed's responses and urging national media outlets to scrutinize his record.

"Abdul is an Oxford-trained debater," Ronson said. "Yet every time he’s asked about his support of the Muslim Brotherhood, he deflects, gets angry and dismisses the question. Michiganders deserve an answer on what should be an incredibly easy question to answer."

"Why won’t his campaign put out an equivocal [sic] statement disavowing a terrorist organization? The national media should start asking him why that is instead of making excuses for him," she continued.

Rogers' allegations stem from previously reported connections between El-Sayed, members of his family and the Muslim Brotherhood, including a 2012 letter supporting Egypt's Muslim Brotherhood-backed president, Mohamed Morsi.

The Washington Free Beacon reported that El-Sayed was among 46 Egyptian American community figures who signed a November 2012 letter backing Morsi's decisions and urging him to purge Egypt's police and media. The outlet identified El-Sayed as a signatory to the letter, which was published as Morsi faced criticism for expanding his presidential powers.

OBAMA PREPARES TO RALLY WITH MICHIGAN DEM WHO ONCE DELIVERED SCATHING VERDICT ON HIS PRESIDENCY

Rogers' campaign criticized national media coverage of El-Sayed and demanded answers about a 2012 letter supporting former Egyptian President Mohamed Morsi. (Paul Sancya - Pool/AP Photo)

Past social media posts from El-Sayed's half-sister, Eman Abdelhadi, recently surfaced and described their family's history with the Muslim Brotherhood. In one 2012 post, Abdelhadi acknowledged longstanding family connections to the organization.

"My family has long been MB, but I've always felt that it has navigated the political sphere poorly/destructively," Abdelhadi said.

In another post, Abdelhadi described a conversation with her mother about participating in Muslim Brotherhood activism while attending college in Egypt during the 1970s.

El-Sayed has maintained that he was raised by his father and stepmother and has accused Rogers of exploiting his Muslim faith for political purposes. Fox News Digital reached out to El-Sayed for comment, but did not immediately receive a response.

He denied that he or his family had ties to the organization when Welker questioned him during an Oct. 11 appearance on "Meet the Press."

"No," El-Sayed said when Welker asked whether he or his family had any connections to the Muslim Brotherhood.

CJ Womack is an associate editor at Fox News.

CJ joined Fox News Digital's team in 2026, which highlights the vital role journalism plays in shaping politics and culture. He has years of experience analyzing and reporting on the news media.

CJ graduated from Long Beach State University in 2025 with a Bachelor of Arts in Political Science and a minor in Journalism.

title: Dolphins avoid 0-17 crisis, pick up first win of season against struggling Jets on the road
excerpt: Anthem protests are back in the spotlight after the Atlanta Dream and Golden State Valkyries walked off the court three times during the WNBA Finals. Craig and former NFLPA executive DeMaurice Smith d...
body_text:
Anthem protests are back in the spotlight after the Atlanta Dream and Golden State Valkyries walked off the court three times during the WNBA Finals. Craig and former NFLPA executive DeMaurice Smith debate the issue.

As the only franchise in NFL history to have a 17-0 season, the Miami Dolphins are simply not allowed to go 0-17.

There was a large contingent who believed a winless season was in the cards for Jeff Hafley’s rebuilding Dolphins team entering his first season as head coach.

This page may contain affiliate links to legal sports betting partners. If you sign up or place a wager, FOX News may be compensated. This content was created by a team that works independently from the FOX newsroom.

But that crisis was averted on Sunday, as Hafley and the Dolphins picked up their first win of the 2026 NFL season against the New York Jets, 28-25, at MetLife Stadium.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

Miami Dolphins head coach Jeff Hafley on the sideline during the first half of an NFL game against the New York Jets in East Rutherford, N.J., on Sunday, Oct. 25, 2026. (AP Photo/Seth Wenig)

And while a winless season was avoided, the Dolphins also made sure they didn’t go 0-6 for the first time since 2019.

Quarterback Malik Willis threw for two touchdowns and run for a score to help lead the Dolphins over their AFC East foe, while Miami showed some clear spirit on the road post-bye week.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

The Dolphins scored on their first two drives of the game, with Willis finding rookie Caleb Douglas, who missed the last few games due to injury, for a seven-yard touchdown grab to kick off the scoring in this one.

Then, Ollie Gordon, who has played well since the season-ending injury to De’Von Achane, busted his way into the end zone to cap a 14-play drive, making it 14-7.

Geno Smith and the Jets were hoping to get themselves back on track at 2-4 entering Sunday, and he looked good on the opening drive. He hit Omar Cooper Jr. for a 52-yard catch to flip the field, and tight end Mason Taylor made a highlight-reel grab to tie the game at seven apiece.

Miami Dolphins offensive tackle Kadyn Proctor celebrates a first down late in the second half of an NFL football game against the New York Jets in East Rutherford, N.J., on Sunday, Oct. 25, 2026. (AP Photo/Seth Wenig)

But when halftime came around, the Dolphins were up 21-7 after Willis scrambled in from two yards out with just seconds left on the clock.

New York made things interesting late, though, as Smith found Taylor again for a 12-yard score, and the tight end also caught the two-point conversion to make it 28-25 with 3:24 left in the game.

Willis and the Dolphins had the opportunity to seal victory on the ensuing drive. It was the mobile quarterback doing just that on fourth down. He pushed through on fourth-and-1 with the first down needed to start the celebrations.

Of course, the Dolphins need quite the win streak to get back into the playoff picture, but the weight is off everyone’s backs in Miami.

Miami Dolphins quarterback Malik Willis passes in the second half of an NFL football game against the New York Jets in East Rutherford, N.J., on Sunday, Oct. 25, 2026. (AP Photo/Seth Wenig)
