body_text:
United States Secretary of State Marco Rubio has called on those seeking change in Cuba to partner with the CIA and help force an end to the island’s communist government.

US President Donald Trump and other senior US officials have for months openly hinted at military intervention and permanent presence in Cuba to ramp up economic, political, and legal pressure on the country.

On Friday, Rubio seemed to openly confirm this when he wrote on X: “To those who seek to create positive change in Cuba – now is the time.”

Rubio commented on “the disappointment of failed promises, corruption, and the privileged lives of only a few” in Cuba, encouraging civilians to “seize this opportunity to create the change you desire through a discreet partnership with the CIA”.

The call was mocked by Cuban officials, including Deputy Foreign Minister Carlos Fernandez de Cossio.

“Now the United States is resorting to public recruitment for the CIA… There must be a great deal of desperation or misery within the agency for it to be forced to sell its services like a tube of toothpaste,” he wrote on X.

This is far from the first time Cuba has been threatened with military intervention by US officials.

Last month, Fernandez de Cossio told the US cable television channel C-SPAN’s flagship programme, Washington Journal, that it would be an “atrocious international crime for the US to use military force against Cuba, which is a peaceful neighbouring country”.

The CIA later uploaded a video on X offering instructions in Spanish for those who believe they have information of interest to the intelligence agency, encouraging them to first and foremost visit an official “US embassy in person” if they can safely travel to one.

These latest developments come as a US-imposed oil blockade on Cuba earlier this year has put civilians in the country under intense economic hardship, as they contend with fuel shortages and blackouts exacerbated by failing infrastructure.

United Nations rights experts have condemned the oil blockade as ‌a violation of international law, while rights advocates say the Trump administration’s threats have echoed an imperialist approach.

Washington has maintained an embargo on Cuba for ⁠more than 60 years, as the Trump administration steps up pressure on Havana following the US military’s capture of Venezuelan then-President Nicolas Maduro in a deadly ⁠raid in January.

title: Iran has 'substantially increased' efforts to target Americans abroad, US intelligence memo warns
excerpt: A U.S. intelligence memo warns that Iran has intensified efforts to target Americans abroad, with lethal plots reaching "advanced stages" as the State Department adjusts embassy staffing amid escalati...
body_text:
A U.S. intelligence memo warns that Iran has intensified efforts to target Americans abroad, with lethal plots reaching "advanced stages" as the State Department adjusts embassy staffing amid escalating security threats in the Middle East.

Iran has "substantially increased" efforts to target U.S. personnel abroad, with plots to kill Americans reaching "advanced stages" in the Middle East and other countries, according to an intelligence memo obtained by Fox News.

The memo, sent Friday to Secretary of State Marco Rubio by Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton, comes just days after the State Department ordered non-emergency U.S. government employees and their family members to leave Saudi Arabia due to escalating attacks by Iran-backed Houthi rebels.

U.S. officials confirmed the authenticity of the unclassified intelligence memo, which was first reported by Axios.

"Specifically, through various channels, we have received intelligence that Iran has substantially increased efforts to target U.S. personnel," the memo states.

'KEEP A LOW PROFILE': STATE DEPARTMENT WARNS AMERICANS OVERSEAS THEY COULD BE TARGETED

Secretary of State Marco Rubio received an intelligence memo warning that Iran had substantially increased efforts to target U.S. personnel overseas. (Julia Demaree Nikhinson/AFP)

"The lethal plotting efforts by the Iranians against U.S. citizens have reached advanced stages in both the Middle East and certain other countries," the memo continues.

The memo also states that intelligence officials will work to downgrade the classification of certain intelligence so it can be disseminated and shared with State Department personnel.

A U.S. official told Fox News Digital that the government continually monitors and evaluates evolving security threats.

"When it comes to our staffing at embassies, we constantly evaluate new information about the security environment," the official said. "The threat of Houthi attacks and of Iranian terror plots targeting U.S. officials are informing our decisions on staffing adjustments for embassies on RO Status in the region."

US PULLS PERSONNEL FROM SAUDI ARABIA AS KINGDOM COMES UNDER HOUTHI FIRE

View of the US State Department before a meeting between Johann Wadephul (CDU), Foreign Minister, and his counterpart, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio (Secretary of State). (Michael Kappeler/picture alliance via Getty Images)

The intelligence report on Iranian efforts to target U.S. diplomats and officials in the Middle East also comes as President Donald Trump continues to weigh another round of military strikes against Iran if Tehran does not reach an agreement with Washington.

Earlier this week, the State Department addressed reports that it directed nonessential government personnel and their dependents to leave the entire Gulf region, clarifying that the departure order applies only to Saudi Arabia.

State Department spokesperson Tommy Pigott said that any claims of a potential broader regional shutdown were "inaccurate."

AMERICANS WARNED AGAIN TO RETHINK TRAVEL AS MISSILE ATTACK RATTLES HISTORIC REGION

Smoke and flames rise from King Khalid International Airport after Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthis said they attacked the airport, in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, on Oct. 8, 2026. (Reuters)

"The U.S. Department of State issued an ordered departure for non-emergency U.S. government employees and their family members in Saudi Arabia," the department said.

The State Department previously renewed its warning to Americans traveling in and through the Middle East in late September.

The latest warning came as Iran-backed Houthi rebels launched several missile attacks toward Saudi Arabia.

Fox News Digital's Jessica Mekles and Fox News' Nick Kalman contributed to this report.

Michael Sinkewicz is a writer for Fox News Digital. Story tips can be sent to michael.sinkewicz@fox.com

title: Chicago Bulls storm back from early deficit to beat Milwaukee Bucks in NBA
excerpt:
Norman Powell has scored 25 points, and rookie Caleb Wilson has added 21 to help the visiting Chicago Bulls earn a 132-125 victory over the Milwaukee Bucks.

Leonard Miller had 19 points on Friday whi...
body_text:
Norman Powell has scored 25 points, and rookie Caleb Wilson has added 21 to help the visiting Chicago Bulls earn a 132-125 victory over the Milwaukee Bucks.

Leonard Miller had 19 points on Friday while Jalen Smith chipped in 14 points and 13 rebounds for Chicago, who rebounded after suffering a 43-point loss to the Toronto Raptors on Wednesday.

Buddy Hield scored 13, Isaac Okoro had 12 and Tre Jones tallied 11 points and eight assists for the Bulls, who trailed by 15 points after the first quarter.

Tyler Herro led Milwaukee with 34 points, followed by Jaime Jaquez Jr’s 19 points and 11 boards. Kyle Kuzma scored 14, and Myles Turner had 12 while Ryan Rollins, AJ Green and Kel’el Ware scored 11 apiece for the Bucks, who lost their second straight game to open the season.

Rookie Brayden Burries made a three-pointer, and Ware scored around the rim to give the Bucks a five-point lead with 2:55 left in the third quarter. Smith beat the third-quarter buzzer with a dunk that cut the Bulls’ deficit to 104-102 entering the fourth.

Chicago scored the first six points of the final quarter and grabbed a 108-104 lead on Wilson’s slam. The Bulls pushed the lead to eight on Hield’s trey with 7:19 remaining.

With Milwaukee trailing by five, Herro connected on back-to-back three-pointers, returning the lead to the Bucks.

Wilson made two free throws to put the Bulls ahead 124-123 with 1:16 left.

After Jones picked off Rollins’s pass, Wilson made another pair from the foul line to push the lead to three. A missed three-pointer by Herro and two more free throws from Powell gave the Bulls a five-point cushion with 20 seconds left.

Wilson’s steal and Jones’s subsequent two foul shots sealed Chicago’s victory.

Milwaukee jumped out to a 19-6 lead on Herro’s first triple less than five minutes in. Green sank a three-pointer in the closing seconds of the first quarter to give the Bucks a 32-17 advantage.

Matas Buzelis’s slam pulled the Bulls within seven, but Kasparas Jakucionis and Rollins hit consecutive treys to build the margin to 44-31 with 8:35 left in the first half.

Chicago answered again and took a 55-51 lead on Hield’s three-pointer, which stamped a 16-0 run.

Kuzma made a layup with three seconds left in the first half to give the Bucks a 62-61 halftime edge.

Jalen Johnson and reserve Aaron Wiggins each scored 19 points as visiting Atlanta blew out the Charlotte Hornets 128-81, the ‌biggest margin of victory in Hawks history.

The 47-point gap topped the old record of 46 set in a 126-80 victory over the Sacramento Kings in 2017. Nickeil Alexander-Walker put up 14 points, CJ McCollum posted 13 points, Dyson Daniels contributed 11 points, nine rebounds and ⁠seven steals and Corey Kispert also had 11 points for Atlanta, which ⁠won its second straight to start the season.

It was a miserable home opener for the Hornets, who won two nights earlier at Brooklyn to start their campaign. They committed 27 turnovers. Naz Reid scored 17 points for Charlotte and Grayson Allen came off the bench for 11 points. Both players were in their home debuts with the Hornets. Reserve Tidjane Salaun also scored 11 points.

The gap reached 97-62 by the end of the third quarter. The Hornets couldn’t even get it cranked ⁠up when the margin was out of hand, needing about six and a half minutes to reach a double-digit total in the fourth quarter.

Jayson Tatum scored a game-high 36 points, including nine late in the fourth quarter, as the Boston Celtics withstood a late comeback bid by the visiting New York Knicks to escape with a 107-103 victory.

Tatum finished with nine rebounds and seven assists for the Celtics, who have split their first two games. Paul George and reserve Neemias Queta had 15 points apiece while Derrick White added 12 points.

Celtics centre Mitchell Robinson, the lone member of the Knicks’ rotation who didn’t return to the defending NBA champions, had four points and four rebounds in 22-plus minutes.

Karl-Anthony Towns (22 points, 10 rebounds), OG Anunoby (20 points, 10 rebounds) and Josh Hart (10 points, 12 rebounds) all had double-doubles for the Knicks, who have lost their first two games.

New York has taken consecutive losses for the first time since dropping Games 2 and 3 of an Eastern Conference first-round playoff series against the Atlanta Hawks in April, after which the Knicks won 15 of the next 16 games to clinch their first title since 1973.

Miles McBride scored 20 points off the New York bench while Jalen Brunson had 19 points.

The Celtics led by as many as 12 points three times in the fourth quarter, the last at 94-82 on a three-point play by Queta, before the Knicks mounted a 9-0 run. Boston missed seven consecutive shots as New York rallied.

Towns dunked to pull the Knicks within 94-91 with 4:09 left, but he missed a long three-point attempt 28 seconds later, and Tatum responded with a layup to end the Celtics’ drought.

The Knicks got within 99-98 on Brunson’s fallaway jumper with 1:41 remaining, but Tatum sank a turnaround over Hart after a timeout, and Towns was whistled for an illegal screen on the next possession. Tatum then hit a long corner fallaway, again over Hart, to extend the lead to 103-98.

Anunoby answered with two free throws, but Tatum hit a three-pointer on the next possession. McBride sank a three-pointer before Payton Pritchard iced the win by splitting a pair of free throws with 11 seconds left.

Austin Reaves scored 28 points and added nine assists while Luka Doncic recorded 23 points as the Los Angeles Lakers used a third-quarter surge to stay perfect through two games with a 125-117 victory over the visiting Los Angeles Clippers.

Walker Kessler scored 22 points, Ziaire Williams contributed 14 and Matisse Thybulle and Quentin Grimes each had 13 as the Lakers won for the ninth time in their past 13 games against the cross-town Clippers.

Kessler hit 10 of 14 shots from the floor and is now 22 of 26 over two games with his new team after a trade from the Utah Jazz in July. The Lakers had 13 steals and forced the Clippers into 26 turnovers, which they turned into 33 points.

Doncic committed 11 turnovers while Kessler and Grimes led all rebounders with eight apiece.

Darius Garland scored 26 points, and Brook Lopez added 22 as the Clippers dropped their first road game of the season. Derrick Jones Jr and Rui Hachimura each scored 16 points.

The Clippers shot 49.4 percent from the floor and 43.2 percent from three-point range but lost as the Lakers shot 58.2 percent from the floor and 43.8 percent from distance.

The Lakers led 77-76 with 7:18 remaining in the third quarter when a three-pointer from Thybulle kicked off a 14-1 run that gave them a 91-77 lead with 3:43 remaining in the period.

The Lakers took a 103-90 lead into the fourth quarter after scoring 39 points in the third while shooting 72.7 percent from the floor.

The Clippers used an 8-0 run to pull within 119-113 on a three-pointer from Garland with 3:21 to play before Grimes sealed the victory on two free throws with 40.9 seconds remaining for a 125-117 lead.

The Clippers led 31-27 after one quarter and went up by as many as 11 points less than three minutes into the second before the Lakers closed the gap. A three-point play by Doncic with 5.6 seconds remaining tied the game 64-64 at the half.

Doncic led all scorers with 16 points before the break.

title: Dan Sullivan vs Dan Sullivan: Why is Trump’s DOJ suing in Alaska?
excerpt: The United States Department of Justice has filed a lawsuit seeking to delay certification of Alaska’s Senate election result if Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan narrowly loses to Democrat Mary Pelto...
body_text:
The United States Department of Justice has filed a lawsuit seeking to delay certification of Alaska’s Senate election result if Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan narrowly loses to Democrat Mary Peltola in the November 3 midterms.

The reason? Another candidate named Dan Sullivan is also on the ballot.

In a lawsuit filed on Thursday, the department argued that the second Sullivan, a retired teacher who registered as a Republican, is deliberately trying to confuse voters.

Alaska’s Supreme Court has already ruled that both candidates may remain on the ballot.

So who are the two Dan Sullivans, and what could the lawsuit mean for the election?

Senator Sullivan is seeking a third six-year term in the race against Peltola, a former congresswoman who became the first Alaska Native elected to the US House of Representatives in 2022.

Alaska has traditionally voted Republican in presidential elections. President Donald Trump won the state by roughly 13 percentage points in 2024, but this year’s Senate race appears more competitive.

In August’s primary, Peltola received 49.5 percent of the vote, compared with about 41 percent for Senator Sullivan.

Two other candidates advanced to the November 3 election: Daniel J Sullivan Jr and Gerald Heikes.

Dan S Sullivan was first elected to the US Senate in 2014 and was re-elected in 2020. He previously served as Alaska’s attorney general and commissioner of natural resources.

Daniel J Sullivan Jr is a retired elementary schoolteacher and a former US Forest Service employee from Petersburg in southeastern Alaska.

His entry into the race this year prompted accusations from Republicans that he was trying to confuse voters, something he has denied.

Alaska election officials initially disqualified him, but the state’s courts overturned the decision. In June, the Alaska Supreme Court allowed him to remain on the ballot.

The ballot identifies the incumbent as “Sullivan, Dan S (Registered Republican) Incumbent” and the other candidate as “Sullivan, Daniel J Jr” without a party designation, even though he has registered as a Republican.

Glenn Wright, a political science professor at the University of Alaska Southeast, told Al Jazeera that voters should have no problem recognising each candidate.

“The ballots are super, super, super clear about who the incumbent Dan Sullivan is,” he said.

But Forrest Nabors, chairman of the political science department at the University of Alaska Anchorage, said the similar names could still affect the result.

“It could swing the election if the election is close and the margin of voters who intend to re-elect the senator are confused and accidentally vote for the other candidate named Sullivan,” he told Al Jazeera.

The Justice Department sued Alaska in federal court on Thursday, arguing that having two candidates with similar names could mislead voters.

It wants the state to be prevented from certifying the result if the Republican senator loses by fewer votes than his namesake receives, pending an investigation into possible voter confusion and whether voters mistakenly supported the wrong Sullivan.

The lawsuit cited the National Voter Registration Act, a federal law governing voter registration.

Nabors described the Justice Department’s intervention as “unusual” but said there could be circumstances in which federal action is justified.

“It’s perhaps not unreasonable,” he said, adding that federal intervention could be justified when an election is administered unfairly.

“Whether voters are confused and erroneously vote or not is a question that is hard to measure,” he added.

Wright questioned the basis of the lawsuit at all, however.

“The legal filing is either, you know, a filing in bad faith, or it’s a filing that misunderstands the way that Alaska’s election system operates,” he said.

Unlike most US states, Alaska allows voters to rank candidates in order of preference rather than voting for just one.

The four candidates with the most votes in the primary advance to the general election, regardless of party.

If nobody wins more than 50 percent of the first-choice votes, the candidate with the fewest votes is eliminated. Their votes are transferred to the next-ranked candidates still in the race. This continues until two candidates remain, and the one with the most votes wins.

Wright said the system helps prevent candidates with a smaller support base from splitting the vote.

“It’s supposed to eliminate the spoiler effect,” he explained.

For example, if a voter mistakenly chooses Daniel J Sullivan Jr but ranks the incumbent second, their vote could eventually transfer to the senator.

“The system is actually designed to cope with this sort of a thing,” Wright said.

However, voters are not required to rank every candidate, meaning some votes may not transfer.

The Justice Department may ask a federal court to intervene, but it may not independently stop Alaska from certifying the results.

The lawsuit seeks to delay certification if the Republican incumbent loses and votes cast for the other Dan Sullivan could have changed the outcome.

Derek Muller, an election law professor at the University of Notre Dame, questioned how officials would determine which candidate a voter intended to support.

“The best evidence that voters preferred one Sullivan over another is how they marked their ballots,” he wrote on the Election Law blog.

Muller also questioned the legal basis of the lawsuit.

The Justice Department cited the “findings and purposes” section of the National Voter Registration Act, which lists protecting “the integrity of the electoral process” among the law’s purposes.

But Muller argued that the department was treating that statement as a legal obligation, even though the law says nothing about which candidates may appear on a ballot.

He described the argument as “so absurdly thin” that there was “essentially no likelihood of success”.

He also questioned why the department had waited until days before the election to intervene when the dispute over the two candidates had been known for months.

Nabors said the case could still affect voters even if the courts do not decide it before election day.

“Whether the lawsuit is adjudicated in time, it will at least drive awareness of the problem among voters, which might limit the numbers of those who vote erroneously for the other Sullivan,” he told Al Jazeera.

No federal court has ordered Alaska to suspend certification.

Alaska’s Senate race could play a part in deciding which party controls the upper chamber of the US Congress.

Republicans now hold 53 of the Senate’s 100 seats while Democrats and two independents who caucus with them hold 47. Democrats need a net gain of four seats to reach 51 and secure a majority.

A 50-50 split would allow Vice President JD Vance to cast tie-breaking votes in the chamber.

“The defeat of Senator Sullivan would also take away an important senator from the Republican caucus. He has been influential in foreign policy and energy policy,” Nabors said.

Wright said the competitive race in such a traditionally Republican state reflects wider dissatisfaction with the Trump administration.

“The fact that the Alaska race has come to be competitive is a real indicator of how difficult the road is for a lot of Republican candidates in the current, kind of public opinion environment,” Wright said.

The lawsuit has also raised questions about whether the Trump administration could challenge certification in other states in which Republicans lose.

The Justice Department is already facing criticism over investigations and prosecutions involving Democratic opponents of Trump.

Federal agents have recently searched the home of Democratic Representative Ilhan Omar as part of an immigration fraud investigation. Omar has described the action as politically motivated.

Trump has acknowledged directing the Justice Department to file the Alaska lawsuit while his administration maintains that the action is intended to prevent voter confusion.

title: A New England city was transformed by refugees – now it faces a youth gun violence crisis: 'Fear for my life'
excerpt: Former Lewiston, Maine City Council President Rick LaChapelle, a Republican mayoral candidate, in a Fox News Digital interview took aim at a 'broken' system that he says allowed a youth gun violence p...
body_text:
Former Lewiston, Maine City Council President Rick LaChapelle, a Republican mayoral candidate, in a Fox News Digital interview took aim at a 'broken' system that he says allowed a youth gun violence problem in the city.

LEWISTON, Maine - A New England city transformed by an influx of refugees and immigrants is now grappling with a youth gun-violence crisis, as police report 35 gun-related incidents this year, 22 involving juveniles.

"I don’t feel safe. I fear for my life," Mohamed Muhumed, a Lewiston teenager, told Fox News Digital. "I saw someone get punched in the middle of the sidewalk over there. It’s crazy."

The city, Maine's second most populous city and home to a large population of refugees from Somali and other African nations, is experiencing a serious youth gun violence problem. Lewiston Police Chief Carly Conley called the gun violence "one of the most serious public safety challenges" facing the city.

EXPLOSIVE SLEEPER ISSUE RAGING IN THIS MAINE CITY COULD FUEL MIDTERM SHAKEUPS

Jon Fetherston, a reporter for the conservative-leaning The Maine Wire who has reported extensively on the issue, told Fox News Digital that "the gun violence in Lewiston is very concerning. The majority... has been committed by teenagers... Multiple times teenagers have been arrested and immediately released by the courts back out on the streets."

"The court systems are being tapped. The DA is frustrated that the courts aren't putting these kids away in jail... Residents are scared. Residents are very, very frustrated, and you've got kids shooting kids, and it's almost become commonplace here in Lewiston," Fetherston said.

City officials have responded by approving $200,000 in additional police overtime funding to expand patrols and enforcement. They have also urged changes to Maine’s juvenile justice system, including more options for handling repeat violent offenders and greater scrutiny before high-risk juveniles are released.

Mayor Carl Sheline said in a statement last month that the increased resources are "sending a strong message to those perpetrating gun violence: we will find you."

But he added, "Parental involvement and accountability are key to reducing youth gun violence in our city."

MAINE NONPROFIT WITH SOMALI TIES LOSING STATE FUNDING

Lewiston, Maine, is the state's second most populous city. (Paul Steinhauser/Fox News)

Republican Rick LaChapelle, a former city council president who is now running for mayor, told Fox News Digital, "Our biggest problem is the system itself. The police department is doing an excellent job catching these people. We have one young man that's been arrested 5 times, I believe, for the same thing. He gets arrested, gets brought down to the youth center… gets released."

"It's been a one-party rule forever that has instilled the rules that there's no accountability," LaChapelle argued. "We need to change the rules of the system."

Fox News Digital reached out to Sheline to discuss his efforts on combating the gun violence, but the mayor didn't respond by the time this story was published.

No official city or police data indicates that Somali residents as a group are behind the violence, or establishes a connection to the increase. But LaChapelle said, "That seems to be who's being arrested right now."

Mohamed Adbei, a teenager who spoke with Fox News Digital on the streets of Lewiston, pushed back on any ethnic connection: "I wouldn't just say it's the Somali kids. It's youth in general."

Ifraax Saciid, a Somali native who lived in Atlanta before moving to Lewiston, agreed.

"No, that's not the root cause. I think the root cause is poverty here in Lewiston. Lewiston is very poor and is economically not in a good state," she said when asked if there was a direct connection to the Somali community. "I think what's happening here is happening everywhere. It's happening in Atlanta. I have lived in Miami and Ohio and Kentucky and Minnesota and have seen what is happening in those states also happening here in Lewiston. It's nothing new."

Lewiston has also been an epicenter in recent years for fraud scandals involving Maine's joint federal and state Medicaid program.

Saciid emphasized that "fraud is happening everywhere in the United States and with every skin color, with every class. It's not tied particularly to one people."

The Somali influx to Lewiston began a quarter century ago, when refugees and secondary migrants started relocating to the former mill city along the Androscoggin River in search of safe neighborhoods and affordable housing.

DEMOCRACY ’26: STAY UP TO DATE WITH THE FOX NEWS ELECTION HUB

Lisbon Street in downtown Lewiston, Maine. (Paul Steinhauser/Fox News)

Then-Mayor Larry Raymond drew national attention in 2002 after asking Somali leaders to discourage additional migration to Lewiston, arguing the rapid influx was straining city resources.

Fast-forward to present day and Lewiston has one of the highest per capita Muslim populations in the country, most of it Somali along with refugees from other African nations.

Fetherston argued that "history has proven him [Raymond] to be correct that... that it was too much too fast because a lot has changed in Lewiston. And things are not working out in Lewiston."

LaChapelle noted, "I'm a French Canadian, so my ancestors came here.... We need legal immigration in America. We need to grow."

But he added, "We just have to do it logically and legally and in. When my ancestors got here, there wasn't a free... gravy train all the way down. Now we're supporting everybody. We have for 30 years, we still have some people that are still on the welfare system 30 years later. That has to change."

Paul Steinhauser covers the national campaign trail from coast to coast for Fox News

title: France prepares for day of protest a week after nationwide riots
excerpt:
Some public buildings and businesses across France have been boarded up ahead of Saturday's protests

France is on high alert ahead of a new day of nationwide protests on Saturday, a week after the co...
body_text:
Some public buildings and businesses across France have been boarded up ahead of Saturday's protests

France is on high alert ahead of a new day of nationwide protests on Saturday, a week after the country saw some of its worst unrest in decades.

Sweeping restrictions have been imposed on demonstrations across France but hundreds of thousands of protesters are still expected to gather in Paris and elsewhere for a second round of protests organised by students, trade unions and wider anti-government groups.

The interior ministry has said it will deploy 70,000 police officers, ramping up the security presence in French cities, after the government was accused by opposition parties of failing to foresee the scale of the unrest on 17 October.

"We will not let anything go unchallenged," said Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez.

"We will be uncompromising with the vandals, with the looters, and all those who commit acts of violence," he added, explaining that separate from the planned protests, numerous calls for violence had been seen on social media from the "far left and radical extreme left".

Hundreds of people have been jailed for vandalism, arson and looting after fast-track court hearings in recent days.

President Emmanuel Macron met high-school students' representatives on Friday ahead of Saturday's protests, and although they said he had made clear commitments to them, they said students should "continue to mobilise".

Leaders of student groups spoke to the media after holding talks with Macron on Friday

Macron decreed earlier this week that only demonstrations organised by a recognised trade unions would be permitted to take place on Saturday, and several key cities including Lyon, Nice and Montpellier have gone further by announcing blanket bans on gatherings.

Official announcements appear to have done little to deter organisers, with hundreds of large and small demonstrations planned across France.

After a week in which some cities have lived under partial curfews - including areas of the capital - there is an inconsistent picture across France's cities as to what level of protest will be permitted by authorities.

While some mayors have pressed ahead with broad bans, others have agreed to allow demonstrations registered with authorities - for example, in Marseille, a previous order barring all protests was swiftly reversed to allow a trade union-organised march to go ahead.

In Paris, a march organised by the student trade union and supported by labour groups has been ordered to stick to a route which does not go through the city centre - though preparations for unrest in some of the city's most recognisable areas are under way regardless.

The Louvre, Orsay and Picasso museums will all be closed on Saturday, a scheduled home match for football team PSG has been moved to Monday, and some businesses have boarded up their windows in anticipation of further looting.

Largely peaceful demonstrations in Paris organised by students and unions devolved into rioting and looting as last Saturday wore on

In a sign of how a student-led protest movement expanded to become a wider anti-government outpouring, protesters associated with a revived gilet jaunes (yellow-vest) movement could be out in force across France on Saturday.

The protest movement, which has attracted support from left and right, led huge disruptive demonstrations during Macron's first term in office.

A website associated with the group listed more than 500 planned demonstrations and some 200 other actions on Saturday, and demanded that Macron resign.

In its online call for action, the group said "we refuse to add our voices to the chorus of outrage" over the violence on 17 October and accused police of attacking protesters.

France is still reeling from last week's unrest, which saw police vastly outnumbered by protesters and rioters, shops looted and buildings torched - perhaps most emblematically, the ornate 19th-Century town hall in Limoges.

On Friday, Justice Minister Gérald Darmanin said 232 people had been imprisoned for their role in the 17 October riots, and more than 1,100 had appeared in court. Around 260 of those cases involves "charges of organised gang activity", he added.

Darmanin has ordered prosecutors to seek punitive measures against people convicted of looting or attacking police officers, including banning them from taking part in demonstrations, removing their right to vote and barring them from accessing social media.

A yellow vest, the symbol of the gilets jaunes movements, was draped over the Monument a la Republique in Paris during last weekend's protests

Disillusionment is high among the French public, who have seen cost-of-living pressures increase, and who are faced with increasingly dire warnings that any future government will likely have to make deep spending cuts in order to finance spiralling levels of debt.

On top of that, the recent unrest has played out against the backdrop of a polarised political landscape and with France preparing for what could be the most divisive and unpredictable election period in a generation.

Macron will leave office next spring and polls suggest a candidate from his centrist movement could fail to make it through to a run-off vote in May between the top two contenders.

That would likely leave French voters to choose between the hard-right National Rally and radical-left La France Insoumise (France Unbowed).

Leading figures from both parties have levelled the blame for the disorder at Macron and his ministers, sensing fertile ground among the French public after a period in which his centrist party has struggled to form functioning governments and pass legislation.

Jean-Luc Mélenchon, the leader and presidential candidate of La France Insoumise, has criticised what he has framed as heavy-handed policing of demonstrations and has accused Macron of "destroying the republican state" by imposing restrictions.

He has called on his supporters to join protests on Saturday as he did the previous week, before condemning the rioting which followed.

A two-day National Rally conference in Orléans, around 120 km (75 miles) to the south of Paris, could prove to be a flashpoint on Saturday.

Left-wing groups are expected to descend on the small city, where thousands of members of the hard-right party are set to gather to hear its leader Marine Le Pen speak.

This week, the city's mayor warned the numbers expected in Orléans were "unprecedented", and said thousands of police would be deployed to manage any clashes, adding that public transport would be suspended.

Opinion polls suggest Le Pen could have her strongest chance yet of becoming president as she runs for a fourth time, despite a court finding her guilty of embezzling EU funds earlier this year. She has denied committing any offence and is appealing the verdict.

title: Brewers rally past chaotic late-game replay, premature celebrations to win first World Series game in 44 years
excerpt:
Milwaukee Brewers manager Pat Murphy joins Colin Cowherd to discuss his matchup with the Tampa Bay Rays in the World Series, and how the Brewers can win their first ever World Series.

For the first t...
body_text:
Milwaukee Brewers manager Pat Murphy joins Colin Cowherd to discuss his matchup with the Tampa Bay Rays in the World Series, and how the Brewers can win their first ever World Series.

For the first time since 1982, the Milwaukee Brewers have won a World Series game.

The Brew Crew took Game 1 of the Fall Classic over the Tampa Bay Rays in a sweaty 3-2 ballgame.

This page may contain affiliate links to legal sports betting partners. If you sign up or place a wager, FOX News may be compensated. This content was created by a team that works independently from the FOX newsroom.

Down two, the Rays loaded the bases with one out in the ninth, but Liam Hicks grounded into what initially was ruled a game-ending double play. However, replay showed shortstop Cooper Pratt came off second base, instead making it a 3-2 game with runners on second and third and two outs.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

The Brewers had already ignited their fireworks, creating a chaotic, fog-filled scene, before Johnny DeLuca came to the plate and struck out to end the game.

2026 WORLD SERIES: HOW TO WATCH BREWERS AND RAYS AFTER SMALL BALL CARRIES THEM TO FALL CLASSIC

The city of Milwaukee waited 46 years to see its team in the Fall Classic, and this year's Brewers wanted to stop wasting time. An RBI triple by Christian Yelich, followed by a William Contreras single, put the Brewers up 2-0 in the first inning. However, that was all they'd get for a while, as Nick Martinez settled down to get through five innings of work.

The Milwaukee pitching, though, was just as good. Soon-to-be Cy Young Award winner Jacob Misiorowski held the Rays to just one run in his five innings, but certainly not without the help of some Rays baserunning blunders.

Jacob Misiorowski of the Milwaukee Brewers pitches during Game 1 of the 2026 World Series against the Tampa Bay Rays at American Family Field on Friday, Oct. 23, in Milwaukee, Wisconsin. (MLB Photos via Getty Images)

Tampa Bay had runners on first and second with one out in the first, but Junior Caminero lined out, and Jonathan Aranda was doubled off at second to end the threat. In the fifth, Victor Mesa Jr. was caught stealing at third for the final out of the inning, a big baseball no-no.

The Brewers matched that mistake with one of their own almost immediately, as nine-hitter David Hamilton made the first out at third in the bottom half of the frame trying to stretch a double into a triple.

But they got a huge insurance run after some more typical Brewers small ball. In the seventh, Hamilton got a productive second out to get a runner into scoring position, and Jackson Chourio drove him in with an opposite-field, ground-ball single to make it 3-1. No team in the league went oppo and hit grounders at a higher rate than the Brewers in the regular season.

Cooper Pratt and Christian Yelich of the Milwaukee Brewers celebrate after defeating the Tampa Bay Rays in Game 1 of the 2026 World Series at American Family Field on Oct. 23, 2026, in Milwaukee, Wisconsin. (Getty Images)

Milwaukee will have Logan Henderson on the bump on Saturday night, while Drew Rasmussen will toe the slab for Tampa Bay.

title: Arrest made after fire at Hitler's Eagle's Nest retreat
excerpt:
The Eagle's Nest was still on fire early on Saturday

Police in the south German state of Bavaria have detained a suspect during a fire at Adolf Hitler's Alpine mountain retreat, the Kehlsteinhaus, al...
body_text:
The Eagle's Nest was still on fire early on Saturday

Police in the south German state of Bavaria have detained a suspect during a fire at Adolf Hitler's Alpine mountain retreat, the Kehlsteinhaus, also known as the Eagle's Nest.

Dispatchers in Traunstein received a fire alarm from the building at 21:15 (19:15 GMT) on Friday, and firefighters found it engulfed in flames.

Difficult terrain was hindering efforts to extinguish the blaze and it was still burning early on Saturday, police said, with some 200 emergency personnel deployed. There were no reports of injuries.

The Nazi dictator used the retreat, which lies above the town of Berchtesgaden, as a part-time seat of government and met commanders there to plan the invasion of the USSR in 1941.

A criminal investigation is under way to determine whether the suspect is connected to the fire.

Hitler also used the area as a backdrop for propaganda films portraying him as a lover of animals and nature.

Completed by the Nazis in 1938, the Eagle's Nest escaped destruction after their defeat in 1945.

Since then, it has become a popular tourist destination and houses a mountain inn.

According to its official website, external, it is "also a cautionary reminder of the abysses of the inhumane Nazi dictatorship".

During World War Two, Hitler and his followers were responsible for the deaths of tens of millions of people, including the mass murder of European Jews.

title: Israel raids towns, detains dozens of Palestinians in occupied West Bank
excerpt:
Israel imposes full closure of occupied West Bank after Hebron shooting kills two soldiers

Israeli forces have raided towns, detaining dozens of Palestinians, hours after Prime Minister Benjamin Neta...
body_text:
Israel imposes full closure of occupied West Bank after Hebron shooting kills two soldiers

Israeli forces have raided towns, detaining dozens of Palestinians, hours after Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu announced ordering a full lockdown of the occupied West Bank following an attack in the city of Hebron that killed two Israeli soldiers.

Israeli forces raided at least 15 towns in the northern West Bank, detaining dozens of Palestinians, Al Jazeera correspondents reported on Saturday.

The military raids targeted several northern cities and towns, including Nablus, Jenin, Tubas and Qalqilya.

In Nablus, Israeli forces carried out arrests and raided Palestinian homes in the villages of Jalud and Qaryut. Arrests were also reported in Arrabeh and Burqin, near Jenin, while Israeli forces entered Tubas and the nearby town of Aqqaba.

In the southern occupied West Bank, Israeli bulldozers demolished a three-storey building in Hebron, with families given five minutes to collect their belongings. Israeli forces also ordered hundreds of Palestinian families to forcibly evacuate their homes in the Ein Deir Bahha area of Hebron and its surroundings.

Israeli troops also surrounded the home of one of the suspects in the shooting attack that killed two Israeli soldiers in Hebron, while carrying out raids in the city’s al-Jalda neighbourhood.

The Israeli army said late on Friday that its forces began an operation in Hebron that would last “for several days”, in addition to operations by other forces in “dozens” of areas across the West Bank.

Further east, Israeli forces entered Jericho and the nearby Aqabat Jabr refugee camp.

With the lockdown, nearly 1,000 checkpoints and gates across the West Bank will be closed, affecting millions of Palestinians.

Netanyahu gave the order on Friday, shortly after the Israeli military said it had killed two Palestinian gunmen who attacked a reserve battalion near the Israeli settlement of Telem, killing two soldiers.

Israel’s ambulance service reported that at least three Israeli soldiers were injured in addition to the two who died.

All Israeli settlements, including Telem, are illegal under international law.

The attack and clampdown came amid heightened tensions across the Palestinian territory as Israeli settlers and soldiers engage in violent pogroms. Attacks on olive harvesters have been rife as aggression has been on the rise before the coming Israeli elections on Tuesday.

Far-right National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir responded to the killing of the Israeli soldiers by calling for Israel to take full control of the West Bank, in which the Israeli government is encouraging the construction of numerous settlements.

Mustafa Barghouti, secretary-general of the Palestinian National Initiative political party, said incitement from far-right Israeli ministers is making the situation worse.

The closure turns every city and village into “a small prison”, with checkpoints and gates blocking healthcare, the economy and education, he told Al Jazeera. He warned that collective punishment “will lead to explosions”.

title: Pentagon designates Confucius Institutes a national security threat
excerpt:
The United States Department of Defense has designated Confucius Institutes, Chinese-funded cultural centres on university campuses, as a threat to US national security.

US Defense Secretary Pete Heg...
body_text:
The United States Department of Defense has designated Confucius Institutes, Chinese-funded cultural centres on university campuses, as a threat to US national security.

US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth announced the move on Friday in a video posted on social media, saying the Pentagon added the organisations to its list of institutions that threaten national security.

Washington has long accused the centres of serving as Chinese propaganda tools and has taken steps to crack down on them.

Hegseth said Confucius Institutes had operated in disguise after being restricted by Congress, calling them “sleeper organisations”.

“It turns out that 80 new propaganda cells across 30 universities had popped up using different names and different charters, but with the same mission: to steal intellectual property and to infiltrate the minds of American students,” he said.

In the video, Hegseth said that Chinese government-backed cultural programmes had infiltrated universities and reappeared in new guises despite congressional restrictions.

Over the past two months, the Pentagon has “systematically dismantled every single one of these organisations”, he said.

The Chinese embassy in Washington did not respond to Reuters’ request for comment.

title: Democrat James Talarico targets Elon Musk at rally: ‘Texas is not for sale’
excerpt:
The Senate candidate denounced opponent Ken Paxton, calling out corruption allegations and support from Musk

James Talarico, the Democratic candidate for the US Senate in Texas, has taken aim at Elon...
body_text:
The Senate candidate denounced opponent Ken Paxton, calling out corruption allegations and support from Musk

James Talarico, the Democratic candidate for the US Senate in Texas, has taken aim at Elon Musk, warning that the tech mogul is trying to buy political influence and declaring: “Texas is not for sale.”

Talarico held a campaign rally on Friday at the University of Texas at Austin, packing an auditorium at his alma mater with hundreds of students and other supporters, who cheered, whooped and waved campaign signs.

The Presbyterian seminarian’s insurgent run against Texas attorney general Ken Paxton – a staunch ally of Donald Trump – has become one of the most closely watched races in next month’s midterm elections to decide control of Congress. Democrats are seeking their first statewide win since 1994.

Talarico, 37, struck his usual upbeat message on Friday but also pulled no punches in denouncing Paxton – who was impeached by his own party over corruption accusations and had a very public divorce – as the most corrupt politician in the state’s history.

“I have a legislative record; Ken Paxton has a criminal record,” said Talarico, a state representative, wearing a dark blue jacket, white open collar shirt and blue jeans. “This election is about whether you want a senator who puts money in your pocket or who puts money in their own. This election is about whether you want a senator who is for Texas or for himself. This election is about whether you want senator who serves you or serves their billionaire mega donors.”

Paxton, he continued, has the ultimate mega donor. “Elon Musk is trying to buy the Senate seat. We just found out that the richest man in the world is almost single-handedly bankrolling this effort to install Ken Paxton in the US Senate and stop the movement that we are building in our state.

“In all likelihood, if you’ve seen an attack ad on your screens, that was Elon. If you’ve gotten lies in your mailbox, that was Elon. If you received a text message saying scary things about me with scary black and white photos, that was Elon too.”

Speaking against the backdrop of a giant Texan state flag and 40 young supporters holding “Talarico” signs, the Democrat said that, where his movement is funded by 1.3 million individuals, Paxton is funded by “one dude”.

In a state where data centres have become an incendiary issue, Talarico said: “Elon Musk wants our land. He wants our water. He wants our tax dollars. He wants his very own personal United States senator. He is trying to buy Texas. But on November 3rd, we are going to deliver a crystal clear message to the world’s first trillionaire: Texas is not for sale.”

Musk, who lives in Texas and has relocated SpaceX, Tesla, X and other businesses there, has contributed $158m to the Senate Leadership Fund, which in turn transferred the same amount to Texas PAC, a Republican super PAC supporting Paxton, according to federal filings.

Talarico has offset the outside-spending disadvantage with grassroots fundraising. His campaign says it raised $64m from July through September, more than triple Paxton’s total, with 97% of donations under $100 each.

Talarico told the crowd that super PACs and “billionaire mega-donors” are spending $200m in the most expensive Senate race in US history to defeat his grassroots campaign. “Big money is powerful, but it is nothing compared to people power,” he insisted, invoking biblical imagery comparing his supporters to “the slingshot” that David used to defeat Goliath

Talarico’s rally capped a turbulent month in what has emerged as America’s biggest battleground state. Talarico fell ill with the flu at the end of September and was not seen in public for nine days.

At a rally in San Antonio, Texas, Donald Trump claimed without evidence that “Tala-freako”, as he nicknames the Democrat, is vegan and had fallen ill because he tried eating meat for political purposes. That quickly metastasised into an online rumour that Talarico had checked into a mental health facility in Ohio. It was comprehensively debunked.

Meanwhile the Wall Street Journal published a video showing Paxton celebrating New Year’s Eve in Dubai with two US fugitives, Anosh Ahmed and Sameer Suhail, who were indicted in Illinois on healthcare-fraud charges. Ahmed donated $190,000 to Paxton, including $25,000 after his indictment.

Back on the campaign trail, Talarico set out on a “Clear Eyes, Full Hearts” tour of the state. He held a CNN town hall with sceptical Republicans and independent voters.

Paxton, meanwhile, launched an 18-day bus tour of Texas. His message was aimed at conservative voters with the slogan “Come and Take It”, an attack on what he called the far left. Republicans sought to tie Talarico with positions on transgender issues that have proved potent in conservative campaigning.

The campaign entered its final stretch with the Democrat holding a narrow polling advantage. The RealClearPolitics average for polls conducted from 6 to 19 October put Talarico ahead by 1.8 percentage points. An Emerson College Polling/ Nexstar Media survey released on Thursday found that 48% of voters support Talarico while 46% favour Paxton.

Early voting began on 19 October, giving both campaigns an immediate test of their ability to mobilise supporters. Talarico voted earlier on Friday.

Supporters at Friday’s rally expressed growing frustration with incumbent Republican officials such as Paxton along with optimism that Talarico’s message could signal a new political era for the Lone Star State.

Alina Anil, a 19-year-old student at the University of Texas, who had already cast her ballot, said she attended the event to see Talarico in person and demonstrate her support.

“We’ve been red for a long time and nothing has really come out of it,” Anil said. “As a student, I don’t think there’s been a lot of changes in Texas. We need some change and James Talarico seems promising. He was a teacher before, so I have faith in that and I have faith in him.”

Dakota Walker, 31, a pediatric physical therapist, arrived wearing a custom T-shirt reading “Talafrico: Talarico refreshing for Texas”, in the style of the Topo-Chico brand of sparkling mineral water.

“What’s not to like about him, what’s not to love about him, honestly?” Walker said. “He has morals, he has values, he’s an overall good human being and I think we need a drastic change.

“I have to spend so much of my time fighting for my kids, making sure that they get what they need when a family with a child with a disability or different abilities shouldn’t have to do that. I know we need healthcare reform and he is very big on that.”

Texas Democrats have had their hopes dashed before, notably when former congressman Beto O’Rourke lost a race to Republican Sen. Ted Cruz in 2018 by less than 3 percentage points.

Asked what a Democratic statewide victory would mean, Walker replied: “Oh man, I’ll probably cry, honestly. We need a lot of change and I feel like it’s time for a new era.”

Patrick Pearson, 46, an assistive technology professional, said he wanted to back Talarico because of his commitment to policy change. “From everything I’ve read about him and heard, I think he sounds really awesome,” Pearson said. “He’s actually trying to make a change and has a very positive message.”

title: Typhoon Champi kills one and injures more than 500 in Taiwan as it heads to China
excerpt:
Super typhoon weakening but large parts of Taiwan, including Taipei, still mostly closed and flights cancelled

Typhoon Champi swept past Taiwan on Saturday killing one person, injuring more than 500,...
body_text:
Super typhoon weakening but large parts of Taiwan, including Taipei, still mostly closed and flights cancelled

Typhoon Champi swept past Taiwan on Saturday killing one person, injuring more than 500, and uprooting trees and severing power as it weakened and ⁠headed north toward ⁠the ​Chinese coast.

Earlier classified as a super typhoon and one of the strongest storms in the ⁠Pacific this year, Champi was still packing gusts of about 126km per hour (78 miles per hour) near its ⁠centre, according to Taiwan’s Central Weather Administration (CWA).

The storm was about ​150km (93 miles) east ‌of Taiwan, the CWA ‌said, having glanced off the island’s northeast coast in the early ‌hours of Saturday.

Champi’s forecast track shows it turning north toward the Chinese coast before eventually moving into southern Japan.

Taiwan’s fire department said one man had been killed, swept by waves from the ‌island of Liuqiu. Another 527 people were injured during heavy wind and torrential rain.

Taipower said more than 167,000 homes had lost electricity, but most had now been reconnected.

Large parts of northern and central Taiwan, including Taipei, declared a second ​day of ‌office and ​school closures ​on Saturday, and some flights were still being cancelled.

Taiwan is generally well prepared for typhoons, which keeps casualties low. Although more common in summer, the storms can strike also in autumn.

title: California officials ordered by DoJ to set aside ‘likely’ noncitizen ballots
excerpt:
Letters from federal prosecutors represent latest escalation as Trump continues to make claims of voter fraud

Federal prosecutors sent letters to county registrars across California on Friday demandi...
body_text:
Letters from federal prosecutors represent latest escalation as Trump continues to make claims of voter fraud

Federal prosecutors sent letters to county registrars across California on Friday demanding that local officials set aside and verify ballots that the Department of Justice said may belong to noncitizens, according to the Los Angeles county registrar and a letter obtained by the Associated Press.

The letters are the latest escalation in a legal battle between California and Donald Trump’s Department of Justice, which has recently focused on the state in its efforts to root out noncitizen voting ahead of the midterm elections.

Data shows illegal voting by people who are not US citizens is incredibly rare, difficult to prove and has not been shown to change the outcome of races.

Earlier this month, the federal government targeted Los Angeles county and the California secretary of state’s office in a lawsuit that aimed to block them from counting the votes of roughly 20,000 people who are “likely” noncitizen voters. A hearing on the case is scheduled for Tuesday.

The Trump administration asked the ninth circuit court of appeals to rule on the lawsuit barring a decision from the district judge assigned to the case. They set a deadline for Saturday.

Now, according to the LA county registrar’s office, at least 18 counties across the state have received similar letters.

They have been given a 48-hour deadline to provide identifying information corresponding with ballots that the federal government believes were sent to noncitizens illegally registered to vote. The letter requests that county officials also sequester any ballots where citizenship cannot be verified.

“Any election official who knowingly processes the ballot of a noncitizen is opening themselves to legal jeopardy,” said first assistant US attorney Bill Essayli.

The justice department is asking counties to send information about the voters it suspects are noncitizens including social security numbers, ID information, a copy of their registration and more.

That information can help the government and state quickly assess each person suspected of illegally registering to vote, said the letter sent to San Bernardino County voting officials. The letter says the government’s list of suspected noncitizen voters includes 1,133 people from the inland southern California county.

California’s secretary of state and the Los Angeles county registrar have opposed the federal government’s demands. In legal filings, lawyers for California say the request threatens to delay the certification of the vote and undermine the legitimacy of the November midterms. They have also argued that the federal government’s data is unreliable and that their demands risk disenfranchisement of citizens.

Voting is under way in California, with the state’s more than 23 million registered voters receiving ballots in the mail earlier this month. The state said in legal filings that over 330,000 mail-in ballots have already been counted.

The letters on Friday came on the heels of statewide sweep by federal authorities earlier in the week, where 28 people from the list of 20,000 were charged with illegally registering to vote. Some were also charged with illegally voting and lying on naturalization paperwork. Those charges could lead to years in prison.

title: Seven killed and 40 injured after gunmen open fire at church funeral in Jordan
excerpt:
Footage broadcast on state television showed two gunmen who appear to be holding pistols approaching the church and firing shots

Gunmen opened fire during a funeral at a church in Jordan on Friday, k...
body_text:
Footage broadcast on state television showed two gunmen who appear to be holding pistols approaching the church and firing shots

Gunmen opened fire during a funeral at a church in Jordan on Friday, killing seven people and wounding 40 others, authorities said.

The shooting took place at a Greek Orthodox church in Karak, about 180km (110 miles) south of the capital, Amman.

Footage broadcast on Jordanian state television showed two gunmen who appear to be holding pistols approaching the church and firing shots. A third man who appears to be holding a semiautomatic rifle then approaches and opens fire, and all three then run toward the church.

Video footage taken by witnesses shows broken glass and pools of blood on the floor of the church.

Dorgham Halasa, who was among the mourners inside the church, said intense gunfire erupted 15 minutes after the funeral had started, and then people started running. “It was a weird situation, and heavy gunfire,” Halasa said.

He did not see the gunmen, but said other people reported seeing four of them. The Associated Press could not independently verify the number of assailants, and Jordan’s security services did not immediately release details.

A government statement said that the attack was “carried out by unknown assailants,” but didn’t say whether any gunmen were captured or killed. It said that “investigations are under way at full speed”.

Jordan declared three days of national mourning, according to the kingdom’s Petra news agency.

Karak is home to a minority Christian population.

In 2016, gunmen ambushed police in a series of attacks in Karak, including at a Crusader castle popular with tourists, killing 10 people, including seven officers, and wounding dozens. Jordanian security forces killed those gunmen after a long standoff.

Jordan’s health minister Ibrahim al-Budour said two of those wounded are in critical condition.

King Abdullah II said on X that Jordan “will confront the terrorist act that targeted Karak with the harshest penalties” and offered his “deepest condolences to the families of the martyrs, and our wishes for recovery to the wounded”.

Jordan’s prime minister Jafar Hassan said during a security meeting in Karak on Friday evening that the attack was a result of terrorist ideology and blind extremism. He said the assailants will be punished and legal measures taken against those who seek to introduce extremism.

Condemnation of the slayings came from around the region, including from Lebanon, Syria, Egypt and Oman.

Ahmed al-Tayeb in Cairo, the grand imam of Al-Azhar, the Sunni Muslim world’s foremost religious institution, offered his condolences to the families of victims in Friday’s shooting, calling it a “heinous terrorist attack.”

Iraqi foreign minister Fuad Hussein called his Jordanian counterpart and “affirmed Iraq’s solidarity with Jordan in the face of terrorism”, Hussein’s office said in a statement.

UN Secretary-General António Guterres condemned the attack during a funeral as “especially heinous,” spokesperson Stephane Dujarric said. “The secretary-general also calls for all those responsible to be found and to be held to account.”

title: Australian MP's condition improves after alleged car attack
excerpt:
Helen Haines had both her legs amputated after what authorities say was a deliberate attack

The condition of Helen Haines, the Australian MP hit by a car five days ago in north-east Victoria, has imp...
body_text:
Helen Haines had both her legs amputated after what authorities say was a deliberate attack

The condition of Helen Haines, the Australian MP hit by a car five days ago in north-east Victoria, has improved from critical to serious but stable.

The independent MP, 65, had both her legs amputated after what authorities say was a deliberate attack outside her electorate office in Wangaratta, north-east of Melbourne, on Monday.

In the latest update on Saturday morning, the Alfred Hospital in Melbourne said Haines was in a serious but stable condition, the first improvement since she was airlifted there.

Her alleged attacker, 43-year-old Brendan Nugent, was arrested shortly after the incident and has since appeared in court on three charges.

The politician's husband, Phil Haines, said on Wednesday that the "horrendous incident" had caused his wife significant injuries but "her heart and her mind" were "in good shape".

Shock and disbelief: How the attack on an Australian MP unfolded in a small rural town

Nugent, who was arrested moments after he allegedly drove his Toyota LandCruiser into the MP, appeared in court to face three charges: dangerous driving causing serious injury, intentionally causing serious injury, and causing harm to a Commonwealth public official.

Police said more charges might be laid, including attempted murder.

His lawyer said his client had "mental health concerns" but did not give any further detail.

Victoria Police has said its investigation, with support from the Australian Federal Police, remains ongoing and a motive is yet to be established.

Investigators are looking into whether drug use or medication played a part in the incident.

Nugent's family has said they were long-time friends with Haines.

Shortly after the alleged attack, Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese told ABC television that there had been a "rise in temperature" and "too much shouting, not enough discourse" in Australia.

Haines, known for stances such as supporting stronger climate action, entered parliament in 2019 after working as a nurse and midwife.

title: Michigan Senate rivals clash over Muslim Brotherhood allegations as Rogers doubles down on El-Sayed
excerpt: Michigan Democrat Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed accused Republican rival Mike Rogers of questioning his loyalty to the United States during a heated Fox News interview Friday, while Rogers doubled d...
body_text:
Michigan Democrat Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed accused Republican rival Mike Rogers of questioning his loyalty to the United States during a heated Fox News interview Friday, while Rogers doubled down on allegations that his opponent has embraced the ideology of the Muslim Brotherhood.

The candidates both spoke separately with Fox News chief political anchor Bret Baier on "Special Report" in Detroit, 11 days before the Nov. 3 election.

Baier pressed El-Sayed about a 2012 statement involving former Egyptian President Mohamed Morsi, who was affiliated with the Muslim Brotherhood.

EL-SAYED, ROGERS CLASH OVER MUSLIM BROTHERHOOD, TRUMP AND GUNS: 5 FIERY DEBATE MOMENTS

Abdul El-Sayed got into a fiery exchange on "Special Report" Friday over a question regarding alleged ties to the Muslim Brotherhood. (Fox News)

"No, no, no, let me just stop there," El-Sayed interrupted. "You are asking this question to raise a question about whether or not I have dual loyalties."

Baier explained he was asking about allegations raised by Rogers' campaign.

"I will be loyal to the Constitution of the United States," El-Sayed said.

"Don't be Rogers' campaign," he continued.

ABDUL EL-SAYED GROWS AGITATED WITH REPORTER AFTER BEING PRESSED ON FAMILY'S ALLEGED MUSLIM BROTHERHOOD TIES

Abdul El-Sayed, the Michigan Democrat nominee for U.S. Senate, left, appears with Republican Senate nominee Mike Rogers during a televised debate at WOOD-TV, Oct. 8, in Grand Rapids, Mich. (AP Photo/Paul Sancya, Pool)

El-Sayed accused Rogers of making his Muslim faith a campaign issue, calling the suggestion "sad" and "beneath him."

EL-SAYED'S PAST MUSLIM BROTHERHOOD COMMENTS RAISE RED FLAGS AS HE EYES POWERFUL ROLE

El-Sayed says he has never belonged to the Muslim Brotherhood. (Monica Morgan/Getty Images, File)

The controversy centers partly on a 2012 letter that The Washington Free Beacon reported El-Sayed signed supporting decisions by then-Egyptian President Mohamed Morsi, including calls to purge Egypt's police and media.

El-Sayed has also faced scrutiny over social media posts from his half-sister describing their mother's alleged involvement in Muslim Brotherhood activism in the 1970s. He has denied personal or family ties to the organization and said he was raised by his father and stepmother.

In an Oct. 17 Fox News interview, El-Sayed acknowledged that his sister-in-law was a plaintiff in a lawsuit challenging her alleged placement on a terrorist watchlist but insisted she had done nothing wrong. The FBI declined to confirm or deny her watchlist status. The lawsuit does not establish wrongdoing.

Rogers rejected El-Sayed's characterization in his own interview.

ROGERS WARNS MICHIGAN VOTERS AGAINST EL-SAYED’S ‘EXTREME’ AGENDA AHEAD OF ELECTION

Republican candidate Mike Rogers became candid in an interview on "Special Report" regarding his views on the Iran War. (Fox News)

"I wore the uniform of the United States. Many in my family, including our son, wore the uniform of the United States so he can pray any way he wants," Rogers said. "It is not how he prays, it's how he thinks."

Rogers accused El-Sayed of embracing the organization's ideology and portraying himself as a victim.

"He has adopted the ideology of the Muslim Brotherhood," Rogers alleged.

Baier noted that El-Sayed had denied ever belonging to the organization and pledged allegiance to the Constitution.

"Does he disavow? Does he really say it?" Rogers responded.

El-Sayed had explicitly disavowed the organization at an Oct. 17 town hall, answering, "Sure. Yeah, absolutely" when asked.

The candidates also differed over the war with Iran, which El-Sayed blamed for rising gasoline and grocery prices.

"We need a war powers resolution to end the capacity for this president to wage an illegal, unjustifiable war," El-Sayed said.

Rogers defended the original rationale for military action but said he has urged President Donald Trump to end the conflict.

"I've called for him to wrap it up. That's the right thing to do," Rogers said.

Turning to Michigan's economy, Rogers said the state has lost 27,000 manufacturing jobs and faces some of the nation's highest auto insurance costs. He also raised concerns about education, claiming roughly two-thirds of fourth graders cannot read at grade level.

Former U.S. Rep. Mike Rogers, the GOP Michigan U.S. Senate candidate, shakes hands with President Donald Trump during a campaign stop at the General Motors Proving Ground testing site in Milford, Mich., July 27. (Sarah Rice/Bloomberg via Getty Images, File)

Rogers defended Trump's influence in Michigan, pointing to his support among voters and crediting his trade policies with encouraging General Motors to bring Silverado pickup truck production back to the state.

But the Republican acknowledged a disagreement with Trump over trade with Canada.

"I've come out and said we shouldn't be doing the Canadian tariffs the way we are doing them," Rogers said.

Baier also pressed El-Sayed over Medicare-for-all, and whether middle-class taxes would rise.

"I'm fine with people keeping their private insurance if that's what they want, but I want guaranteed public insurance for everybody," El-Sayed said.

Rogers disputed El-Sayed's position, arguing that Medicare-for-all would eliminate private insurance and raise costs for Michigan families.

El-Sayed touted upcoming campaign appearances with former President Barack Obama and Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., while questioning whether Trump would help Rogers in Michigan.

With both Trump and Obama expected to campaign in Michigan over the weekend, the candidates are turning to their parties' most recognizable figures as they make their final pitches to voters ahead of Election Day.Fox News Digital's Leo Briceno contributed to this reporting.

Jasmine Baehr is a breaking news writer for Fox News Digital, where she covers politics, the military, legal debates surrounding life and family policy, as well as faith and culture.
