title: Minister says 32 government services offline due to PHP code flaw – UK politics live
excerpt:
Organisations around the world scrambling to fix a critical security flaw in the programming language PHP used by the majority of websites

Some 32 government services are offline and four are partial...
body_text:
Organisations around the world scrambling to fix a critical security flaw in the programming language PHP used by the majority of websites

Some 32 government services are offline and four are partially unavailable while work is carried out to address potential cybersecurity issues, a minister has said.

As the Press Association reports, organisations around the world have been scrambling to fix a critical security flaw in the programming language PHP used by the majority of websites.

Downing Street on Thursday said no large UK public-facing critical services have been affected, but some “limited” government websites have gone dark while issues are resolved. National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) experts are working with OpenAI, whose technology was used to discover the vulnerabilities, and partners around the globe to address potential problems, a No 10 spokesperson said.

In the House of Lords, Liz Lloyd, the tech minister, said:

double quotation markThe information I have is that 32 government services are unavailable and four are partially unavailable.

Lloyd said that “has largely resulted from precautionary measures taken to protect systems while security updates and mitigations are applied”.

double quotation markWork has already taken place across government to identify and fix potential exposures to our systems, and our experts are continuing to work closely with both OpenAI and international partners on this issue.

Here is our story about the global impact of the problems identified in the PHP programming language. It’s by Robert Booth and Aisha Down.

Yesterday Steve Witkoff, the property developer appointed by Donald Trump as his lead foreign policy envoy, described Vladimir Putin as a “humanitarian”. Andrew Roth has more about that here, in a piece pointing out that this is an extraordinary lie.

Douglas Alexander, the Scottish secretary, was giving interviews this morning. Asked if he agreed with Witkoff’s description on LBC, he was reassuringly blunt. He replied:

We see him as somebody who illegally invaded Ukraine at the start of this conflict, who has been responsible for conduct by his government that included attempted assassinations on UK soil.

So we simply do not recognise the description of Vladimir Putin as a humanitarian.

In contrast, we are crystal clear that we stand foursquare behind Volodymyr Zelensky and the people of Ukraine in their battle for freedom.

At the No 10 lobby briefing, a No 10 spokesperson also argued that Witkoff had got it wrong. Asked about Witkoff’s comment, the spokesperson said:

double quotation markWe do not recognise that characterisation … Putin has killed thousands of people, Ukrainians and his own. He’s starving children and the elderly of heat and warmth and destroying critical national infrastructure.

The Conservative party seems to have missed the bit in the ONS report on the crime figures where it said “crime against individuals and households has generally decreased over the last 10 years”. (See 9.54am.) Chris Philp, the shadow home secretary, has issued a statement saying:

double quotation markCrime is spiralling out of control under Labour. Record numbers of sexual offences, knife crime and shop theft show what happens when criminals know they can get away with it. This is a direct consequence of Labour cutting police numbers by 2,000 and letting thousands of prisoners out of jail early.

The Tories justify this claim by looking at the ONS report and picking out all the worst bits (a technique not unfamiliar in the world of journalism). Their briefing highlights four figures in particular. Here is an extract.

double quotation markSexual offences have reached the highest level on record under Labour, with the police now logging around 600 of them every single day. Police in England and Wales recorded 218,994 sexual offences in the year to June 2026, the highest annual total since the series began in 2002-03 …

Police are recording more rapes of women than at any point since records began, at a rate of around 142 every day. There were 51,731 recorded rapes of women aged 16 or over in the year to June 2026, the highest figure since the series began in 2004-05 …

More people are being caught carrying knives and blades than at any point since records began. Police recorded 30,216 offences of possessing an article with a blade or point in the year to June 2026, the highest figure since the series began in 2008-09 …

Thefts and robberies from shops have reached a record high under Labour, with more than 1,500 recorded every single day. Police recorded 519,516 shoplifting offences and 31,089 robberies of business property in the year to June 2026, a combined 550,605 and the highest total since the series began in 2002-03.

But these claims are highly selective – to the point of being misleading.

On sexual offences, and rape, the ONS report points out that much of the increase over time is due to more offences being recorded, and not necessarily more of them taking place. It says “there has been a general increase in police recorded sexual offences over the last decade, largely because of improvements in police recording practices”. And it includes a specific warning about drawing the wrong conclusions from the figures.

double quotation markPolice recorded sexual offences are not a good indicator of trends over time. Improvements in police recording practices, the introduction of new offences, and increased reporting by victims have contributed to the level of offences in recent years.

On knives, while more people may be carrying them, the Tories have ignored the figures suggesting fewer criminals are actually using them. The ONS says:

double quotation markKnife-enabled crime recorded by the police decreased by 6% in year ending (YE) June 2026 (to 48,615 offences), compared with YE June 2025 (51,567 offences). Levels remained 12% lower than YE March 2020 (55,170 offences).

And, on shoplifting, the Tories are again presenting the data in a misleading way. The ONS says:

double quotation markFollowing a period of increases in shoplifting, there has been a 2% decrease (to 519,516 offences) in YE June 2026 when compared with the previous year (530,336 offences).

The Tories have justified their “record high” claim by combining the shoplifing figures with the figures for robberies from business properties. They describe this as “shop crime” – even though many business properties are not shops. And the ONS has a caveat about these figures too.

double quotation markThe number of robbery of personal property offences fell by 7% (to 57,193 offences) compared with the previous year, however, overall robbery increased by 10% (to 88,282 offences) mainly because of improvements to recording practices for robbery of business property.

And the ONS says, with shoplifting, more offences are also now being recorded than in the past.

double quotation markRecent increases in police recorded shoplifting likely reflect both growth in offences and improved reporting resulting from closer engagement between police and retailers. Reporting rates for shoplifting are known to be very low and police are actively encouraging the reporting of all incidents and the submission of supporting evidence, such as CCTV, to strengthen intelligence, identify offenders, and link related offences.

The Office for National Statistics has also published a report on the gender pay gap. It says:

double quotation markThe gender pay gap for full-time employees has continued to decline in the UK. It was 6.8% in April 2026, down from 7.2% in April 2025. This compares with 9.4% a decade ago and 16.4% 25 years ago.

This chart shows the pay gap trend over time.

Patrick Maguire was not the only person to interview John Healey yesterday. Robert Peston, ITV’s political editor, spoke to the chancellor too, and he has written a blog about the most interesting points to emerge. This is what Peston says about Healey’s comments about the banks. (See 10.41am.)

double quotation markSecondly, I asked Healey whether he sees the banks as making excessive profits, which would be the coherent justification for him to increase the surcharge on bank profits – as he is expected to do in the Budget next week.

He said: “You know the banks are the engine of investment in this country. The banks are doing well at the moment and that is good to see.

“It’s good for Britain – and the budget is where I’ve got decisions to take across the economy, across the tax system. I will set those out on Wednesday next week.”

This sounded like he will increase the surcharge but doesn’t have an economic rationale for doing so.

There has been a “significant increase” in the proportion of adults in England and Wales who have experienced domestic abuse, the Press Association report. In its report on today’s crime figures (see 9.54am), PA says:

double quotation markSome 9.6% of people aged 16 and over are estimated to have been the victim of domestic abuse in the year to March 2026, or around 4.7 million people.

This is up from 7.8%, or around 3.8 million people, in the year ending March 2025.

The rise indicates “real change” in the prevalence of domestic abuse and is a “significant increase”, according to the Office for National Statistics (ONS) which carried out the survey.

The jump has been driven by a rise in partner abuse, experienced by 7.9% of people aged 16 and over in the latest figures, compared with 6.1% in the previous year.

Some “minor changes” to the way the survey is carried out are likely to have influenced the size of the increase, the ONS said.

But their best assessment is there has been a genuine rise in the level of domestic abuse.

While there has been a jump in the prevalence of partner abuse, figures for family abuse are broadly similar, at 2.8% of adults in the year to March 2026, compared with 2.7% in the previous 12 months.

Meghan Elkin, ONS head of crime statistics, said: “While minor survey changes and the usual uncertainty around gathering data on this sensitive topic are likely to have affected these estimates, our assessment is that the rise in domestic abuse includes real change.

“More data points are needed to further understand the uncertainty and what this tells us about trends in domestic abuse.”

Kemi Badenoch has criticised the government for not sending a minister to address the Police Federation’s conference.

Addressing the federation this morning, she said she was “not scared to wade in” and not scared to “back the police”.

double quotation markToo often these days, we fail to recognise sacrifice and service. Whether it’s hounding brave and elderly veterans through the courts, hounding police officers who try to do the right thing, or even ordinary members of the public who step in to help only to find that they’re in trouble themselves.

It’s no wonder the people in this country are becoming too scared to wade in, too scared to do the right thing. Well, I am different. I am not scared to wade in, and I am not scared to back the police.

I think it is telling that for two years in a row, the Labour government has not sent anyone to address this conference – not the policing minister, not the home secretary.

But Badenoch also said she would not promise police officers a big pay rise.

double quotation markNow, I know that you would also like a massive pay rise as well.

I’m sorry that I can’t promise that just yet – at least not on day one.

I am not going to stand here and promise something without a plan to pay for it.

Too many politicians have done that, and it only leads to disappointment.

Offenders who refuse to face their victims’ families in court for sentencing could be stripped of privileges or kept in cells for weeks under government changes granting wider powers to judges in England and Wales, Geneva Abdul reports.

Kalyeena Makortoff is the Guardian’s banking correspondent.

CS Venkatakrishnan, CEO at Barclays, seems to have admitted defeat over bank tax hikes, which are expected to be a headline measure in Healey’s budget next week.

When asked whether the bank might consider tilting assets or investment out of the UK and to the US - where it also has operations - as a result of higher taxes, Venkatakrishnan gave his full backing to the chancellor.

double quotation markI recognise that the chancellor and the government has been entrusted with an important duty by the public and the people. And they have to balance a host of considerations. He [Healey] is the man in the arena, and I deeply respect the responsibility he bears on his shoulders and wish him well.

His long term goal is the same as our long term goal, which is to get growth.

Second, we are already a bank, which makes, effectively, half of our money elsewhere [outside] the UK. And so this is not a question of a financial hit to us. It’s bearable. It is a question of proportion and it’s a question of market signaling. But as I said, I deeply respect the responsibility that the chancellor has and he has our full support and backing.

Bank bosses have been lobbying intensively against bank tax rises since narrowly escaping higher levies during last year’s budget.

That includes JP Morgan boss Jamie Dimon, who said earlier this year he could scrap plans for a new £3bn London headquarters if the UK government became hostile to banks. News of the tower – which will house more than half of its 23,000 UK staff – was unveiled just days after former Labour chancellor Rachel Reeves spared the sector of further tax rises in her 2025 autumn budget.

Here are some more lines from Patrick Maguire’s interview with John Healey in the Times. This passage sums up the overall picture very well. Maguire writes:

double quotation markSo what is the chancellor now concentrating on? One could be forgiven for thinking him utterly unreconstructed: a party man and proud of it. There is no such thing as Healeyism, he says when the conversation turns to Anthony Crosland’s evangelism for the mixed economy: “I’m just Labour.”

“Just Labour” is exactly what the bond markets fear — and, indeed, it is what gives Kemi Badenoch hope of pulling off a comeback to rank alongside Lazarus and Bobby Ewing for utter implausibility.

As explained earlier, while not going into specifics, Healey was keen to present himself as someone reducing the burdens facing businesses – especially smaller businesses. (See 9am.) But here are some other lines.

Healey argued that his budget next week would refute the claim made by Andy Haldane, the former Bank of England chief economist, about Labour not having the right policies to promote growth. In an article for the Financial Times, Haldane said Conservative policies were better for the economy, partly because they were more likely to support “cuts to business and employment taxes and regulation to unleash animal spirits”. In his write-up, Maguire says:

double quotation markIt was Haldane who also said, memorably and mercilessly, that the markets had concluded that this was a “traditional tax-and-spend socialist government with better TikTok videos”. At Westminster, this sort of criticism is at risk of curdling into thick and immovable consensus. What does Healey say to that? “I’d say to Andy Haldane,” he growls, fixing me with a cold stare, “speak to me next Thursday.” And, for the record, he speaks explicitly of “making an argument for how you bring welfare costs down” — albeit not via the “crude cuts” that were Starmer’s undoing.

Healey hinted that he was sympathetic to arguments that Labour should drop its plan to let younger workers qualify for the full national living wage. In his article Maguire says:

double quotation mark[Healey] is “acutely conscious”, too, of the “trade off” between an ever-increasing minimum wage — particularly for the youngest workers — and levels of employment.

He knows the many businesses who “want to employ young people” sometimes cite that upward ratchet as a reason they cannot.

Healey defended the part he played in bringing down Keir Starmer. Healey resigned from Starmer’s government over defence spending, and this contributed to the loss of support for Starmer in the parliamentary party that led to him standing down. Referring to this period, Healey said:

double quotation markThe country was ready for a change … Wherever you stood on the spectrum of the [parliamentary Labour party], there was a recognition that we needed a change.

He also argued that changing leader had been good for the party.

double quotation markWe have a very rare moment now. We’re in the middle of a parliament, the second half of a parliament, and we’ve got a chance of a new hearing. People are at least willing to listen again … the Labour party is actually quite determined and disciplined, and in any party, the second half of a parliament starts concentrating minds.

The Office for National Statistics’ latest report on crime figures is out. It covers crime in England and Wales in the year ending June 2026 and it starts:

double quotation markCrime against individuals and households has generally decreased over the last 10 years with some notable exceptions, such as fraud.

This chart shows some of the key figures. The crime survey figures are based on what people tell researchers about the crimes they have experienced; the other figures related to the crimes reported to the police.

At this stage of the budget process, John Healey has almost certainly made all his key decisions. But, just in case he hasn’t, he could try our budget interactive. It allows you to make a decision on some of the options facing the chancellor, and then it will tell you what the impact would be on budget headroom, and how the markets and the polls might react.

Good morning. A week today John Healey, the chancellor, will be doing a media round defending the budget he is presenting on Wednesday next week. Ahead of that, he has given an interview to Patrick Maguire from the Times. As you would expect, there is no real detail in it about the measures he will be presenting to MPs. But the big picture message is very clear – and quite surprising, coming from a chancellor serving a PM who in some respects is steering left compared to his predecessor. Healey says that he wants to be on the side of bloody-minded entrepreneurs who make a profit, he acknowledges that government has made their life harder over the past two years, and he suggests that cutting the ‘cost of living’ for business is just as important as cutting the real cost of living for families.

In the quote that gives the Times its splash headline, Healey says:

double quotation markI want to be a chancellor who backs business in Britain making a profit, and those entrepreneurs who, in the end, are the ones who challenge the status quo, come up with innovative ideas and are trying, some of them through sheer bloody-mindedness, to keep going through these sorts of pressures …

If you’re not making a profit, you’ve got nothing to put back into the business. And for the people who start up these businesses, the ones who really thrive and grow, they have to make a profit — and they will be much more inclined to put it back into their own business. But we want it to grow here and stay here.

And this is what he says about the government has recently been putting “a lot of pressure” on business.

double quotation markIf you talk to any of the businesses that have come in and have either had one-to-ones or round tables with me, I have recognised that in recent times there’s been a lot of pressure: employment law, regulation, tax, input costs, supply chains.

And so when I talk about the cost of business, and recognising that in the same way as we’re recognising the cost of living pressures, I’m conscious of that as I go into the budget for both businesses and households.

All chancellors – including all Labour chancellors – say they want to help businesses make a profit. But many people in the business community suspect that, when they face fiscal pressure, Labour government will usually default to treating business as a cash machine.

Healey’s comments about wanting to be seen as “a chancellor who backs business” and about how tax rises and the Employment Rights Act have increased costs sound like an implicit rebuke to Rachel Reeves, his predecessor. In his interview Healey defends her decision to increase employer national insurance, saying she had to deal with the “dereliction of duty” of the last Tory government on the economy. But Healey still gives the impression of wanting to be seen as markedly more pro-business than Reeves.

In his interview Healey does not give details of how he will cut costs for business next week. But, in his write-up, Maguire says:

double quotation mark[Healey] is expected to use the budget to make significant cuts to regulation on businesses that one senior Treasury source described as “the sludge choking firms”. Reporting requirements are likely to be abolished for many smaller enterprises, The Times understands.

9.30am: The ONS publishes crime figures for England and Wales and – separately – annual gender pay gap figures.

10am: Ofgem chief executive Tim Jarvis and Department for Energy and Net Zero permanent secretary Jonathan Brearley give evidence to the Commons public accounts committee about achieving clean power by 2030.

10.15am: Kemi Badenoch gives a speech at the Police Federation’s annual conference.

Morning: Andy Burnham is in Manchester where he is getting a flu jab, and also holding a meeting with mayors at No 10 North about mayors retaining revenue from business rates.

11.30am: Downing Street holds a lobby briefing.

Lunchtime: Miatta Fahnbulleh, the energy secretary, speaks at a lunch at the Commons hosted by lobby journalists.

I’m afraid we are no longer able to have comments open below the line every day on this blog. If you want to contact me, please email politics.live@theguardian.com. You can use this email to flag up corrections, comments for publication, questions or complaints.

title: What is PHP and why did it spark a global cyber-security scramble?
excerpt:
For more than a decade, serious flaws had gone undetected in the technology underpinning much of the internet.

It took artificial intelligence (AI) to bring them to light and caused a global cyber-se...
body_text:
For more than a decade, serious flaws had gone undetected in the technology underpinning much of the internet.

It took artificial intelligence (AI) to bring them to light and caused a global cyber-security alert.

The vulnerabilities lie within a programming language called PHP, which has been used internationally since the 2000s to build websites.

Governments and cyber-security agencies around the world scrambled to contain the fallout of this discovery on Wednesday, and have urged website operators to install a new emergency fix or consider taking their platforms offline.

Cyber-security firm Wiz - one of the companies whose researchers uncovered the vulnerabilities - described the flaws as the "most severe" ever detected by AI.

OpenAI, whose technology was used to find the flaws, called the discovery "one of the most impactful security issues in recent memory".

Most people may not have heard of PHP - short for PHP: Hypertext Preprocessor - but they most certainly interact with it daily.

PHP powers a vast number of platforms, including online shops, Wikipedia and WordPress – the content management system behind many websites like blogs.

When you visit a website like Wikipedia, PHP is the code that collects information you need and presents it in a way you can read on the web, Paul Spain, chief executive of Gorilla Cyber Security, told the BBC.

But due to a flaw that could allow attackers to take control of affected web servers without authentication and steal sensitive data, everything built on PHP was left exposed.

AI could make such attacks easier and faster, Spain said, estimating that the flaw could affect "millions and millions" of websites.

It would be "disastrous" if hackers or countries weaponised the flaw and seized private data from websites, said cyber-security researcher Jill Slay from the University of Adelaide.

The alert has disrupted services globally, from gaming platforms to government portals and online forums.

That includes Wikimedia - the organisation behind the online encyclopaedia Wikipedia - which took down a number of its systems as a precautionary measure.

Sites and pages have been taken offline by the Finnish government, Edinburgh council and the BBC, with the Netherlands' cyber-security agency also pulling its website.

Websites like the University of Geneva's were taken offline on Wednesday

A number of Scotland's public organisations, including councils and health boards, have also taken their websites offline.

Some experts warn the vulnerability could leave poorly maintained websites, particularly those belonging to smaller organisations with limited security resources, at greater risk.

More attempts to exploit these flaws are likely in the coming weeks since the technical details are now being made public, cyber-security researcher Salil Kanhere from UNSW Sydney said.

Developers of the PHP platform on Wednesday rolled out patches to fix the vulnerabilities that had been lurking in their software for years.

"All PHP users are strongly encouraged to update immediately," the company said.

Authorities and security organisations around the world have echoed those warnings to website operators to secure their platforms.

The US National Security Agency told all organisations that use PHP to take their systems offline if they were unable to patch them immediately, adding that the flaw could provide a "direct path" to exploit a system's database.

"These risks are serious enough to require immediate patching across United States Government departments and agencies," the agency said.

The UK's National Cyber Security Centre gave similar advice and told organisations to check for "backdoors installed by an attacker".

Its counterparts in the EU, Singapore and Australia have also issued similar alerts.

Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi urged people to check if their publicly available websites ran on PHP.

Japan's Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi urged people to check if their publicly available websites ran on PHP

"We have an urgent request for everyone to take action tonight," Takaichi wrote on X.

"If it is difficult to apply the fix patch promptly, temporarily suspending websites and similar measures can be considered an effective way to reduce risk," she said.

Tech companies are also racing to secure their systems.

E-commerce giant Amazon said it was targeted in multiple attempts days before the public disclosure of the PHP issue. It is unknown how the potential attackers knew about the vulnerability.

The vulnerabilities were found by researchers at the security firms Calif and Wiz.

The researchers used advanced AI tools that are able to analyse code and find flaws much faster than humans or older systems can.

"Modern software is incredibly complex, and some vulnerabilities can remain undetected for years," Kanhere said.

"The underlying bugs weren't new; what changed was our ability to find them," Kanhere said.

Details of the discovery leaked online this week, forcing the PHP platform's developers to rush out its announcement of the security flaw and its huge scale.

The incident "highlights how AI can uncover security flaws" but also how it can "help attackers rapidly develop offensive tools and exploits," OpenAI said in a blog post.

The ChatGPT-maker said it had released a program to check if the PHP platform is secure.

"Many of these flaws stem from the way software were built in the past, which were built for functionality and not with security in mind," said Ryan Ko, at the University of Queensland's Cyber Research Centre.

Website owners are being urged to secure their websites with the latest version of PHP.

The PHP software patch is a small, routine fix for most tech teams, Spain said.

The US National Security Agency has urged "heightened awareness" in the coming weeks and to closely monitor updates from software vendors.

"Vigilance in applying patches related to those systems is paramount," it said.

The onus lies mainly on website operators, but users should stay alert for any security advice issued by affected services, such as requests to change passwords, Kanhere said.

He warned people to be alert to any phishing messages exploiting the publicity around the incident too.

King warns malicious online actors are evolving tactics

Make sure use of AI is safe, data watchdog warns

title: Cookies and weapons: Women in Yemen’s Taiz find ways to help the city’s defence
excerpt: Taiz, Yemen – As Houthi fighters tighten their siege on the government-held southwestern Yemeni city of Taiz, women who initially organised food deliveries for soldiers defending the city have begun r...
body_text:
Taiz, Yemen – As Houthi fighters tighten their siege on the government-held southwestern Yemeni city of Taiz, women who initially organised food deliveries for soldiers defending the city have begun raising money to buy weapons and ammunition.

The initiatives have emerged spontaneously since the resumption of fighting in early September in the western countryside of Taiz governorate, between Saudi-backed forces of the internationally recognised government and the Iran-backed armed group.

At first, women volunteers came together to bake cookies for fighters on the front lines.

The aim was “to strengthen the relationship between the supportive social base and the members of the national army and pro-government popular resistance forces stationed at the front lines in defence of their besieged city, which is subjected to daily shelling in preparation for an invasion,” said Amira al-Saghir, an activist involved in the campaign.

The cookie-making initiative attracted widespread participation among women volunteers, drawing encouragement and support on social media. It coincided with a broader community campaign to supply fighters with food and other basic necessities, as well as weapons, with people contributing from districts and villages across the governorate.

In Yemen, a conservative country and the poorest in the Middle East, the vast majority of women do not participate in active fighting in the civil war, which began in 2014. Instead, these initiatives allow women to take part in what they see as the defence of their city against an invading force, and support for the men who are fighting.

After nearly four years of relative calm following a United Nations-brokered truce in April 2022, Houthi forces launched a major ground offensive in western Taiz in early September. The armed group rapidly captured territory along Yemen’s Red Sea coast, including the strategic port city of Mocha on September 10 , expanding its presence around Bab al-Mandeb strait, a vital shipping route.

The Houthis, also known as Ansar Allah, Arabic for Supporters of God, subsequently advanced towards other parts of Taiz governorate, taking control of key routes into the provincial capital and effectively surrounding the city. Government forces have since launched counteroffensives, with control of some areas remaining contested.

The renewed siege has severely restricted the movement of people and essential supplies into the city, triggering shortages of food, fuel, and medicine.

As the fighting intensified, the women’s initiatives expanded. What began with baking cookies and organising food convoys to supply arms kitchens gradually evolved into efforts to buy ammunition for fighters.

Women involved in the initiatives told Al Jazeera that they felt they had been “forced” to act because of the risk of their city falling to the Houthis.

The change began as more rural districts began falling to the Houthis, leading to some donors making their contributions conditional on part of the money being used to buy ammunition for fighters.

Al-Saghir believes the shift was encouraged by information and criticism circulating on social media suggesting that government fighters in Taiz lacked sufficient ammunition to continue defending the city and surrounding front lines.

The initiatives soon took off, encouraging more women to get involved. Among them was Huriya Wabel, a humanitarian activist.

“After we saw that those [Houthi] militias … are waging a war of extermination against our city, we felt that we had to take a serious stand to support the army, not just with food and clothing, but with weapons as well, especially since a siege has been imposed on Taiz and supplies can no longer reach it easily,” Wabel told Al Jazeera.

“We also found many civilians who wanted to participate in the fighting alongside the army in defence of the city, but they did not have weapons,” she added. “So it became incumbent upon us to help by focusing more of our activities on this aspect at this stage.”

For Khadija al-Majidi, the move from providing humanitarian supplies to delivering military equipment is a response to the growing threat facing Taiz.

“When the enemy reaches the gates of your city and imposes a complete siege on it in preparation for storming it by force, and everyone in it – including you, your children, and members of your family – is threatened with being killed, captured, or displaced … then what do you expect from us?” the activist told Al Jazeera. “Did you expect us to carry flowers for the criminal who came from the farthest reaches of the country to destroy our city and kill us?”

When Al Jazeera spoke to al-Majidi, she had just returned from the fighting around Jabal Sabir, the mountain overlooking Taiz from the south.

It was al-Majidi’s second trip to the front that day, delivering ammunition and other military supplies, which she valued at $3,000, to the commander on the front, along with winter clothing, shoes, food, and other necessities.

She said that after more than 10 years of living through Yemen’s devastating war, she no longer felt afraid to visit active battlefronts.

“Repeated visits to the front lines play a major role in removing fears, given what we see on the ground of the heroes’ courage and bravery in defending the city and their confidence in victory,” she added.

As fundraising expands, the women’s department of Taiz’s Supreme Council for Popular Resistance launched a campaign on October 8 , aiming to equip 10,000 pro-government fighters with rifles and ammunition.

The council has called for contributions from Yemenis across the country and abroad to support the initiative.

The campaign reflects the state of the fighting in Taiz, with government forces facing daily Houthi attacks, as they try to conduct their own counter-attacks.

But the longer the siege continues, the more difficult the military and humanitarian situation becomes in the city.

Al-Saghir and al-Majidi both explained that while many of the donations they receive come from Yemenis living abroad, people on the ground are also giving whatever they can, despite the humanitarian crisis in Taiz.

Al-Saghir said one woman whose husband was fighting in the army donated a wedding ring, while al-Majidi recounted stories of other women donating their gold jewellery.

Al-Majidi recalled a woman arriving at her home carrying envelopes containing Yemeni and Saudi currency.

The woman had written on the envelopes, “God willing, we will win. Buy ammunition for the heroes with this.”

title: Man United’s Carrick not worried about his job despite ‘unacceptable’ loss
excerpt: Michael Carrick has admitted that Manchester United were difficult to watch during an “unacceptable” 4-1 Champions League thrashing by Como, but insists he is not concerned about losing his job as man...
body_text:
Michael Carrick has admitted that Manchester United were difficult to watch during an “unacceptable” 4-1 Champions League thrashing by Como, but insists he is not concerned about losing his job as manager.

The three-time European champions were outclassed by the Italian debutants at the Stadio Giuseppe Sinigaglia on Wednesday, as the embarrassing defeat extended their winless run to seven matches in all competitions.

Carrick’s position has come under scrutiny amid United’s slump, which has included their worst start to a league season for 40 years, but he told a news conference that he was not fearing for his position.

“I have not given my own position any thought,” Carrick said.

The Old Trafford boss insisted that his apology to the travelling fans at the end of the game held no extra significance as pressure builds on his position.

“I always go over to the fans regardless,” Carrick said.

“It wasn’t a particularly different reason why I went over. I think it’s the appreciation and acknowledgement of what they have gone through and what they have done over a period of a few weeks now. But particularly tonight.”

United fell behind within two minutes to a Nico Paz goal, becoming the first English team ever to concede in the opening two minutes of two consecutive major European matches, having gone behind one minute into a 2-0 defeat by Atletico Madrid last week.

Cesc Fabregas’s side romped into a deserved 4-0 lead in northern Italy before substitute Joshua Zirkzee pulled back a stoppage-time consolation and Carrick admitted he was alarmed by the manner in which his team were outplayed.

“For us to play in that way, it’s not acceptable,” he said. “It wasn’t a good performance at all. We wanted to build on what we brought and the performance we had at Leeds.

“That bit of intensity, that spirit, that aggression, that real willingness to give everything. Tonight was the total opposite performance. I have to say, it was tough to watch.”

“There’s a lot going through my mind, watching that,” he continued. “Genuinely, it’s difficult to understand how it can be so different [from the Leeds performance].

“It shouldn’t be like that. We can all play well, we can all have poor performances, but to do it in that manner is really not right at all.”

Next up for Carrick’s side is a home Premier League game against Bournemouth on Sunday.

“I’m frustrated, more than frustrated, I’m really angry, to be honest,” Carrick said.

“You’ve got to move on, you’ve got to deal with what’s next and see what that looks like. At this moment in time, there’s a lot to do before that next game to get the team ready because that was a difficult night for everyone tonight.”

title: The world is $365 trillion in debt, and the interest bill is climbing
excerpt:
Hundreds of thousands of people have taken to the streets across Europe in recent weeks, angry at rising living costs, low wages, unaffordable housing and underfunded schools.

Protests in France, Bel...
body_text:
Hundreds of thousands of people have taken to the streets across Europe in recent weeks, angry at rising living costs, low wages, unaffordable housing and underfunded schools.

Protests in France, Belgium, Italy and Portugal have sometimes descended into clashes, looting and fires, although many protests have remained peaceful.

France has been at the centre of the unrest. More than 550,000 people demonstrated nationwide on Saturday, according to the Interior Ministry, amid weeks of student protests over education and living costs.

The unrest has turned the spotlight on a fiscal squeeze that governments are struggling to control. Years of heavy borrowing have left many European countries deeply in debt, and that debt is getting more expensive.

France’s borrowing costs are the highest since 2002, and the more governments spend on interest, the less they have for the schools, hospitals and pensions that protesters want.

In this visual explainer, Al Jazeera looks at how governments borrow, where France ranks among the most indebted countries, and the trillions that governments spend on interest.

Governments borrow money much like people do, but instead of going to a bank, they sell bonds.

In return, the government pays the buyers interest and promises to repay the full amount on a set date.

A 10-year bond is a loan the government pays back after a decade. Its yield – the return investors earn for lending – is the most closely watched measure of how much markets trust a country to manage its debt.

When bond prices fall, yields rise, making borrowing more expensive. Like a family facing a higher mortgage rate, a government then spends more on interest and has less money for essentials, such as schools, hospitals and roads.

Ten-year borrowing costs for major European economies have not been as high as 5 percent since the early 2000s, shortly after the euro was launched.

During the eurozone debt crisis of 2010 to 2012, only struggling countries such as Greece, Italy and Spain paid that much or more, and yields above 7 percent pushed Ireland and Portugal into bailouts.

France now pays around 5 percent to borrow for 10 years, compared with 3.41 percent for Germany. The widening gap shows investors want a higher return for lending to France.

The chart below shows 10-year borrowing costs across the euro area and the UK. France now pays more than Italy and Greece, two of the countries hit hardest by the eurozone debt crisis. Only the UK, which is outside the euro, pays more.

The United States has by far the largest government debt, at $41.4 trillion, or 127 percent of its economy, or gross domestic product (GDP). The US benefits from borrowing in dollars, the world’s dominant reserve currency, which supports global demand for its debt. But its borrowing capacity is not unlimited.

China follows with $22.5 trillion, or 104 percent of GDP, while Japan owes $8.7 trillion and has the highest debt ratio among major economies, at 199 percent of GDP. The UK’s debt stands at $4.4 trillion, or 102 percent of GDP.

France ranks fifth globally, with debt of $4.2 trillion, or 118.5 percent of GDP. That is more than Italy’s $3.7 trillion, although Italy’s debt is larger relative to its economy, at 138 percent. Germany owes $3.5 trillion, just 65 percent of GDP.

The  IMF projects France’s public debt to rise to 121.8 percent of GDP by 2030, complicating efforts to put the country’s public finances on a sustainable path.

The table below ranks countries by government debt. Use the search box to find yours.

Global debt, including that of governments, households and companies, rose by $10 trillion in the first half of 2026 to more than $365 trillion, according to the Institute of International Finance (IIF). That is roughly $44,000 for every person on Earth. Much of the increase came from emerging markets.

Paying for that debt is costly. Advanced economies paid more than $3.3 trillion in interest on their government bonds over the past year. That is more than the world spends on defence ($3.1 trillion), artificial intelligence ($2.6 trillion) or clean energy ($2.3 trillion).

For the public, rising interest costs mean less money for services such as schools, hospitals and pensions. Governments may have to raise taxes or cut spending to cover the bill. Higher government borrowing costs can also push up interest rates on mortgages, car loans and credit cards.

title: ‘Stupid talk’: France rejects Trump’s attempt to blame unrest on migration
excerpt:
Paris, France – As France reels from violent clashes during protests, riots and looting, the blame game is on.

One argument making waves across the political spectrum – and across the Atlantic – is t...
body_text:
Paris, France – As France reels from violent clashes during protests, riots and looting, the blame game is on.

One argument making waves across the political spectrum – and across the Atlantic – is that migrants and open-border policies are responsible.

“If Europe doesn’t close its borders and bring the criminals out, like the people that are protesting, Europe is finished,” United States President Donald Trump said at the White House on Monday. “When I look at France, when you look at Italy, when you look at all the turmoil and the hatred – that’s not about school. That’s about people coming into the countries that hate the country.”

French President Emmanuel Macron has since slammed “stupid comments by many, including foreign leaders”, but did not name Trump. Speaking during a visit in Qatar, he said there was no evidence of foreign interference behind the riots.

Young student protesters in France were unimpressed by Trump’s intervention.

Bilal Narjissi, a 17-year-old student at the Paul Eluard high school near Paris, one of the first to witness protests, called it “stupid talk”.

“They can think whatever they like. We’re focusing on the main subject, which is the students’ demands,” Narjissi said. “The far right has to say these kinds of things because they base their politics and political programmes on instilling fear.”

Emmanuel Dupuy, president of the Institute for European Perspective and Security Studies, a think tank on diplomacy and political analysis, said Trump’s argument was aimed at American voters.

“It’s an artificial argument used as a political tool in the context of midterm elections,” he said. “They are trying to argue that what is happening in France would happen in the US if Democrats get elected.”

Trump’s comments came after largely peaceful high school student demonstrations in France descended into chaos over the weekend when rioters attacked city halls and looted stores, marking the most violent unrest in France in years.

More than 2,000 people were placed in police custody – the vast majority of them minors – and thousands of businesses were ransacked. Accused of letting the situation spiral, French authorities imposed partial and temporary curfews in certain cities across the country, including in areas of Paris.

While concerns over dilapidated buildings, overcrowded classes and teacher shortages were at the fore, the protest movement quickly catalysed wider discontent over the cost of living and social unease.

Italy, Albania and Spain have seen similar demonstrations.

French authorities have not linked crime with migration. The state does not share the identities of people arrested and sent to trial.

Under constitutional laws aimed at equality, it is illegal to collect data on ethnicity and race.

Both far-right leader and presidential hopeful Marine Le Pen and politicians from the centrist bloc, including Macron and Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu, have accused hard-left groups of fomenting disorder.

The wave of protests seems to have struck a nerve across the European bloc, too.

Hungarian Prime Minister Peter Magyar said it was now “clear to everyone why Hungary takes the toughest possible stance on immigration”, posting on X a video showing buildings burning in France.

Without explicitly referring to events in France, Poland’s Prime Minister Donald Tusk also weighed in. “Poland will not repeat the mistakes of other European countries, nor will it pay for them,” he asserted on X a day after the mass demonstrations and looting in France. “We will be uncompromising on security.”

Dupuy said the origin of those who joined the violence was beside the point.

“These protesters were high school students; then professional black bloc and looters joined, too – whether they came from a third or fourth generation of former migrants is irrelevant,” he said. “Eventually, this is a problem of integration, not immigration.”

The US is in campaigning mode as it gears up for key elections in early November that will determine who dominates Congress.

With all eyes on midterms, Republicans seem eager to capitalise on unrest in Europe to rally support for Trump’s Make America Great Again (MAGA) movement and its tough policies on immigration and border measures.

“Western liberals imported the third world into France and other countries in the name of diversity and compassion,” US Vice President JD Vance said on X. “They ignored fundamental questions of assimilation and compatibility.”

Some critics have argued that Trump is trying to divert attention from the US’s cost-of-living crisis. Costs are rising in the US amid the Iran war he launched and the subsequent closure of the Strait of Hormuz, which has sent energy prices to new heights.

What is happening in France, Trump said, should be a cautionary tale for American voters.

“If you want to see what is at stake in this election, just look at what’s happening in France,” he said, doubling down at a rally in the US state of Kansas.

title: Ukraine’s access to Starlink a decision for Elon Musk, Rubio says
excerpt: United States Secretary of State Marco Rubio says decisions about Ukraine’s access to Starlink are in the hands of its parent company, SpaceX, and CEO Elon Musk, not the White House, in response to cl...
body_text:
United States Secretary of State Marco Rubio says decisions about Ukraine’s access to Starlink are in the hands of its parent company, SpaceX, and CEO Elon Musk, not the White House, in response to claims it was involved in restricting Kyiv’s access to satellite internet services.

Rubio’s comments on Wednesday may increase scrutiny of US decision-making to potentially throttle the high-tech system, which allows Kyiv to intercept incoming projectiles and target Russian launchers.

The Wall Street Journal reported on Tuesday that Musk had ordered a slowdown of Starshield, a military-grade version of Starlink that Ukraine relies on for defence against Russian missile attacks.

The Journal quoted one person as saying Musk, US President Donald Trump and White House officials discussed the matter beforehand and two people as saying Musk and the president discussed the matter in the days after the slowdown.

The Reuters news agency has quoted two US officials and a Western official briefed on the matter as saying the decision ultimately came from the White House.

This version was also confirmed by Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy but denied by the Trump administration.

Zelenskyy adviser Serhii Beskrestnov wrote on the Telegram messaging app on October 14 that SpaceX had imposed a limit of 160 kilometres per hour (100 miles per hour) on Starshield services. That affected guidance systems for drones that Ukraine uses to intercept Russian drones flying at far greater speeds.

“Our defence forces received no prior warning regarding this restriction, and it has led to the disruption of a number of missions,” Beskrestnov said.

Ukraine’s Ministry of Defence confirmed the resumption of services on October 15.

Rubio told reporters during a trip to India on Wednesday that he was not aware if the administration knew about the decision beforehand but said it was “irrelevant”.

“The bottom line is that that is governed by a private commercial contract as to how their stuff can be used and what speeds they’ll allow it to be used at,” he said.

Musk had previously said on X that “any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS (President of the United States).”

Trump, asked by reporters on Wednesday whether Musk ordered the slowdown, said he did not know who did it but “I was not involved.”

Pentagon chief Pete Hegseth on Tuesday also portrayed the Starlink cutoff as a commercial matter.

“There are terms of service that ultimately need to be complied to, and that’s where Starlink has the option to make those decisions,” he said.

One significant point of confusion relates to the difference between SpaceX’s Starshield and Starlink products. Starshield is essentially a military-grade version of Starlink developed for the Pentagon.

Rubio suggested on Saturday that Ukraine never had access to Starshield while Zelenskyy has said both services had been disrupted in Ukraine.

title: Man charged after allegedly making threats at Hannah Beazley’s electorate office while armed with nunchucks
excerpt:
Perth man charged with ‘being armed in a way that may cause fear’ – days after Helen Haines was allegedly attacked with 4WD outside her Victorian office

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily...
body_text:
Perth man charged with ‘being armed in a way that may cause fear’ – days after Helen Haines was allegedly attacked with 4WD outside her Victorian office

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

A man has been charged after allegedly threatening staff and wielding nunchucks at the electoral office of the Western Australian local government minister, Hannah Beazley.

The Perth incident came days after the federal independent MP Helen Haines was hospitalised with severe injuries following an alleged attack outside her electorate office in Wangaratta in Victoria on Monday.

Electoral staff at Beazley’s Victoria Park office called police after a man caused a disturbance on Wednesday afternoon.

Police said they received reports the man was making verbal threats while in possession of an “improvised martial arts weapon” described as “nunchucks”.

They arrested the 56-year-old man nearby and took him into custody. On Thursday he was charged with being armed in a way that may cause fear, making unlawful threats and cannabis possession. Nobody was injured in the incident.

The man was refused bail to appear at Perth magistrates court on Thursday.

Beazley was not in the office at the time but told reporters on Wednesday evening her staff were “rattled” by the “confronting situation”.

“He was [allegedly] being very threatening. He did want access to me, I believe, but we don’t know his motivations at all,” the minister said.

Beazley said there had been two staff members in the office at the time. The man allegedly attempted to lean through the security screen but her staff were a safe distance away, she said.

“It’s not the first time I’ve had threats made against me.

“My primary concern is the welfare of my staff, obviously. That was very rattling for them. They called the police.”

The prime minister, Anthony Albanese, said Hannah Beazley was a friend “because I’m a good friend of her dad”, the former Labor defence minister Kim Beazley.

“This is far too prevalent,” Albanese told Perth radio on Thursday. “It’s not who we are as Australians. We can have our discussions and debates and settle those issues at the ballot box.”

The governor general, Sam Mostyn, speaking generally on Thursday, discussed the gendered dynamics of threats and abuse directed at women in high-profile positions.

“Like any woman who has stepped up into any position across any part of our society, there is a unique and pernicious form of attack that comes our way,” Mostyn told ABC TV.

“I still receive that online. In fact, I was just saddened this morning to see some of the comments on my own Instagram page, in capitals with expletives, once again questioning the very nature of what it is that I do.

“Women across the country know that there are certain things that are reserved for women … that go to our gender and they are often vicious and just despicable.”

A community vigil was held for Haines in Wodonga on Wednesday evening after it was revealed the MP had lost both her legs following Monday’s alleged attack.

Haines’s predecessor as the federal member for Indi, Cathy McGowan, said on the sidelines of the event the community was grappling with “mixed emotions”.

McGowan had spent time with Haines’s staff and she told Guardian Australia they were “all crying together because of the emotion that’s been building up”.

“The people here tonight don’t want violence … but that’s not to say when violence happens in their communities they know what to do about it,” McGowan said.

“There’s a lot of violence in our communities, there’s a lot of violence online … there’s nothing new about this.

“What the attack on Helen has brought to our mind is, this is us. We can’t just pretend that everything’s OK in the regions and we’re doing fine.”

Haines’s chief of staff, Kaz Rourke, said on Thursday that the team was “devastated” by Monday’s alleged attack.

“Helen is adored by her team. She is a remarkable leader, a truly wonderful boss and someone we all care about deeply,” Rourke said in a statement.

“Most of us were in the office when the incident occurred and some of us were involved in Helen’s immediate care, so this has been deeply traumatic for the team.

“We are receiving a great deal of support and my priority right now is making sure Helen’s staff are as OK as they can be. I’m so very proud of them and know Helen would be too.”

Rourke said Haines’s staff were planning to reopen the electorate office “later next week”.

title: El Salvador’s Bukele threatens Haitian gangs over abducted soldiers
excerpt:
El Salvador has initiated a military operation to rescue four Salvadoran soldiers abducted by gangs in Haiti, President Nayib Bukele announced in a post on X, without elaborating.

Bukele, known for h...
body_text:
El Salvador has initiated a military operation to rescue four Salvadoran soldiers abducted by gangs in Haiti, President Nayib Bukele announced in a post on X, without elaborating.

Bukele, known for his intense crackdown on gang violence in El Salvador, warned in Wednesday’s statement that a more forceful response was coming if the personnel were not released alive and well.

“Do not take our word for empty threats,” the president wrote, addressing the gangs allegedly responsible for holding the four men. “We have already finished with the gangs in El Salvador, and we can finish with you too.”

Gangs in Haiti opened fire on an armoured vehicle carrying the men three days earlier, in the first major attack since an international gang suppression force began operating in the violence-wracked Caribbean country last year.

The four men, aviation technicians with the United Nations-backed Gang Suppression Force (GSF), have been missing since they fled the burning vehicle in the Santo area of Croix-des-Bouquets, Port-au-Prince.

Haiti’s government issued a news release on Wednesday evening saying the release of the abducted soldiers was an “absolute priority”.

It was not immediately clear if Haitian authorities received any confirmation that the Salvadoran soldiers are alive.

The government said a meeting was held at the prime minister’s office “to assess the ongoing interventions and determine the necessary measures to strengthen operations, in close collaboration with the Gang Repression Force”.

A spokesperson for the GSF did not immediately respond to a message seeking details

The UN-backed force is still fighting gangs in the community where Sunday’s attack occurred, warning residents in the area to remain indoors.

No one has claimed responsibility for the attack on the Salvadoran troops, which comes as Haiti prepares for its first general election in more than a decade. It also showcases the power of the gangs that control an estimated 70 percent of the capital, Port-au-Prince.

El Salvador is among several countries – including Chad, Jamaica and Guatemala – to form part of the gang suppression force, with more than 2,000 troops on the ground in Haiti.

Gang violence has displaced nearly 1.5 million people in Haiti in recent years. More than 5,700 people have been killed or injured from January through mid-September this year, and more than 230 have been kidnapped, according to the UN.

The area where the armoured vehicle was targeted is controlled by gangs, including Chèn Méchan; Kraze Barye, led by Vitel’Homme Innocent; and 400 Mawozo, led by Lanmo Sanjou.

Both gang leaders have been sanctioned by the UN and the US.

title: How Arab parties could hold critical balance of power in Israeli election
excerpt:
Students in Nazareth are handing out leaflets encouraging Arab Israelis to vote in next week's election

At rush hour in Nazareth, the largest Arab-majority city in Israel, students are handing out le...
body_text:
Students in Nazareth are handing out leaflets encouraging Arab Israelis to vote in next week's election

At rush hour in Nazareth, the largest Arab-majority city in Israel, students are handing out leaflets by the roadside urging motorists to vote in next week's closely fought, general election. Polls indicate that Arab parties could be left holding a critical balance of power.

Disaffection has often driven down past turnout among Arab Israelis - who account for about a fifth of the population and often describe themselves as Palestinian citizens of Israel. But this election, there is a strong push to get rid of the most right-wing governing coalition in the country's history - an alliance between veteran Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and far-right and ultra-Orthodox parties.

"I see it as our duty to bring down this extremist government. They treat us as second-class," says Arkan Badran, 23, who is with the students giving out flyers. "I call on all young men and women to vote for Arab lists, which represent us, because this is our future."

All but one of the leading Jewish parties have ruled out forming a coalition government with Arab parties

Most opinion polls indicate that neither Netanyahu and his partners nor the main "Change Bloc", led by centre-right former military chief Gadi Eisenkot, has a clear path to a parliamentary majority.

If they are right, after the election anti-Netanyahu parties wanting to form a governing coalition would either have to go back on pledges not to work with the prime minister or make a deal with Arab-majority lists.

A major sticking point is that Eisenkot has so far ruled out forming a government with Arab parties, citing a lack of shared values.

Israel's politics and society have been changed by the deadly, unprecedented Hamas-led assault on the country on 7 October 2023, and subsequent war in Gaza. There is increased mistrust of and hostility towards the country's Arab minority.

Salman Mousa accuses ministers of "systematic discrimination and incitement" against Arab Israelis

"After October 7, we were treated as enemies of this country," says Suha Salman Mousa of the Mossawa Centre in Nazareth, which advocates for equal rights for Arab citizens. "There was shrinking space for freedom of speech. There were major arrests, there was also firing of people from their workplaces because they put something on social media or they went out against the war on Gaza."

Salman Mousa accuses ministers of "systematic discrimination and incitement" against Arab Israelis. Civil society groups say they have disproportionately cut budgets for Arab communities. The government says reductions are needed to fund wartime defence and security spending.

There have also been politicised campaigns against Arab physicians working in Israeli hospitals and racially motivated attacks on Arab bus drivers by Jewish Israelis.

Some electioneering has sought to capitalise by deepening social divisions. The far-right Finance Minister, Bezalel Smotrich, has vowed to "Judaise" parts of the northern Galilee and southern Negev regions where most Arabs live, likening this to expanding settlements in the occupied West Bank.

The majority of Arab Israelis are descendants of Palestinians who remained within what became Israel during the war that surrounded the creation of the state in 1948, when hundreds of thousands were forced from or fled their homes. Israel's current government often frames them as a threat to the state's Jewish identity.  Recently, the prime minister has claimed that his rivals plan to team up with Arabs and form a "dangerous government".

To make this point, his campaign has put up billboards, including one at a road junction at the main entrance to Nazareth. They suggest a choice between: "Right or Palestine" - with pictures of main opposition figures, including right-wingers, depicted as representing the latter not the former. The Netanyahu campaign has also used AI-generated videos to present his opponents embracing Arab leaders.

Radio Nas anchor Mohammed Magadli says Benjamin Netanyahu is trying to delegitimise Arab parties

At Radio Nas, a popular Arabic-language station in Nazareth, I meet news anchor Mohammed Magadli, who is also an analyst for Israel's Channel 12. His father, Raleb Magadli, served as Israel's first Muslim minister between 2007 and 2009, representing the Labour party.

I ask the younger Magadli what he makes of Change Bloc leaders refusing to join forces with Arab parties.

"In a word its racism. But if we're trying to explain why, it's because of the political interests of Benjamin Netanyahu," he says. "He's trying all the time to pull the legitimacy of the Arab parties - because they're Arab, because they're Palestinian. This is affecting the majority of the Jewish parties in Israel."

Polls this week have suggested that both Eisenkot's bloc and Netanyahu's religious-nationalist bloc could each win around 50 seats of the 120 in Israel's parliament while 13 or 14 seats in total could go to Arab-majority groupings.

These are the Joint Arab List, a coalition of Hadash, Balad and Taal, and the smaller United Arab List, an Islamist party headed by politician Mansour Abbas.

United Arab List leader Mansour Abbas wants Arab parties to reach a "position of influence"

While Abbas's party was originally created as part of the Islamic Movement in Israel - which has socially conservative values - he has become known for joining with Jewish partners. He prioritises solving the problems of Arab Israelis and speaks relatively little of Palestinians in the West Bank and Gaza.

Abbas has had a taste of power. In 2021, he became a minister in a previous, short-lived Israeli government led by Naftali Bennett - now a right-wing member of Eisenkot's bloc.

For this election, he has taken the surprise step of giving the number two position on his slate to a Jewish former police official and centrist member of parliament, Yoav Segalovitz. Abbas believes Eisenkot and others will be more open to an alliance with his party after the election and insists he wants to join the next government.

"We've reached the conclusion that parliamentary representation is not enough to serve Arab society. We decided to take responsibility, to become part of the solution to our problems and to offer hope to both Arabs and Jews," he tells me.

"That's why our approach has been driven by a desire to reach a position of influence, not merely representation."

The Joint List talks of providing an electoral "safety net" to those who could replace Netanyahu's government

Meanwhile, the Joint List - which is made up of secular parties and advocates for equal rights for Arab Israelis, an end to Israeli military occupation of Palestinian territories, and a two-state solution to the Israeli-Palestinian conflict - aims to wield a position of influence within the opposition.

It talks of providing an electoral "safety net" to those who could replace the Netanyahu government, in return for support on important policies.

A main issue in this election for Arab Israelis is rampant gang crime.

In September, a poll by the Israel Democracy Institute think tank found that this was the most important factor for 53.5% of Arab citizens when deciding which party to vote for.

Murders within the community reached a record high of 252 last year – about five times higher than the number of Jewish Israelis who were killed, according to the Abraham Initiatives, a Jewish-Arab organisation that promotes coexistence.

Arab Israelis accuse the government of inaction on the issue of gang crime

In Jaffa, a mixed Arab-Jewish neighbourhood which is now joined to Tel Aviv, Ziad Samouni shows me where his son, Hussein, was shot dead by two gunmen on a motorcycle near his home last November.

No arrests have been made in his case. With a low percentage of cases solved, Arab-Israelis accuse the government of inaction.

"It seems they're interested in making sure we reach a situation where the killer is never caught, allowing Arabs in Arab society to keep killing one another," says Samouni, who is now part of a support group, Israeli-Palestinian Bereaved Families for Peace.

The Israeli police told the BBC its investigation into Hussein's murder remained active, adding that it took "every case of violence and crime with the utmost seriousness."

"As a father who's lost a son, of course, I want this bloodshed to end," Samouni tells me. "I wish every Arab citizen who believes there needs to be a change sees that this is a time to go to vote."

Ziad Samouni's son Hussein (2nd L) was shot dead last November but no arrests have been made

This month, Israel's Supreme Court overruled a decision by the Central Elections Committee to disqualify the United Arab List and the Joint List as well as two of their members.

The committee, which is dominated by the governing coalition, argued that they broke a law banning candidates who deny the existence of Israel as a Jewish state. The parties and their representatives strongly denied it.

With just days to go before voting, back in Nazareth, some motorists display flags for their preferred party on their cars.

The stakes are high in this election: Arab citizens could yet decide who wields power in Israel, and they also see this vote as key to their own future in the country.

Israel's far right find fertile ground among first-time voters

The murderous crime wave sweeping Israel's Arabs

title: Airbnb guests freed from chores involving ‘significant effort’ under new global rules
excerpt:
Accommodation platform acts after long-standing guest complaints over doing dishes, taking out rubbish and stripping beds

Airbnb hosts will no longer be able to ask guests to strip beds or wash dishe...
body_text:
Accommodation platform acts after long-standing guest complaints over doing dishes, taking out rubbish and stripping beds

Airbnb hosts will no longer be able to ask guests to strip beds or wash dishes under the accommodation platform’s new rules.

The changes, which apply to Airbnb reservations covered by the platform’s global policy, including bookings in Australia, will come into effect on 20 November and limit chores imposed on guests.

Airbnb had long fielded complaints from guests about having to pay cleaning fees, which can be hundreds of dollars, and still complete a list of chores for their host.

Since April 2025, cleaning fees have not been shown to guests. Instead, hosts have been allowed to choose to factor cleaning costs into the total price of the stay.

In a community policy update posted on its website this week, Airbnb said hosts would “generally” no longer be allowed to ask guests to complete tasks that “require significant effort or time or would typically be performed by a cleaner”.

Examples of such tasks include stripping beds of linen, taking rubbish offsite, and washing and putting away dishes, the company said.

The updated guidelines state that hosts can now set seven standard house rules which must be displayed in full at the time of booking – and can also add other “reasonable” requests.

Examples of house rules include check in and check out times, limits on how many guests can stay at the property, smoking restrictions, quiet hours, and whether or not pets are allowed.

Reasonable requests depend on “relevant local considerations”. For example, it may be reasonable to ask guests to limit shower time due to local water restrictions, or to dispose of rubbish in an animal-proof container.

While guests shouldn’t be asked to wash and put away dishes under the new guidelines, hosts can ask them to put used dishes in the sink.

“House rules help guests understand what hosts expect, but we’ve heard from our community that they can be confusing, onerous and hard to manage,” an Airbnb spokesperson said.

“So we’ve redesigned them to make them easier to discover and clearer to set, alongside a new policy that keeps requests reasonable, with no surprises.”
