title: Iran determined to keep uranium amid increased war odds, flurry of meetings
excerpt:
Tehran, Iran – There has been a flurry of diplomatic activity in the Middle East in recent days, with hopes of a diplomatic breakthrough to end the United States and Israel war on Iran.

Pakistan’s ar...
body_text:
Tehran, Iran – There has been a flurry of diplomatic activity in the Middle East in recent days, with hopes of a diplomatic breakthrough to end the United States and Israel war on Iran.

Pakistan’s army chief Asim Munir was in Tehran on Wednesday to discuss the war and recent tensions in Yemen. It comes against the backdrop of fears of a new breakout in conflict in the region.

Despite this, Tehran has held firm to its position that the war will not end, and the Strait of Hormuz will not reopen, until the US accepts its conditions.

Iran maintains an unyielding stance on its contentious nuclear programme, which was a factor in the Trump administration’s decision to launch the war on February 28.

“Not a single gram of enriched uranium will be removed from Iran,” Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, said late Tuesday after meeting Munir.

But he did not rule out downblending the highly enriched uranium inside the country under supervision from monitors, something Iran has offered before.

Iran’s authorities present the decades-old nuclear programme as a sovereign right and an achievement gained despite strikes, sabotage and assassinations. Rezaei described it as “national wealth” on Tuesday.

Iran has also used low-enriched uranium for civilian purposes like manufacturing radiopharmaceuticals and for power generation at the Bushehr plant in cooperation with Russia.

The authorities argue that surrendering the nuclear programme under military pressure would amount to capitulation, if it did not guarantee that Iran would not be left exposed to more attacks.

US President Donald Trump has repeatedly emphasised since the start of the war that he wanted to dismantle the Iranian nuclear programme. US Vice President JD Vance, however, suggested earlier this month that a “meaningful” reduction in the level of enrichment capacity may satisfy US demands.

Before Israeli and US attacks on Iran’s nuclear facilities in June 2025, the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) estimated that Tehran possessed 440 kilogrammes (970 pounds) of uranium enriched up to 60 percent. A nuclear bomb would need enrichment of more than 90 percent.

The attacks, followed by further US-Israeli strikes on nuclear sites in 2026, severely damaged Iran’s nuclear infrastructure. With the IAEA unable to inspect key facilities, the current size, condition and whereabouts of much of Iran’s enriched uranium stockpile remain unverified.

Tehran has refused access to the IAEA to inspect its nuclear facilities since the war started, accusing the agency of advancing Western interests through adopting resolutions and referring the nuclear file to the United Nations Security Council.

Iranian authorities maintain they are not pursuing a bomb. But senior Iranian officials, like Rezaei, have publicly questioned the validity of being a party to the international nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty if Iran’s nuclear facilities and other infrastructure continue to be attacked.

Still, Iranian officials have hosted numerous foreign diplomats this week. Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov was in Tehran on Monday after attending a meeting with Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) countries a day earlier. There were also indications of visits to Tehran by other Arab officials.

US Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth is also reported to have met Israeli security officials earlier this week. These meetings did not appear to have decreased the prospects of renewed war.

But speaking at a conference for Iranian exporters in Tehran on Wednesday, Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi cautioned that the country faces threats of more attacks and expansive economic sanctions.

“The reality is that the country is truly in war conditions and the war continues. We have not reached peace conditions and are away from it, so all decisions must be made within war conditions,” he said.

Parliament speaker and chief negotiator Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf told Munir that Iran had “nothing new” to tell Washington and expected realisation of conditions offered in New York last month to reopen the Strait of Hormuz within seven days.

Mediators did not publicly divulge details of their proposals to Tehran this week, but were told the US needed to build trust by accepting Iran’s conditions. These include returning to the June memorandum of understanding and recognising an Iran-Oman deal over temporary transit in the Strait of Hormuz.

In addition to a pledge for immediate talks on a bigger deal regarding Iran’s nuclear issue, the memorandum included removing the US naval blockade on southern Iranian ports, waivers for oil sanctions, unfreezing Iranian assets and halting military action in Lebanon and other regional hotspots.

Ellie Geranmayeh, a senior policy fellow and deputy head of the Middle East and North Africa programme at the European Council on Foreign Relations, said it was clear that Tehran would be unwilling to give up its enriched uranium without guarantees of sanctions relief.

“The Iranians have made it very clear, and I see no evidence that’s changing, that they are willing to negotiate over the fate of the highly enriched uranium or access for international monitors, but that has to be directly linked with a very clear implementation protocol for US sanctions relief,” she told Al Jazeera. “We are very far from those types of negotiations at this stage.”

US media cited unnamed officials as saying on Tuesday that the Pentagon was sending the USS Theodore Roosevelt carrier strike group and a Marine unit to the Middle East. That would present President Trump with a range of strike options after the US midterm elections on November 3.

Over recent weeks, Trump and his officials have further discussed a range of military operations, including hitting Iran’s Pickaxe Mountain to diminish nuclear facilities inside, and dropping the “mother of all bombs” on nuclear and energy facilities. They have also previously raised the idea of seizing Iran’s southern islands on the Strait of Hormuz and assassinating more Iranian officials.

Iran’s state-run Press TV cited an unnamed security official as saying on Wednesday that decision-makers in Tehran have chosen to advance “without any limitations or restraint” if there are more US and Israeli attacks or assassinations.

Geranmayeh pointed out that Tehran had also helped its ally, the Houthis in Yemen, with their advances along the Bab al-Mandeb strait, and even considered potential preemptive strikes to rattle the US ahead of the election.

“One thing we should be watching out for is Israel and the US combining forces on military attacks after the Israeli elections and the US midterms,” she said, after Trump backed Netanyahu’s election bid.

title: Elon Musk’s Super Pac spends $500,000 to back New York Republican in midterms
excerpt:
Incumbent Mike Lawler is fending off a challenge from Democrat Cait Conley in state’s 17th congressional district

Elon Musk’s Super Pac has spent more than $500,000 in New York’s highly competitive 1...
body_text:
Incumbent Mike Lawler is fending off a challenge from Democrat Cait Conley in state’s 17th congressional district

Elon Musk’s Super Pac has spent more than $500,000 in New York’s highly competitive 17th congressional district race to help Mike Lawler, the Republican incumbent, hold on to his seat.

Lawler, a moderate Republican, is fending off a challenge from Democrat Cait Conley in the Hudson valley. It is among the most-watched races that could determine whether Republicans hold on to their majority in Congress.

America Pac, the Super Pac founded by Musk, has spent hundreds of thousands of dollars over the last year to boost Lawler’s campaign, according to Federal Election Commission filings.

Most of that spending has funded voter outreach efforts such as texting, printing, and postage and digital media-related services. Gothamist was the first to report on Musk’s spending.

Musk, the Republicans’ largest donor so far this midterm cycle, has spent millions of dollars on conservative candidates. Since the beginning of July, Musk has funneled $276m into Republican groups and America Pac, the New York Times reported earlier this month.

The funding is helping push Republican candidates to the finish line as they try to convince disgruntled voters to back the conservative party again. Polling shows Republican candidates are at a slight disadvantage this cycle because many have grown frustrated with the cost of living under Donald Trump.

America Pac’s spending on Lawler’s race is notable because Musk’s Pac spent more than $2m to help re-elect Lawler in 2024.

Conley, Lawler’s Democratic opponent, and the former head of the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, has accused Lawler of protecting Musk rather than regulating artificial intelligence.

“AI poses a very real threat to the safety and security of the American people, and it’s long past time that Congress took action to regulate it,” Conley wrote on X. “But Mike Lawler is standing in the way, because he’s looking out for his trillionaire backer Elon Musk.”

Ciro Riccardi, Lawler’s campaign manager, told Gothamist that they had “no say over what America PAC or any other outside group spends in this race” – referencing a law that prohibits campaigns from coordinating directly with Super Pacs.

Palestinian farmers are still being blocked from accessing their olive groves by Israeli settlers and the military during this year’s harvest in the occupied West Bank. Volunteers supporting farmers have also been detained, including US congressional candidate Brad Lander and activist Andrey X.

title: French politician calls out Victor Wembanyama for supporting, encouraging French protestors
excerpt:
The mayor of Nice, France, rebuked Victor Wembanyama for supporting the ongoing protest movement in France, accusing the NBA star of encouraging unrest.

"French celebrities like the basketball player...
body_text:
The mayor of Nice, France, rebuked Victor Wembanyama for supporting the ongoing protest movement in France, accusing the NBA star of encouraging unrest.

"French celebrities like the basketball player Victor Wembanyama, who called for supporting the riots of October 17, bear a historic responsibility," Ciotti wrote on X. "They must be condemned."

For background, the protests began in September with high school students claiming they were demanding better conditions in French schools, including more resources, improved facilities and relief from overcrowded classrooms. The movement has since expanded into a broader protest against government spending cuts, drawing support from university students, labor unions and members of France's "Yellow Vest" movement.

KYRIE IRVING, VICTOR WEMBANYAMA LIKE MAMDANI'S VIDEO CALLING NETANYAHU A 'WAR CRIMINAL'

The unrest escalated significantly on Oct. 17, when an estimated 550,000 to 800,000 people participated in demonstrations across France. Rioters broke out in several major cities, including Paris, Lyon and Marseille. Rioters and looters clashed with police, set fires, damaged public buildings and looted businesses.

Earlier this month, Wembanyama, who was born in France, wrote on Instagram that he'd "really love to" join the protests.

"These are systemic inequalities, problems that are so deep," he added when asked about the demonstrations during a preseason postgame press conference on October 8.

"I’m glad that high school students, young people in general, are making their voices heard, because I hear them and I support them. And I hope the people at the very top will do the same."

Then, on Oct. 16, the eve of the nationwide demonstrations, Wembanyama posted a cryptic image of the White Rabbit from "Alice in Wonderland" pointing to his watch. Some in France interpreted the post as signaling anticipation for the Oct. 17 demonstrations, though Wembanyama did not explain its meaning.

Wembanyama has not publicly commented on the protests since the widespread violence on Oct. 17.

Victor Wembanyama stands with his arms crossed during the national anthem before Game 1 of the 2026 NBA Finals against the New York Knicks. (Adam Pantozzi/NBAE)

As the emerging face of the NBA, Wembanyama has shown he's more LeBron James than Michael Jordan in his approach to political issues. Last January, he said he ignored the advice of Spurs public relations and spoke out against ICE in America anyway.

"PR has tried, but I'm not going to sit here and give some politically correct [answer]," Wembanyama told reporters. "Every day I wake up and see the news, and I'm horrified. I think it's crazy that some people might make it seem like or sound like the murder of civilians is acceptable."

During the NBA Finals, Wembanyama drew attention for crossing his arms during the playing of the U.S. national anthem. Later in the series, he reportedly stayed off the court entirely during the anthem.

VICTOR WEMBANYAMA CROSSING HIS ARMS DURING U.S. NATIONAL ANTHEM IS A PROBLEM FOR THE NBA | BOBBY BURACK

It would behoove the NBA for its biggest star to not align himself with polarizing political causes. James did little to help his own or the league's popularity when he embraced political activism.

I suspect Wembanyama's commentary and demonstrations, whether about America or France, won't help the league's popularity either.

Victor Wembanyama #1 of the San Antonio Spurs looks on during the game against the New York Knicks during Game Five of the 2026 NBA Finals on June 13, 2026 at Frost Bank Center in San Antonio, Texas. (Jesse D. Garrabrant /NBAE via Getty Images) ((Jesse D. Garrabrant /NBAE via Getty Images))

One must also wonder how informed Wembanyama is about the issues on which he comments. This tends to be the question when athletes and celebrities speak out about complicated issues.

His initial support was for students protesting conditions in French schools. Fine. However, the movement he encouraged has since grown into something much larger and, at times, much more violent.

Wembanyama was willing to lend his considerable platform to the demonstrations when they represented a cause he supported. Now that those demonstrations have been accompanied by widespread violence, he ought to use that same platform to condemn it.

So far, he hasn't. Nor has he responded to Mayor Ciotti's criticism of him.

title: Thousands march for school funding in Greece
excerpt:
Milan’s youth follow France in violent cost-of-living protests

Thousands of students and teachers ‌have rallied across cities in Greece, demanding more funding for ⁠education, including better facili...
body_text:
Milan’s youth follow France in violent cost-of-living protests

Thousands of students and teachers ‌have rallied across cities in Greece, demanding more funding for ⁠education, including better facilities and smaller ⁠class sizes.

The demonstrations echo a wave of youth-led protests across Europe this month, including in France and Albania, where anger over rising costs and alleged corruption has led to clashes with police and major property damage.

Greek police said about 10,000 demonstrators, including school and university students, rallied peacefully in central Athens and the capital’s suburbs on Wednesday.

“From Greece to France, we want public, free education,” protesters chanted as they gathered outside Parliament, where students staged an overnight sit-in nearby before the rally.

Others joined the protests in Thessaloniki, Patras, Larissa and other cities ⁠across Greece in solidarity with growing demonstrations in France and elsewhere in Europe, where rallies demanding educational resources have morphed into angry demonstrations over soaring living costs.

In Greece, the protests add pressure to ⁠Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis and his centre-right government as the country prepares to hold elections in mid-2027 amid a weakening economy.

Greece struggled with a serious debt crisis from 2009 to 2018, during which the government agreed to spending cuts in exchange for three European Union and International Monetary Fund bailouts worth about 290 billion euros ($326bn).

But the measures have impacted Greek workers, who are among the poorest in Europe and struggle with stagnant wages, high rents and rising energy costs.

The average monthly salary of 1,500 euros ($1,685) sits at 2009 levels, with many young Greeks having been priced out of housing in ⁠cities by skyrocketing rents.

“Surviving here is very difficult; the ⁠rent is really high, the houses are really small. Our parents can’t make ends meet to pay for our rent, the electricity, for our life here,” university student Georgia Foukidou, 21, who joined the protest in Athens, told the Reuters news agency.

The protests on Wednesday included strikes by primary and secondary school teachers protesting low pay and staff shortages, while substitute teachers demanded permanent positions and reduced class sizes. Public sector workers and other unions also joined the demonstrations.

Education Minister Sofia Zacharaki said prior to the protests that she was listening to student demands, noting that the government was spending more than 733 million euros ($823m) on new student residences and facilities upgrades.

Mitsotakis’ government has also pledged about one billion euros ($1.12bn) in state subsidies and other benefits to offset increased energy costs for households and businesses due to the Iran war and inflation.

title: Epstein’s attorney and accountant accused of ‘facilitating and concealing’ his crimes in lawsuit
excerpt:
New Mexico lawsuit claims ‘in exchange for furthering Epstein’s criminal project, his associates received generous salaries’

The attorney general of New Mexico on Wednesday filed a civil lawsuit agai...
body_text:
New Mexico lawsuit claims ‘in exchange for furthering Epstein’s criminal project, his associates received generous salaries’

The attorney general of New Mexico on Wednesday filed a civil lawsuit against Jeffrey Epstein’s longtime attorney, Darren Indyke, and Epstein’s longtime accountant, Richard Kahn, accusing them of having “facilitated and concealed” Epstein’s crimes, and is seeking to stop them from being paid by Epstein’s estate while the litigation plays out.

The lawsuit, filed in the US district court for the district of New Mexico, names Kahn and Indyke as defendants both in their individual capacity, and in their capacity as co-executors of Epstein’s estate. The complaint also names Epstein’s estate, and the 1953 Trust, which holds the estate’s assets.

“Epstein, with the help of his associates, trafficked, isolated, and abused survivors at alluring locations” including at Epstein’s ranch in Stanley, New Mexico, known as Zorro Ranch, the complaint claims. It goes on to allege that “in exchange for furthering Epstein’s criminal project and remaining silent about it, his associates received generous salaries, access to elite social circles, and lavish gifts, including being named beneficiaries of his multimillion-dollar estate”.

In a statement on Wednesday, an attorney for Indyke shared a statement on behalf of both Indyke and Kahn saying that they “emphatically reject the New Mexico Attorney General’s allegations that they were complicit in or in any way knowingly facilitated Mr Epstein’s sexual abuse or trafficking – conduct that by all accounts occurred behind closed doors, in secluded locations, and at times when neither Mr Indyke nor Mr Kahn was present.

“Not a single woman has ever accused Mr Indyke or Mr Kahn of committing sexual abuse or witnessing sexual abuse, nor claimed at any time that she or anyone else reported to them any allegation of Mr Epstein’s abuse,” the statement added. “The New Mexico Attorney General’s complaint does not allege anything to the contrary.”

The statement goes on to say that “neither the New Mexico Attorney General nor anyone from his office asked to speak with Mr Indyke or Mr Kahn to seek relevant information from them before filing this baseless lawsuit, raising serious questions about the thoroughness of the Attorney General’s investigation and the motivations for his lawsuit”.

Earlier this year, Kahn and Indyke told the US House committee investigating Epstein that they had no knowledge of Epstein’s crimes during their employment.

Among the demands the lawsuit seeks is a court order preventing Indyke and Kahn from receiving estate payments while the case proceeds.

The complaint alleges that both men profited personally from their relationships with Epstein. It alleges that from 2011 to 2019, Indyke received more than $16m from Epstein and related entities and that Kahn received more than $10m.

In a statement on Wednesday, Raúl Torrez, New Mexico’s attorney general, said that Epstein “did not operate alone, and his death does not end the pursuit of accountability for the people who helped make his crimes possible”.

“The allegations in this lawsuit describe a network of people and financial arrangements that helped sustain and conceal the abuse of vulnerable girls and young women, including here in New Mexico,” he said. “Those who allegedly enabled this exploitation should not be allowed to profit from it while survivors continue to live with its consequences.”

In the complaint, Torrez wrote that “through this action, the State seeks to hold these individuals accountable to the fullest extent possible and to ensure that Epstein’s assets are distributed to the survivors of his horrific crimes”.

Several survivors of Epstein’s abuse signed a letter on Wednesday in support of Torrez’s lawsuit “because it can expose what roles Indyke and Kahn played in Epstein’s operation, examine how they handled survivors’ claims, and prevent Epstein’s trusted loyalists from being rewarded for their roles in Epstein’s organization”.

“Survivors deserve accountability and answers under oath. Epstein’s chosen confidants should not get the last word – or the money,” they added.

At a news conference on Wednesday about the new filing, Epstein survivor Anouska De Georgiou thanked Torrez for “standing with survivors”.

“We have carried this burden for long enough,” she said. “It is time for those responsible to answer for their part in it.”

The announcement on Wednesday comes amid a separate ongoing dispute between New Mexico officials and the Department of Justice over files Torrez is seeking as part of the state’s investigation into Epstein’s possible crimes in the state, including at his ranch outside Santa Fe, where multiple survivors have said they were abused.

Torrez sued the Department of Justice in August, accusing the department and Todd Blanche, the attorney general, of “stonewalling” the state’s investigation, which was reopened in February. Torrez asked the court for access to unredacted Epstein-related files held by the justice department, and said in its filing his prosecutors had requested access to the records but had “faced sustained resistance” from the department.

The case is ongoing and the justice department recently filed a motion to dismiss, arguing that “decisions about law-enforcement information sharing are committed to the agency’s discretion” and that turning over unredacted files would violate victims’ privacy.

Epstein’s Zorro Ranch came under renewed scrutiny after the justice department’s release of roughly 3m files related to Epstein late last year and early this year. The Guardian reported in early February that the newly disclosed Epstein files contained thousands of references to Zorro Ranch, and numerous photos of men and young girls at the property, and that several survivors of Epstein’s abuse had also previously given testimony about abuse they say they were subjected to there.

The Guardian investigation also revealed that, unlike Epstein’s other properties in Palm Beach, in New York and on his private Caribbean island, federal authorities had apparently never searched the New Mexico ranch.

Epstein, who died in a Manhattan jail in 2019 while awaiting trial on federal sex-trafficking charges, bought the property in New Mexico 1993. It was later sold by his estate in 2023.

In late February, Torrez announced that New Mexico would reopen its investigation into Epstein’s activities at the ranch, after the state’s initial investigation was put on hold in 2019 at the request of federal prosecutors in New York, who were pursuing the investigation into Epstein’s sex-trafficking operation that led to his arrest. In March, New Mexico authorities launched a search of the ranch.

Torrez has said that he wants to establish what took place at Zorro Ranch. New Mexico lawmakers also established a “truth commission” to examine activities at the ranch.

title: Bibas family relative takes fight to ICC after mother, two young boys murdered by Hamas
excerpt:
Secretary of State Marco announced Friday that the Trump administration is sanctioning International Criminal Court, arguing it does not have the power to prosecute American citizens and leaders.

The...
body_text:
Secretary of State Marco announced Friday that the Trump administration is sanctioning International Criminal Court, arguing it does not have the power to prosecute American citizens and leaders.

The International Criminal Court has so far turned a blind eye to the family of Shiri Bibas and her young sons, who were brutally murdered by Iran-backed Hamas terrorists after being forcefully taken from their homes during the Oct. 7 attack on Israel.

The Bibas boys — Ariel, four, Kfir, nine months, and their mother, Shiri — became the faces of the Israeli hostages held by terrorists in Gaza. All three were brutally murdered and now the mother's uncle, Maurice Shnaider, wants justice.

Before the court's Chief Prosecutor, Karim Khan, was removed for misconduct, Khan oversaw the issuance of controversial arrest warrants in 2024 for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, former Israeli Defense Minister Yoav Gallant, and Hamas terror commander Mohammad Deif, alleging they had committed a variety of war crimes and crimes against humanity.

ICC PROSECUTOR WHOSE NETANYAHU WARRANT FUELED MAMDANI ARREST THREAT IS FIRED OVER SEXUAL MISCONDUCT

This combination of pictures created on February 20, 2025, shows posters bearing the portraits of Israeli hostages Shiri Bibas (C) and her two sons Ariel (L) and Kfir (R), held in the Gaza Strip since the October 7, 2023 attack by Hamas terrorists. The three were brutally murdered by terrorists.  (AFP Via Getty Images)

Khan’s ICC only sought to grant "selective justice" according to legal expert Elliot Malin, who told Fox News Digital that he filed two cases with the Office of the Prosecutor in 2025 requesting warrants against the leaders he accuses of truly practicing war crimes, including genocide, in Israel and Gaza.

Malin, president of Stratos Council, filed his first case with the ICC in Sept. 2025. It requested that the court investigate and issue warrants for two Iranian officials for "crimes against humanity, war crimes and genocide committed in Israel and Gaza on and after Oct. 7, 2023." Malin said that "It is very clear that the Islamic Republic is the principal to these proxies who are operating as agents of the regime… and we should hold the Islamic Republic directly accountable."

The request for investigation and warrants was filed on behalf of Shnaider, whose filings say he has lost five generations of his family "to acts committed with the intent to destroy Jews," including the Holocaust.

MIKE WALTZ FIGHTS BACK TEARS REVEALING WHAT HAMAS HOSTAGE REFUSED TO DO BEFORE RELEASE

Hanukkah candles were lit in The Hostages and Missing Square, on Dec. 9, 2023, in Tel Aviv, Israel at places set at a festival table for the Bibas family, an Israeli family including 11-month-old baby Kfir, his 4-year-old brother Ariel and their parents Shiri and Yarden. They were being held hostage by Hamas in the Gaza Strip.  (David Silverman/Getty Images)

On Oct. 7, Shnaider told Fox News Digital that he turned on the news to see his niece, Shiri Bibas, "being taken away" with her young children into captivity. Bibas and her children were later murdered as hostages. Shnaider says that he prays that Bibas "didn’t witness how they did what they did to a four-year-old and a nine-month-old."

Shnaider’s sister and brother-in-law were also murdered at Kibbutz Nir Oz on Oct. 7. He explained that they "were burned inside the house in a brutal way that you cannot imagine, you cannot explain, you cannot answer." By the time of his sister and brother-in-law’s burial, he explained that "there was hardly anything left" to put in the caskets.

Shnaider says that the grief from the horrific losses of his family on Oct. 7 "doesn’t compute in my body," leaving him "choking" with tears. Though Shnaider acknowledges that he will never understand the rationale behind hate, he said that "the most I can do is fight them in the way I can." He believes it is now up to the ICC "to put a stop to it." If the ICC fails to do so, Shnaider says the court "should be condemned" for its bias.

Flag with the logo of the International Criminal Court (ICC) on March 29, 2022, in Den Haag, Netherlands.  (Alex Gottschalk/DeFodi Images via Getty Images)

While the case against Iranian leaders was filed on behalf of just the Shnaider family, Malin advocates filing a case on behalf of each family who lost relatives during the attacks of Oct. 7.

In Dec. 2025, Malin filed a second case, requesting investigation and arrest warrants for over a dozen Hamas members for a myriad of "war crimes, and crimes against humanity committed against Palestinians in Gaza."

IDF PUSHES BACK ON CLAIM IT TARGETS JOURNALISTS IN GAZA, SAYS 170 WERE PART OF TERROR GROUPS, INCLUDING HAMAS

Iran internet blackout hardens into permanent digital repression system as regime treats citizens' access as an existential threat after protests. ( Stringer/Getty Images)

Malin says it is also important to hold Hamas leaders "directly accountable for the crime of genocide." He explained that Hamas attackers’ own words prove that there was no military goal during the Oct. 7 attacks, which largely killed civilians.

Malin said Hamas attackers told Oct. 7 victims that they would continue attacks into Israel "until there are no Jews left in Palestine," and during phone calls to family, an attacker celebrated specifically having killed Jews.

"They’re not talking about soldiers. They’re not talking about people who, in the course of combat or conflict, would be allowed to be targeted. They’re talking about civilians," Malin said.

Malin added that the individuals now trying to justify Hamas’ actions on Oct. 7 "are now justifying the actual crime of genocide."

Hamas terrorists emerge in a show of strength escorting Red Cross vehicles carrying 3 Israeli hostages to be released as part of the cease-fire deal.  (TPS-IL)

The case against Hamas leaders also notes their particular role in the deaths of innocent Gazans during the conflict that followed Oct. 7. "The goal there is to raise light of Hamas’ criminal conduct against Palestinians in Gaza," Malin said. He pointed out Hamas’ use of civilians as human shields and their torture of civilians, which he says "we have years of evidence for."

Malin said that the ICC has not responded to either of the cases he has filed. "If we don’t shed light on that at the ICC and the ICC refuses to do anything about it, then the only question for me… is what is the purpose that you serve?"

TRUMP ADMINISTRATION SANCTIONS SITTING PRESIDENT OF THE INTERNATIONAL CRIMINAL COURT FOR 'ABUSES OF POWER'

Malin argues that though the Iranian officials, one of whom was killed during the ongoing conflict with the U.S., were from a state that is not party to the statute, because the ICC has jurisdiction over Gaza, it is responsible for overseeing crimes committed there.

In response to questions about their response to Malin’s filings, the Office of the Prosecutor for the ICC told Fox News Digital, "On the Situation in the State of Palestine the Office of the Prosecutor (OTP) is actively investigating all crimes committed within the Court’s jurisdiction since 13 June 2014. The investigation is ongoing, and the Office continues to collect evidence in that context."

Iran’s Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei. (Fox News)

The statement added, "The OTP carries out its mandate independently and impartially, in accordance with its founding treaty, the Rome Statute," it continued. "The Office does not disclose details of the investigation to ensure the integrity of its processes and proceedings and to maintain the safety and security of all concerned, including victims, witnesses, the Office's staff and all those who cooperate with the Office and support its activities."

Malin said that Khan sought warrants against senior Israeli and Hamas leaders for the crime against humanity of extermination, which he described as "genocide without the intent [to commit genocide.]"

That warrant was denied for Israeli leaders, but ultimately approved for Deif, though he had been previously killed in an Israeli air strike.

Earlier this month, Secretary of State Marco Rubio imposed sweeping financial sanctions against the court. In a recorded video, Rubio charged, "Our message is clear: The United States and the American people are not subject to the jurisdiction of this fake ICC."

Beth Bailey writes on the United Nations, worldwide antisemitism, and regions in conflict for Fox News.

title: Russia to send first diesel tanker to the US amid Trump deal
excerpt:
Russia will send its first tanker of diesel fuel to the United States on Thursday, Russia’s Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak told reporters amid a deal with US President Donald Trump.

The vessel...
body_text:
Russia will send its first tanker of diesel fuel to the United States on Thursday, Russia’s Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak told reporters amid a deal with US President Donald Trump.

The vessel will have 40,000 tonnes of fuel, but Novak, who made his remarks on Wednesday, did not name which US port the fuel would be delivered to.

Russia lifted its ban on diesel exports on October 9, which Moscow originally put in place to tackle the country’s shortages as Ukrainian-led drone strikes hindered production capacity.

The shipment comes despite setbacks for Russia’s diesel output. Earlier this month, Ukraine’s Ministry of Defence said that drone strikes knocked out at least half of Russia’s oil refining capacity, forcing cuts at Russia’s top diesel-producing refineries.

“Additional shipments will follow, of course. There were agreements reached between the two leaders. We will meet the United States’ needs, to the extent of our capabilities,” the RIA Novosti news agency quoted Novak as saying.

That was echoed by US special envoy Steve Witkoff, who has been meeting Russian President Vladimir Putin for talks in St Petersburg.

“We are preparing deliveries of several vessels, the tankers, right now. They will go one after another. The financial component should be provided,” he said, adding that Russia would also be able to supply fertilisers in “large quantities” to the US market.

US President Donald Trump had previously said that Moscow would export 300,000 tonnes, or 2.25 million barrels, followed by 500,000 tonnes in November and 1 million tonnes “immediately thereafter”.

US consumers have continued to face high prices at the petrol station, particularly for diesel fuel, a pressing point as the country heads into midterm elections in less than two weeks. The average price for a gallon of diesel is $6.31 ($1.70 per litre), according to the American Automobile Association (AAA). While prices remain well over the $6 mark, they are on the downturn. The average price a month ago was $6.51.

title: Burnham backs mandatory suicide prevention training for social workers after parent-carer Matilda Davis’s death
excerpt:
Former art teacher, who cared for her disabled son, ‘received almost no support’, said her local MP Manuela Perteghella

Andy Burnham has backed mandatory suicide prevention training for social worker...
body_text:
Former art teacher, who cared for her disabled son, ‘received almost no support’, said her local MP Manuela Perteghella

Andy Burnham has backed mandatory suicide prevention training for social workers after the “devastating” death of Matilda Davis, a parent-carer who killed herself minutes after meeting professionals.

The Guardian revealed in August how the “absolutely inspirational” 36-year-old had taken her life after feeling “completely exhausted” and failed by England’s social care system.

Davis, a former art teacher, had told multiple professionals she was struggling to cope with the significant care for her seven-year-old son and “paralysed with anxiety” about her looming divorce from her estranged husband.

She died on 3 October last year, minutes after an emotional meeting with social workers who had not received suicide prevention training.

Burnham was asked about Davis’s case at prime minister’s questions on Wednesday and said he supported the extension of this training to all local authorities in England.

Manuela Perteghella, the Liberal Democrat MP for Stratford-upon-Avon, where Davis lived, said: “My constituent Matilda Davis was a wonderful and devoted mum and a full-time carer for her disabled seven-year-old child. Despite providing round the clock care, she received almost no support leaving her physically and emotionally exhausted.

“Last October, social workers visited Matilda and she took her own life 15 minutes after they left. She was 36.”

Perteghella highlighted University of Birmingham research showing that 41% of parent-carers have contemplated suicide, and asked Burnham to meet her and Matilda’s family to discuss “mandatory suicide prevention training for local authorities and other measures so that no more normal families suffer such a devastating loss”.

Burnham replied: “I will ensure that a minister meets the honourable lady to discuss that proposal because I find myself in agreement with it.”

The prime minister praised the Lib Dem leader, Ed Davey, for his work campaigning on behalf of unpaid carers, whose failure by the state has been brought into light by an award-winning Guardian investigation into the carer’s allowance scandal.

Burnham said these carers, who often gave up work and other commitments while saving the government billions of pounds to look after severely disabled loved ones, could often “sink under their responsibilities and find it very, very difficult”.

He added: “Sadly in the case of Matilda, [Perteghella’s] constituent, obviously a devastating situation. I will arrange that meeting and I thank [Perteghella] for raising it in the House [of Commons] today.”

At Davis’s inquest in March, social workers admitted they did not ask her whether she had thoughts of suicide despite knowing she was in significant distress, nor was she directed to crisis organisations.

As a result, the coroner, Deborah Sewell, issued a rare prevention of future deaths notice ordering Warwickshire council to make suicide prevention training mandatory for 600 members of staff, primarily social workers.

Davis’s brother, Joel Harley-Davis, said the family was “really reassured” by Burnham’s response and that his sister would have been “proud” to make a positive difference.

“We all believe that this training would have been enough to save Matilda’s life,” he said. “If those social workers had asked her [whether she was considering ending her life] Matilda was so honest she would have said yes.

“This needs to be made mandatory – you can’t leave it up to councils to decide whether to put it in place because it creates a postcode lottery. It doesn’t need to be this really expensive thing. All the literature and advice says that if in doubt about whether someone is suicidal, ask that direct difficult question.”

Guidance issued by the mental health charity Mind states that it is best practice not to “skirt around the topic of suicide” and instead ask direct questions such as: “Are you having suicidal thoughts?” when speaking to someone who might want to kill themselves.

Harley-Davis, 30, said his sister felt “failed and let down” by England’s social care system and was passionate about advocating on behalf of other parent-carers. He added: “Matilda was an incredibly stoic individual but that’s not to say she didn’t need someone to offer that respite.

“Matilda needed that professional support and a degree of empathy and I don’t think she got that, especially on the day she died.”

In the UK and Ireland, Samaritans can be contacted on freephone 116 123. In the US, you can call or text the National Suicide Prevention Lifeline on 988, chat on 988lifeline.org, or text HOME to 741741 to connect with a crisis counsellor. In Australia, the crisis support service Lifeline is 13 11 14. Other international helplines can be found at befrienders.org

title: Secret sex video rocks University of North Carolina at Charlotte fraternity, 1 arrested: Police
excerpt: Leaked text messages shake up the ongoing Cornell University fraternity sexual assault investigation as Fox News correspondent Bryan Llenas shares new details as this major development comes amid wide...
body_text:
Leaked text messages shake up the ongoing Cornell University fraternity sexual assault investigation as Fox News correspondent Bryan Llenas shares new details as this major development comes amid widespread student protests on the Ithaca, New York campus demanding accountability and justice.

Police said a 19-year-old was taken into custody after allegedly filming a University of North Carolina at Charlotte student during sex and sent the video to a fraternity group chat.

Officials accused Alexander Michael Evanoff of using his cellphone on Sept. 19 to secretly record a "sexually explicit video" of a woman while the two had sex, then sharing it without her consent. He was charged with one count of disclosing private images and two counts of felony secret peeping.

After Evanoff and the woman had sex, he allegedly sent a video of the sexually explicit recording to a Sigma Alpha Epsilon fraternity group chat, which had 32 members.

WOMEN'S COLLEGE SOCCER TEAM MAKES DISTURBING DISCOVERY IN LOCKER ROOM CEILING

Alexander Michael Evanoff, 19, was charged with one count of disclosing private images and two felony counts of secret peeping after allegedly recording a sexual encounter with a University of North Carolina at Charlotte student and sharing the video with a fraternity group chat, according to police. (MCSO)

During an interview with law enforcement, according to the affidavit, Evanoff allegedly admitted to intentionally recording the sexual act and sending it to the fraternity group chat.

He also acknowledged to detectives that he didn't request or obtain the victim's permission to create or distribute the video.

A view of the University of North Carolina at Charlotte campus, where a female student was allegedly secretly recorded during a sexual encounter before the video was shared in a fraternity group chat, according to police. (University of North Carolina at Charlotte/Facebook)

When the woman confronted Evanoff about the alleged recording, she asked if sending it to the fraternity group chat made him "appear cool," to which he "responded affirmatively" and apologized.

LISTEN TO THE NEW 'CRIME & JUSTICE WITH DONNA ROTUNNO' PODCAST

Evanoff was arrested Monday and released Tuesday on $10,000 bond, according to court and jail records.

The University of North Carolina at Charlotte campus. A 19-year-old man was arrested after allegedly recording a sexual encounter with a female student and sharing the video with members of a fraternity, police said. (University of North Carolina at Charlotte/Facebook)

A University of North Carolina at Charlotte spokesperson told WSOC that Evanoff isn't a student.

"The individual who has been charged is not currently enrolled at the University. The alleged conduct in this case, if true, is reprehensible. It is not what we expect or will tolerate from members of our campus community," the spokesperson said.

Fox News Digital reached out to the university, Evanoff's attorney and Sigma Alpha Epsilon for comment.

Adam Sabes is a reporter for Fox News Digital. Story tips can be sent to Adam.Sabes@fox.com and on Twitter @asabes10.

title: Likely voters prefer Democrats to Republicans in latest poll ahead of midterms as Trump’s popularity continues to sink – live
excerpt:
Likely voters prefer Democratic candidates over Republicans running for office by 11 percentage points, new poll shows; Trump campaigns in South Carolina

Send us your questions about immigration and ...
body_text:
Likely voters prefer Democratic candidates over Republicans running for office by 11 percentage points, new poll shows; Trump campaigns in South Carolina

Send us your questions about immigration and the midterms

New polling from the New York Times and Siena University shows that likely voters prefer Democratic candidates over Republicans running for office by 11 percentage points.

Meanwhile, Donald Trump’s approval rating dropped to a new low for this particular survey – 36%.

Notably, according to the Times’ polling, the perception of either party has shifted over the last two years. The number of people who consider Democrats as the party of the working class has grown by five points – from 48% to 53%. While it’s dropped by five points for Republicans – from 45% to 40%.

Donald Trump has welcomed the news that UK government has approved the controversial Jackdaw gasfield in the North Sea.

“Great news for the wealth and prosperity of the United Kingdom, and the wonderful region of Aberdeen. The UK has started drilling in the North Sea, one of the greatest and most prosperous areas of OIL in the World,” the US president wrote on Truth Social.

He added that the UK should go “FULL BLAST”, and the move to resume offshore extraction would “make the UK very wealthy again”.

As my colleagues reported earlier today, Andy Burnham, the UK prime minister, said the Jackdaw project will “protect hundreds of jobs and help keep millions of homes warm this winter”. This comes after fierce opposition from several Labor MPs and environmental groups throughout the country.

Trump has long pushed for Britain to expand oil and gas drilling in the North Sea, instead of relying on wind turbines. He frequently clashed with Burnham’s predecessor, Keir Starmer, who argued that energy sustainability relied on renewable sources and moving away from fossil fuel dependence.

The Israeli military has detained about 80 US, Israeli and British volunteers helping Palestinians harvest olives near Bethlehem, including the New York Democratic congressional nominee Brad Lander, several rabbis and Israel’s former deputy attorney general.

“I’ve been detained by the IDF, along with a group of rabbis and volunteers,” Lander posted from a bus taking him to a police station. “We were simply harvesting olives in a grove near Nahalin in the West Bank. The occupation is a crime under international law. Harvesting olives isn’t a crime under any law I know.”

Lander, who is Jewish and an outspoken critic of the Israeli government, describes himself as a liberal Zionist. He believes in the vision of Israel as a safe, Jewish home, but argues that it cannot be a true democracy while it denies Palestinians their human rights and freedom.

An ally of the New York City mayor, Zohran Mamdani, Lander’s critical approach to Israel was a key factor in his resounding primary victory against Dan Goldman, a prominent supporter of Israel.

He condemns Israel’s continued occupation of the West Bank and Gaza, supported the restriction of US military aid to Israel and believes that Israel’s military campaign in Gaza after the 7 October 2023 Hamas attacks amounts to genocide.

Settler militants have unleashed extreme violence on Palestinians attempting to harvest olives from their trees across the occupied West Bank, and anyone accompanying them.

A vicious assault on a US photojournalist and attacks on European diplomats and a French mayor over the weekend drew international condemnation and calls for the Israeli government to crack down on militants.

New polling from the New York Times and Siena University shows that likely voters prefer Democratic candidates over Republicans running for office by 11 percentage points.

Meanwhile, Donald Trump’s approval rating dropped to a new low for this particular survey – 36%.

Notably, according to the Times’ polling, the perception of either party has shifted over the last two years. The number of people who consider Democrats as the party of the working class has grown by five points – from 48% to 53%. While it’s dropped by five points for Republicans – from 45% to 40%.

Meanwhile, as my colleague Jakub Krupa reports, French president Emmanuel Macron blasted “unacceptable” and “stupid” comments on the protests and riots in France from foreign leaders, accusing them of “campaigning at our expense”.

This comes after Donald Trump has explicitly linked the protests to mass migration, without any evidence to support his claims.

Speaking to reports in Doha, Macron slammed the comments without mentioning any leaders by name. “We saw images generated by artificial intelligence depicting scenes that never actually occurred in France,” he said. “Some people even claimed that we had been overrun by hordes of migrants and Islamists – which is completely false.”

As we bring you more from Steve Witkoff’s meeting in St Petersburg with Russian officials, it’s worth noting that it takes place after a day of talks with Volodymyr Zelenskyy, Norwegian prime minister Jonas Gahr Støre and Alexander Stubb, Finland’s president, in Oslo.

Trump’s special envoy will relay the proposals discussed on Tuesday – including calls for a trilateral summit between Zelenskyy, Vladimir Putin and Donald Trump in order to hammer out a lasting deal.

Trump, however, appeared skeptical of any progress for peace when speaking to reporters in the Oval Office on Tuesday. “Russia is a big machine. They just keep grinding forward, and that’s what they’ve done,” the US president said. “We want Zelenskyy to make a deal. He can make a deal … In my opinion, it’s just really just going to get worse.”

Donald Trump will begin his day in Washington, and host a roundtable at the White House at 2.30pm ET.

He’ll then continue he midterm campaign blitz by heading to Clemson, South Carolina, where he’ll rally for Darline Graham – the Republican nominee for US Senate who is hoping to secure a full term for her late brother’s seat. Trump won the Palmetto state by almost 18 points in 2024.

A reminder that Darline was appointed by the South Carolina governor to carry out the remainder of Lindsey Graham’s time in office after his death in July. However, she now faces a competitive race against Annie Andrews, a paediatrician and the Democratic nominee, in a contest that has become rancorous in recent months.

My colleague Jakub Krupa over on our Europe live blog is staying abreast of the Witkoff and Putin meeting in St Petersburg.

Trump’s envoy is trying to advocate progress on peace talks after meeting yesterday with Zelenskyy in Norway.

We’re not expecting much though – both sides are still launching daily drone and missile strikes.
 
 
 The first comments from the Kremlin on the meeting so far say Russia will analyze the US proposals but “much depends on Ukraine” and “if Ukraine does not make necessary decisions, situation for them will be worse.”

As voters struggle with the rising cost of living and gas prices up 45% since the Iran War, Trump on the campaign trail this week has also repeated his $5,000 cash promise to every American adult if the Republicans win the House and Senate.

That’s a $1.2 trillion cash splash. Lawmakers in his own party have questioned where the money will come from while Democrats have called it blatant vote-buying scheme.

The White House says the payments will be funded by foreign trade deals, investment by foreign countries and government shares in private companies and oil and gas.

There’s also scepticism among voters as to whether they’ll actually see the cheque. Some have pointed out that previous government dividends promised by Trump – such as tariff revenues- never materialised. Meanwhile voters are facing rising inflation and a national average price of gas is more than $4 a gallon.

Roughly half of registered voters say Trump does not keep his promises, according to September AP-NORC poll.

The US president has just posted on Hubbard’s release, saying: “Welcome home Stephen, it’s great to have you back.”

The statement posted on his Truth Social says the prisoner release was the result of a direct request Trump made to Putin in a telephone call last week.

“Stephen is on his way back home and will soon be with his family,” the statement reads.

double quotation markThe United States, out of respect for President Trump, was not required to give anything in return - an unprecedented situation for Russia.

There was no “swap” necessary for this release. This major return should have taken place long ago through the Biden Administration, which got nowhere in its negotiations with the Kremlin. Stephen is on his way back home.

US envoy Steve Witkoff announced this morning that Russia authorities had freed Stephen Hubbard, the first American known to be convicted of fighting as a mercenary in Ukraine.
 
 
 Hubbard, who grew up in Michigan, had been living with his Ukrainian wife in the eastern Ukrainian city of Izyum. He was arrested when the Russians briefly took over the city at the start of the war in 2022.

In 2024, he was sentenced to nearly seven years in prison by a Russian court. But he has always denied being involved with any combat or military unit, saying that the Russians just took him from his house.

Trump yesterday had flagged Hubbard’s release saying he’d spoken with Putin in regards to the 74-year-old. “It’s time to have Mr Hubbard back,” he said.

Good morning and welcome to our coverage of US politics. With 14 days until the mid-terms, we’re heading into the final straight.

President Donald Trump attended a rally last night in North Carolina, where Democrat Roy Cooper is leading Trump’s pick Michael Whatley by a considerable margin.

Undaunted though, Trump said the pollsters “never poll us right” and he predicted “some amazing results”. He repeated his $5,000 cash “goodie” to voters if Republicans retain control of both the Congress and Senate. He’s got another rally in South Carolina later today.
 
 
 Overnight he’s also posted on data centers – saying that companies building the energy-intensive sites should pay a “dividend” to the communities where they’re located, including several proposed warehouses in Michigan, where the president will head to on the weekend.

Trump has been pushing rapid AI expansion but in a nod to how unpopular these water and electricity-guzzling centres are with locals who have to live near them, he’s been hinting at community benefits.

Trump said the “new and giant” centers “are mandated by me to make their own electricity , and ‌give or sell any excess back to the local community, or grid”.

Meanwhile US envoy Steve Witkoff is in St Petersburg for a meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin on Ukraine; some earlier wrangling by Trump has succeeded in the release of US schoolteacher Stephen Hubbard, who was captured by the Russians and accused of having fought for Ukraine.

Stay with us for all the day’s developments.

title: Macron accuses Trump and other foreign leaders of making ‘stupid comments’ about France unrest
excerpt:
Leaders criticised for spreading misleading information as France prepares for further protests this weekend

Emmanuel Macron has accused Donald Trump and other foreign leaders of making “stupid comme...
body_text:
Leaders criticised for spreading misleading information as France prepares for further protests this weekend

Emmanuel Macron has accused Donald Trump and other foreign leaders of making “stupid comments” about France’s street unrest for political gain, as the country prepared for more protests this weekend.

Speaking during a visit to Qatar, the French president did not name names but said “manipulation of information” after Saturday’s riots had led to “comments that are as unacceptable as they are stupid, from many people, including foreign leaders”.

Asked if he was referring to Donald Trump, Macron replied: “Among others.” The US president has blamed France’s violence on “migrants, jihadists and communists” as he campaigns for his Republican party before midterm elections.

Macron told reporters in Doha that some leaders “in the middle of election campaigns, whether here in the region or on the other side of the Atlantic” were “naively spreading narratives that certain circles are clearly trying to promote”.

They were “using our country for their own political campaigns”, the French president said. “And we don’t need that. We already have difficulties to deal with.”

He said AI-generated images were circulating “depicting scenes that never actually happened in France. We’ve had people claiming that we were invaded by hordes of migrants and Islamists, which is completely false.”

The Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, who faces elections next weekend, has also said that France had been hit by an “invasion of extremist Islam”. Analysts have dismissed claims that migrants were the main factor in France’s protests.

Macron and his government are struggling to get on top of a crisis that has erupted six months before presidential elections to choose his successor. The government has admitted it “lost control” over widespread rioting on Saturday.

Largely peaceful demonstrations over the cost of living rapidly descended into rampant violence and extensive looting, especially in Paris, Marseille, Lyon and Limoges, where the town hall was set on fire and partially destroyed.

The unrest has prompted several countries to issue travel warnings for France and rattled already nervous financial markets, with the yield on the French government’s benchmark 10-year bonds passing 5% on Wednesday, its highest since 2002.

Macron pledged to prevent any repeat of last weekend’s convulsions, as the gilets jaunes (yellow vest) grassroots protest movement formally filed plans for a march through the centre of Paris ⁠on Saturday that is likely to be the ⁠government’s next big test.

Student groups have also called for protests on the same day to push demands for greater investment in education. The gilets jaunes activists aim to revive their nationwide 2018 campaign against rising living costs and declining public services.

“Those who want to cause disorder in city centres next Saturday will be prevented from doing so,” Macron told reporters in the Gulf, where he was seeking energy deals to help offset rising fuel costs. “There must be no wavering at the top of the state.”

Government ministers have promised a “massive” and vastly reinforced security operation after acknowledging shortcomings in their initial response last weekend, with some troops expected to be deployed alongside police reinforcements.

Partial night-time curfews imposed on Monday and Tuesday in areas prone to violent protests and looting in cities around France, including Paris, Marseille and Lille, have helped ensure relative calm and were expected to be renewed on Wednesday.

France’s main trade unions have separately called a nationwide mobilisation for 5 November. Sophie Binet, the head of the CGT union, said: “There is huge and legitimate anger, and the answer to that situation is not repression. It is a political response.”

Macron insisted France “doesn’t need a state of emergency”, saying it “has the means” to control any further unrest. Union representatives met the prime minister, Sébastien Lecornu, on Wednesday but no concrete announcements followed.

Sometimes violent protests in European countries including Italy and Belgium have added to concerns that anger over living standards risks spreading across the continent where with many nations, including France, face budget problems.

Italy’s government has ordered 500 troops to Milan to stem street violence there.

title: Musk pledges $10bn in SpaceX shares for US children: Who really gains?
excerpt:
Elon Musk has pledged to give one SpaceX share to every child in the United States next year – a gift that could be worth more than $10bn.

“This will be the first of many,” the world’s richest man wr...
body_text:
Elon Musk has pledged to give one SpaceX share to every child in the United States next year – a gift that could be worth more than $10bn.

“This will be the first of many,” the world’s richest man wrote on X on Monday.

About 73 million children under 18 live in the US, according to US Census Bureau data.

At Friday’s closing price of $146.03, the pledge would be worth about $10.7bn.

President Donald Trump thanked Musk on his Truth Social platform, and claimed the shares would be given to children “through TRUMP ACCOUNTS”, the tax-friendly investment accounts for children created under his signature tax and spending law last year.

The pledge comes two weeks before the November 3 midterm elections.

Musk is the biggest known donor in the run-up to those elections, having given more than $276m to Republican groups since July.

Musk has not said which children will qualify, when the shares will be handed over, or how.

So how might the giveaway work, and who stands to gain?

SpaceX, the world’s seventh-largest company, began trading on the Nasdaq in June at an initial public offering price of $135 per share.
That price has been volatile. SpaceX shares have fallen 35.3 percent since peaking days after the listing.

The shares are currently trading at around $146 a share. Every $1 move in the share price will change the gift’s value by about $73m.

Musk owns 4.8 billion shares in SpaceX outright, according to a filing with the US Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) in August.

Including unvested awards and stock options, his stake rises to about 6.4 billion shares, or 48.4 percent of the company.

Giving away 73 million shares would reduce his outright holding by about 1.5 percent, barely affecting his control of the company. That’s because his voting power, which is currently about 82 percent because SpaceX has two classes of shares, would fall by only 0.1 percentage points, according to a Bloomberg Opinion calculation.

It would be the largest single gift linked to Trump accounts so far.

Trump said the shares would be held in Trump accounts, and Musk thanked Brad Gerstner, the tech investor behind the accounts, for “helping enable this”.

Nearly 70 million Trump accounts have been opened, one for every child under 18 with a Social Security number, according to the White House. Investments held in Trump accounts can roll up with tax deferred until they are withdrawn when a child turns 18. Alternatively, they can be rolled into a tax-friendly IRA – a retirement account for adults – and continue with the tax-friendly status.

Under Treasury rules published on September 30, donors can now gift individual company stock to children via the accounts. Families and friends making regular contributions to a child’s Trump account are limited to investing low-risk index funds.

Families cannot refuse the shares on behalf of their children and generally cannot sell them for five years, or until the end of the year the child turns 17 if that comes sooner.

Musk cannot sell or trade most of his SpaceX shares until June 2027, the Wall Street Journal reported.

The accounts carry the president’s name, and Trump has tied himself closely to the gift.

He thanked Musk on Truth Social, saying the pledge was “exactly what was envisioned when we created TRUMP ACCOUNTS”.

The White House has presented the accounts as a signature achievement of Trump’s tax law, noting that “every single Democrat voted against” the legislation.

The pledge also marks a public reconciliation. Musk and Trump fell out in 2025 over Trump’s tax-and-spending bill, a rift Trump later called a “little dispute”.

Children will be gaining a share for free, but the gift could also save Musk money.

Donors who give appreciated stock to charity avoid capital gains tax and can usually claim a deduction, the US broadcaster CNBC reported.

As SpaceX’s founder, Musk paid very little for his shares, and selling $10.7bn of them could mean a tax bill of up to about $2.5bn.

It is “a popular practice for particularly high-income taxpayers that would otherwise be paying a high rate”, Will McBride, chief economist at the Tax Foundation, told the broadcaster in May.

Ann Lipton, a law professor at the University of Colorado Boulder, told Inc. magazine that millions of shareholders unable to sell would also have an interest in SpaceX’s success and in “minimising its regulatory burdens”.

For Mitchell Downey, an economist at Stockholm University’s Institute for International Economic Studies who studies political influence in the US, the more striking part of the pledge is what he called “the horseshoe aspect of this” – the idea that right-wing and left-wing policies can curve around and meet.

For decades, progressives have backed the concept of Child Development Accounts, investment accounts for every newborn designed to reduce inequality in wealth, he said. The idea was associated with groups such as the Democracy Collaborative but struggled to gain federal support. Now the idea may become more mainstream as a result of Musk’s gift and Trump accounts.

“It always felt like it might be out of reach,” Downey said. “But I don’t see how Musk’s proposal would be possible without building some infrastructure like this.”

The pledge comes just two weeks before the November 3 midterm elections, which will decide control of the two houses of Congress. All seats in the House of Representatives and one-third of the Senate are up for re-election.

Trump’s approval rating has meanwhile fallen to a record low of 33 percent, according to a Washington Post-ABC News-Ipsos poll, with many political observers expecting to see the Republicans lose seats to the Democratic Party as a result.

Musk, who campaigned with Trump in 2024 and spearheaded the president’s Department of Government Efficiency initiative to reduce the size of the federal workforce, has contributed heavily to Republican candidates in advance of the midterm elections.

Downey said he does not believe the pledge raises legal concerns.

“Individuals are allowed to spend their money in support of a politician,” he told Al Jazeera. “The law only gets violated when either it isn’t publicly reported, or it is part of an explicit and documented quid-pro-quo.”

But he said it does raise ethical concerns, though not ones unique to Musk’s approach.

Those concerns relate to “the outsized role that external donors play in US elections”, Downey said. In his view, they apply much like when someone spends heavily on television advertisements for a candidate.

Downey said the precedent was “hard to assess”.

Because Musk is the richest person in modern history, he said, it is perhaps unsurprising that he is “doing something that involves more money than other very rich people have done”.

He pointed to the Gates Foundation’s spending over the past three decades as “a different type of ‘gift to the public’”. The difference, he said, is that the Gates Foundation focuses funding on health crises in countries in Africa and South Asia – not on voters in the US.

Last year, Gates pledged to “give away virtually all my wealth through the Gates Foundation over the next 20 years to the cause of saving and improving lives around the world”.

title: Europe’s far right seizes on protest violence to push authoritarian anti-immigration agenda
excerpt:
Nationalist leaders are framing unrest as consequence of failed liberal governance and open borders

Europe’s far-right leaders have jumped on the violence that rocked numerous cities last weekend, fr...
body_text:
Nationalist leaders are framing unrest as consequence of failed liberal governance and open borders

Europe’s far-right leaders have jumped on the violence that rocked numerous cities last weekend, framing it as the inevitable consequence of failed liberal governance and open-border policies and insisting only they can restore law and order.

Months away from key elections in Spain, France and Italy, authoritarian nationalists are eager to weaponise the wave of street unrest, originating in peaceful protests over the cost of living and deteriorating public services but hijacked by violent rioters.

Those in opposition have not held back. In France, where cities such as Paris, Marseille and Lyon faced widespread rioting and looting, the far-right National Rally (RN) has denounced centrist incompetence and promised a crackdown.

The party’s president, Jordan Bardella, said the government was “impotent”. The RN leader, Marine Le Pen, said on Wednesday the state was “collapsing” and had “lost control of everything” amid “migratory, budgetary and security chaos”.

Ahead in presidential polls and seeking voters beyond her base, Le Pen has resisted explicitly racialising the unrest, but has framed it more broadly as a result of state and policy failures leading to “anarchic immigration” and “a total loss of authority”.

In Germany – where there were no major protests – the far-right Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) has stoked fears rioting could spill over the border. Its co-leader Alice Weidel said France’s “violent excesses” were a “warning for Germany”.

Weidel also linked the unrest to immigration, posting: “The dangerous mix of mass migration and leftwing extremism threatens to lead to civil war-like conditions here too … There will only be a turnaround on migration with the AfD!”

In Portugal, populists have used peaceful housing and cost of living protests to warn against “importing” instability. André Ventura of the far-right Chega party said the nation must “refrain from importing into Portugal climates of instability and protest”.

In Spain, where the housing crisis has led to huge protests and a Madrid encampment, and prompted the socialist prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, to call a snap election next month, the far-right Vox party has sought to demonise the protesters. “They’re not defending the right to housing, or asking for work, they’re serving Pedro Sánchez,” the party’s leader, Santiago Abascal, said. “They’re Sánchez’s militias.”

Vox has also attempted to link the housing issue to migration. In a message posted on social media last month, the party falsely suggested that the 87-year-old woman whose eviction sparked the mammoth protests would have had a home had she been an immigrant from north Africa.

In Belgium, where cost of living protests also escalated into street clashes in Brussels and Liège, the far-right Flemish nationalists of Vlaams Belang framed the rioting as a failure of integration and open borders, characterising it as “imported violence”.

Italy’s prime minister, Giorgia Meloni, has adopted another strategy – as head of a far-right government she has headed for four years, she cannot simply blame failures of the state. Instead, she has expanded her law-and-order agenda, and framed rioters as extremists.

“Demonstrating is a right, but setting our cities ablaze is not,” Meloni said after rioting in Milan and Bologna. “Hooligans have exploited the protests to sow chaos, attack those responsible for ensuring security, and hold entire cities hostage.”

Meloni has previously enacted sweeping security measures aimed at hindering public dissent, including jail terms for blocking roads, tough sentences for resisting police officers, and pre-detention for demonstrators thought likely to cause trouble.

This week she passed emergency decrees creating an offence of violent participation in ⁠a demonstration, imposing tougher penalties on ⁠rioters and organisers of violent groups, and penalising parents whose children take part in vandalism and looting.

But she too has highlighted immigration as a factor, noting that “nearly half of those stopped or arrested” after the Milan riots were “of immigrant background, including individuals born abroad and second-generation children of immigrant families”.

Beyond Europe’s orthodox far-right parties, anti-immigration polemicists have gone further, interpreting the violence not as state and policy failures but as evidence of a looming civilisational war fuelled by multiculturalism and non-EU immigration.

Éric Zemmour, the founder of France’s Reconquête! (Reconquest) party, demanded an immigration halt and the deportation of “foreign delinquents”, declaring: “These are not riots, but the warning shots in an ethnic war. Either we establish absolute order or we yield.”

The far-right narrative has been reinforced by similar comments from the US, where both the president and vice-president have sought to turn the unrest in France in particular into a cautionary tale for voters before midterm elections.

Donald Trump described France as a once-great nation that had been “conquered, looted, and burned to the ground by migrants, jihadists, and communists”, adding on social media that immigration “has shattered that once great country”.

JD Vance echoed the same view, saying: “Western liberals imported the third world into France and other countries in the name of diversity and compassion.” In doing so, they “ignored fundamental questions about assimilation and compatibility”, he said.

Deborah Cole in Berlin, Angela Giuffrida in Rome and Sam Jones in Madrid contributed reporting
